organizations would participate in wholesome outdoor sports on a big playing field.
They would play to their heart's content. Soon, to have a field day meant to indulge
yourself in any way you wanted. Even today, some schools have a “field day.”

name: fifth wheel
meanings: [{"name":"an unwelcome or extra person","examples":["He felt more and more like a fifth wheel at the office.","If he comes with us, he'll just be a fifth wheel.","I don't like living with my son and daughter-in-law. I feel like a fifth wheel.","Bill always begs to come on camping trips with us, but really, he's a fifth wheel."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This is a proverb that was first used in France in the 16th century. A unicycle
has one wheel; a bicycle has two wheels; a tricycle has three wheels; and wagons and
cars have four wheels. No vehicle needs five wheels. The fifth wheel is a surplus thing,
good for nothing. In the same way, if two persons are going out on a trip, an
extra person who tags along could be called a “fifth wheel.”

name: fight tooth and nail
meanings: [{"name":"to fight fiercely, furiously, and ferociously; to try very hard to get something you want","examples":["The counselor had to separate two campers who were fighting tooth and nail.","We fought tooth and nail to get the route of the new road changed.","They fought against the robber tooth and nail.","The dogs were fighting each other hammer and tongs."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This vivid expression goes far back to a Latin proverb that became a French
saying centuries later and finally came into English in 1562. When wild animals fight,
they bite and claw each other. Sometimes people fight fiercely, as if they were animals
fighting a deadly battle “tooth and nail.”

name: fill the bill or fit the bill
meanings: [{"name":"to be just the perfect thing that is needed; to be very competent, effective; be suitable","examples":["The decorator said that a tall potted palm in this corner would fill the bill.","That box will fill the bill nicely.","Jane: I need some string. Tom: Here's some twine. Will it fill the bill?","I need cloth to make a shirt. This muslin ought to fit the bill."],"media":[]}]
origin:
One of the many meanings of “bill” is a list of acts being presented in a
theater. In the 1800s an audience expected to enjoy a full bill of singers, dancers,
jugglers, and comedians. To be sure that the audience was satisfied with the evening's
lineup, the theater manager sometimes added acts to “fill the bill.” Today the meaning
has broadened to anything or anyone that meets a need or is just right for a purpose.

name: finger in every pie
meanings: [{"name":"to have a part in something; to be involved in many matters, businesses, or activities","examples":["He is a sharp talent agent who has a finger in nearly every pie in show business.","Ms. Katie has her finger in every pie when it comes to music, dance, and theater."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The person who made up this saying might have been thinking of people who
can't decide what pie they want — blueberry, pecan, peach — so they stick a finger in
every pie to get a taste of each. Think of each pie as a different business or project,
and when you put your finger into a “pie,” you have a part interest or responsibility
in that activity. People often participate in many activities to make extra profit for
themselves.

name: fish or cut bait
meanings: [{"name":"do one thing or another, but stop delaying; make a choice; act now or give someone else a turn","examples":["He's been promising voters that he'll support women empowerment, now it's time to fish or cut bait.","Are you using that microscope or not? Fish or cut bait.","Decide whether you're going to watch or help. Fish or cut bait."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This idiom, popular since the 1800s, is a metaphor that refers to a person who
holds a fishing rod but doesn't fish. Someone else could use that rod and catch some
fish. The procrastinator might be asked to either drop the line into the water and fish,
or cut the bait from the line and let another angler have a chance.

name: fish out of water
meanings: [{"name":"a person who is out of his or her usual place; someone who doesn't fit in or is helpless in a situation; someone who is uncomfortable in a specific situation","examples":["I want to help the new girl from Russia. She must feel like a fish out of water.","I felt like a fish out of water at my new school.","I didn't have any friends that were like me. I just always felt like a fish out of water.","The country boy felt like a fish out of water in the big city."],"media":[]}]
origin:
For thousands of years people have known that a fish belongs in water. That's
its natural habitat. So a person who is in an unfamiliar or uncomfortable setting will
feel like a fish out of water.

name: fit as a fiddle
meanings: [{"name":"in good health; in fine shape","examples":["My grandmother is nearly ninety, but she's still fit as a fiddle.","I feel (as) fit as a fiddle this morning.","You may feel sick now, but after a few days of rest and plenty of liquids, you'll be fit as a fiddle.","Grandson: Are you sure you'll be able to climb all these stairs? Grandmother: Of course! I feel as fit as a fiddle today."],"media":[]}]
origin:
his expression dates from at least the early 1600s. “Fit” has always meant
“in good health.” But why was it joined with “fiddle” in this simile? Probably because
“fit” and “fiddle” are a good example of alliteration, and a fiddle that's fit (well tuned
and in good shape) can play terrific music.

name: fit like a glove
meanings: [{"name":"to fit a person or thing perfectly; to be exactly right","examples":["I love these pants because they fit like a glove and they're so comfortable.","These new curtains match your bedspread perfectly. They fit your bedroom like a glove."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression from the 18th century first referred only to gloves. If a glove
fit, it wasn't so loose that it fell off, and it wasn't so tight that it was hard to pull on. It
fit perfectly and kept your hands warm. Today, not just a glove can “fit like a glove.”
A shirt that goes well with your outfit or a chair that complements your living room
can fit like a glove. One person can be so right for another person that you can say,
“She fits him like a glove.” An expression with a similar meaning is “suits you to a T.”
The T probably refers to the T-square a draftsperson uses to measure things precisely.
However you say it, if something “fits you like a glove” or “suits you to a T,” it's a
perfect match.

name: fix your wagon
meanings: [{"name":"to punish someone; to get even with someone; to plot against someone.","examples":["Nicole borrowed my homework sheet and then left it at home. I'll fix her wagon.","If you ever do that again, I'll fix your wagon!","Tommy! You clean up your room this instant, or I'll fix your wagon!","He reported me to the boss, but I fixed his wagon. I knocked his lunch on the floor."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Some people think this idiom may have come from the days of the great
westward migration in America in the 1800s, when the covered wagon was the main
means of transportation. One meaning of the word “fix” is to take revenge upon or get
even with. It might also mean tying up and holding secure, as in tying up a wagon so
it cannot roll away. Today, “fix someone's wagon” means to plot against that person
to do something bad to him or her.

name: flash in the pan
meanings: [{"name":"a temporary success which yields no long-term results; a person who fails to live up to earlier potential","examples":["People thought she was going to be a great concert violinist, but Dana was just a flash in the pan.","Sadly, their success was just a flash in the pan.","The band was just a flash in the pan with one hit in 2003."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1600s there was a popular gun called a flintlock musket. When the
trigger was pulled, sparks were supposed to make the gunpowder in a small pan on
the gun go off and explode the main charge. But sometimes there was only a flash in
the pan and no big explosion. Today a “flash in the pan” is any person who showed
great early promise (“sparks”) but who never lived up to his or her full potential
(“explosion”).

name: flotsam and jetsam
meanings: [{"name":"anything or anyone that is not wanted or not considered to be important or useful","examples":["I'm clearing out my room of all the flotsam and jetsam.","a notebook filled with flotsam and jetsam.","The homeless sleep in doorways and stations - we step over their bodies like so much human flotsam."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The words “flotsam” and “jetsam” date from the early 1500s. Flotsam means
all the wreckage and cargo floating in the ocean after a shipwreck. Jetsam is cargo
and equipment floating in the water that was thrown overboard to lighten a ship in
danger of sinking. By the 19th century these words meant any kind of junk or debris
on land or sea, thrown out or not. The near-rhyming sound of the words helped make
this idiom popular.

name: fly-by-night
meanings: [{"name":"selling for quick profit, then disappearing; a swindler or unreliable person","examples":["The store where I bought that defective computer was a fly-by-night operation.","The carpenter we hired was a fly-by-night worker who did a very bad job.","You shouldn't deal with a fly-by-night merchant."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Fly-by-night was an ancient term that described a woman who was thought
to be like a witch. Witches were supposed to fly at night on brooms, and the term came
to mean anyone who flies hurriedly from an activity. In the late 1800s this expression
was made up to describe a person or business that sneaked away in the middle of the
night to avoid paying bills or making good on promises to customers.

name: fly by the seat of your pants
meanings: [{"name":"to do something by instinct and feel without any earlier experience or instruction","examples":["I had to entertain Dad's friends from Italy. I didn't know their language, so I just flew by the seat of my pants.","I had no idea how to do it – I was just flying by the seat of my pants."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This phrase was popular among members of the U.S. Army Air Corps in
the 1930s. Often, there were few or no instruments on the planes and sometimes the
instruments didn't work. So a pilot had to sit tight (on the seat of his pants) and
fly an airplane by instinct. Today if you're doing any kind of project and there are
no instructions, you may have to “fly by the seat of your pants.” You proceed by
intuition, natural talent, or common sense.

name: fly in the ointment
meanings: [{"name":"a single thing or person that is spoiling a situation that could have been very positive or enjoyable","examples":["The food, the music, and the decorations were perfect, but her camera broke. That was the fly in the ointment.","I'm looking forward to Sunday, the only fly in the ointment being the fact that I'll have to sit next to my mother-in-law."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Thousands of years
ago, people realized that a tiny nuisance can sometimes ruin something pleasant.
Ointment is a creamy substance that soothes, softens, or heals the skin. Finding a fly
in the ointment would certainly ruin it.

name: fly off the handle
meanings: [{"name":"to lose your temper; to become furiously angry","examples":["When Dr. Anthony discovered that someone had sneaked a look at the report cards, he really flew off the handle.","He tends to fly off the handle when people disagree with him.","Every time anyone mentions taxes, Mrs. Brown flies off the handle.","If she keeps flying off the handle like that, she'll have a heart attack."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Many Americans in the early 1800s used handmade tools with axheads to
chop down trees and build houses. The tools were often crudely made and the axhead
would fly off the handle during furious chopping. The flying axhead is much like an
angry person out of control.

name: fly the coop
meanings: [{"name":"to escape; to leave suddenly and secretly; to get out or get away","examples":["I tucked my little brother into bed, but the next time I looked, he had flown the coop.","In the morning the suspect had flown the coop.","These chickens want to fly the coop — literally!","I couldn't stand the party, so I flew the coop."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A coop is an enclosure or cage for poultry or small animals. If a chicken “flew
the coop,” it escaped its pen. In the late 1800s and early 1900s “coop” was also a slang
word for jail, so this expression often referred to what an escaped prisoner did. Today
it is used in connection with any person or animal that secretly escapes or runs away.

name: foam at the mouth
meanings: [{"name":"to be uncontrollably furious, like a mad dog","examples":["Dad was foaming at the mouth when he found out that Gerry had slipped out of the house.","She was almost foaming at the mouth when she heard about the cost of the car repairs.","Walter was foaming at the mouth with rage."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A dog with rabies or distemper foams at the mouth. A bubbly saliva forms
around the lips, and the dog behaves in a crazy manner. As long ago as the 1400s
people began describing furious people as “foaming at the mouth,” as if they were
mad dogs.

name: follow your nose
meanings: [{"name":"to go straight ahead in the same direction","examples":["When he asked me the way to the cafeteria, I told him to follow his nose.","Just follow your nose until you get there; you can't miss it.","Turn left, then just follow your nose and you'll see the shop on your left."],"media":[]},{"name":"to proceed without plan or reflection, obey one's instincts","examples":["Take a chance and follow your nose - you may be right!","You don't need my advice—just follow your nose."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying was being used as early as the 15th century, maybe even earlier.
Your nose is in the middle of your face, pointing straight ahead of you. So, if you
“follow your nose,” you proceed directly ahead. This saying usually has nothing to do
with the nose's ability to smell things. However, someone directing you to the school
cafeteria, a perfume factory, or a skunk farm might also tell you to “follow your nose,”
even if you have to take three lefts and a right.

name: food for thought
meanings: [{"name":"an interesting idea worth thinking about carefully","examples":["The unexpected test results have given us food for thought.","The sign said, “If all else fails, read the instructions.” That was food for thought.","Thank you for your suggestion – it gave us a lot of food for thought."],"media":[]}]
origin:
People have used this metaphorical saying since the early 1800s. In it, we
think of the mind as a mouth that “chews” not food, but ideas. So ideas are the “food
for thought.” We sometimes use a related idiom, “to chew over an idea,” which means
to think about it seriously.

name: forty winks
meanings: [{"name":"a short nap","examples":["I just need forty winks and I'll be able to work all night.","I could use forty winks before I have to get to work."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Since the 1300s, “wink” has referred to sleep, but probably just a short period
of sleep because when you wink you close and open your eyelids quickly. In the works of William Shakespeare, the number forty didn't always mean the number
after thirty-nine. It meant an indefinite number or “few.” The phrase “forty winks”
was first used in 1872 in an issue of the famous British humor magazine Punch.

name: from the four corners of the earth
meanings: [{"name":"from all over the planet; from everywhere; from all over","examples":["When John F. Kennedy died, people came to his funeral from the four corners of the earth.","From the four corners of the Earth, people come to this city to work and help create a truly modern metropolis.","People came from the four corners of the earth to see the sight."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Some ancient
peoples thought that the planet Earth was flat and had corners. So when they referred
to the “four comers of the earth,” they meant some place near the edge of a rectangular
map, the farthest ends of the world.

name: from soup to nuts
meanings: [{"name":"the whole thing from beginning to end; covering every detail or part of something; including everything:","examples":["We've got acts in this talent show from soup to nuts: jugglers, acrobats, singers, magicians, tap dancers, you name it!","The book provides a soup to nuts look at the current political scene.","The entire procedure from soup to nuts is changing.","The whole building, soup to nuts, cost less to build than that parking lot."],"media":[]}]
origin:
For centuries any foods served at the beginning or end of a meal stood for the
entire thing: the start and finish and everything in between. This expression was “from
eggs to apples” and “from pottage to cheese.” In the United States, in the middle of the
20th century, the expression developed into “from soup to nuts.” At many meals, soup
is often the first course and a dessert with nuts is sometimes the last. The expression
does not have to refer only to meals, however. It could be the selection of goods for
sale or classes offered.

name: from the word go
meanings: [{"name":"from the very beginning","examples":["The bridge-building project had problems with funding right from the word go.","We were in trouble (right) from the word go.","She was failing the class from the word go.","I knew about the problem from the word go."],"media":[]}]
origin:
At the start of many races, someone shouts, “Ready, set, GO!” So, since the
mid-1800s in the United States, “from the word go” has meant from the outset of
something.

name: full of beans
meanings: [{"name":"lively, happy and energetic, high-spirited","examples":["After final exams, some of us were exhausted and others were full of beans.","We were young and full of beans.","I've never known anyone be so full of beans before breakfast."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Just as the expression “feel your oats” means to be lively and frisky, being “full
of beans” is a similar food-related idiom. Eating lots of beans has a gastrointestinal
effect on some people that may make them a little more lively. The origin may also
be from the days when the racehorses were fed beans. This lively expression has been
bouncing around since the 1800s.

name: full of hot air
meanings: [{"name":"being foolish and talking nonsense; pompous; vain; full of nonsense; talking nonsense.","examples":["I don't believe a word he says. He's full of hot air.","Oh, shut up, Mary. You're full of hot air.","Don't pay any attention to Bill. He's full of beans."],"media":[]}]
origin:
When you talk, warm air comes out of your mouth. Large balloons that carry
people in baskets are kept afloat by hot air. This idiom from the mid-1800s puts those
two ideas together. If you want to describe a pompous person who is all puffed up
(like a balloon), you could say he or she is “full of hot air” (that's coming out of his
or her mouth).

name: full steam ahead
meanings: [{"name":"proceed with all possible speed and power","examples":["The captain of the team shouted, “Full steam ahead!” to get his tired players out onto the field.","The work started slowly, but now it's full steam ahead.","The campaign is going full speed ahead.","Full steam ahead! Let's see how fast this will go!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the early days of trains, about 150 years ago, locomotives were powered
by steam engines. Ocean liners crossed the seas propelled by steam. Thousands of
steamboats sailed up and down America's major rivers. Mark Twain was a pilot on
a steamboat on the Mississippi. There was even a car that ran on steam. When the
captain of a ship or the engineer of a train shouted, “Full steam ahead!” it meant “Put
the steam boiler up to maximum pressure so we can go faster.” (For that reason, the
captain could also shout, “Full speed ahead!”) This expression became very popular
after Rear Admiral David G. Farragut used it at the Battle of Mobile Bay during the Civil
War in August 1864 to get his fleet moving forward quickly. Today you can use this
expression while working on any project. The opposite of “full steam ahead” is to “run
out of steam” when you're exhausted and can't go another step.

name: get a handle on something
meanings: [{"name":"to understand and be able to deal with something","examples":["Rachel had a lot of trouble with geometry, but I think she's getting a handle on it.","I can't quite get a handle on the way this machine works.","It seemed like she had a good handle on the situation.","By coming in early, staying late, and working weekends she started to get a handle on the problem."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This bit of American slang became popular in the mid-1900s. Did you ever try
to lift up a heavy, bulky object that had no handles? How do you get a secure grip on
it? The answer is to attach a handle to it. Today this expression refers to any difficulty
you need to deal with or get control of. When you finally “get a handle on it,” you
start to solve the problem.

name: get a kick out of something
meanings: [{"name":"to enjoy doing something; to get a thrill out of something","examples":["My grandmother really gets a kick out of playing these video games with me.","We just got a big kick out of seeing our names in the paper."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A famous songwriter, Cole Porter, made this 20th-century American saying
popular in his 1934 song, “I Get a Kick Out of You.” The title means “I really enjoy
being with you.” In this expression “kick” has to do with a thrill, not striking
something with your foot. There are two variations on this idiom: “get a bang out of
something” and “get a charge out of something.” All three words — “kick,” “bang,”
“charge” — suggest something that will really shake you up.

name: get away with murder
meanings: [{"name":"to do something bad, wrong, or illegal and not get caught or punished","examples":["The company had been getting away with murder for years before the scandal broke.","You will spoil your son if you let him get away with murder. You should punish him for his back-talk.","That guy always gets away with murder—just because he's cute."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American expression from the late 2oth century is really an exaggeration.
It can refer to any offense, major or minor, that you're not punished for, such as
chewing gum in class, cheating on a test, or stealing. But, figuratively speaking, if
you can get away without being punished for murder, you can probably get away with
less serious crimes.

name: get down to brass tacks
meanings: [{"name":"to go straight to the basic facts of the matter; begin the most important work or business; to get started with the essentials","examples":["Let's get down to brass tacks. How much does this computer cost?","Let's get down to brass tacks. Who's paying for all this?","We finally got down to brass tacks and decided to work out a schedule for the project."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Although this idiom has been widely used since the early 1900s, word experts
are not sure what “brass tacks” stand for. The phrase might refer to copper bolts on a
boat that have been scrubbed clean, or to brass-topped tacks used in the upholstery
trade. If you get down to business by discussing the most basic, essential, and practical
realities, then you're “getting down to brass tacks.”

name: get in on the ground floor
meanings: [{"name":"to be part of some big or important project or business at its start","examples":["He was able to get in on the ground floor of the computer industry.","Miss Cohen got in on the ground floor with a new women's clothing company.","This is our chance to get in on the ground floor of an industry that's going to be big."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying probably originated in the financial world of the late 1800s. It's an
advantage to get in at the beginning of an enterprise. As the company succeeds and
prospers, so will you. After all, you were there at the start and helped it grow. The ground
floor is where you enter a big building. After that, there's no place to go but up.

name: get into the swing of things
meanings: [{"name":"fully involved and comfortable with (a regular activity, process, etc.)","examples":["Barrie didn't join in many activities at first, but now she's gotten into the swing of things.","After a while, she got into the swing of her new job.","I've been away on vacation but I should be (back) in the swing of things in a few days."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1500s the phrase, “in full swing,” meant to be very active in something.
“Swing” could have come from the motion of a children's swing or a clock pendulum.
In the 1800s a new expression developed that was based on the old one: “get into the
swing of things.” That meant getting involved with whatever was going on, especially
socially.

name: off the hook
meanings: [{"name":"to free yourself or someone from a distasteful obligation; to get out of trouble; to evade a punishment","examples":["I don't want to babysit tonight, so I hope my sister will get me off the hook.","He denied leaking the documents to get himself off the hook.","If you ask me, they let him off the hook too easily.","Thanks for getting me off the hook. I didn't want to attend that meeting. ","You're off the hook tonight.","Don't think you're off the hook on taxes just because you were paid in cash."],"media":[]}]
origin:
(Typically: be ~; get ~; get someone~; let someone~.) This expression comes from fishing. If a fish is caught on a hook, it desperately
wants to be off the hook. In the same way, if people are in trouble, have unwanted
obligations, or are about to be punished, they want to “get off the hook” by ridding
themselves of all these burdens.

name: get out of my face
meanings: [{"name":"stop standing in front of me in a provocative manner, close to my face, arguing with me, or disapproving of my actions","examples":["You'd better get out of my face right now or you'll be sorry!","I said no! Now get out of my face!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
his recent, vivid African-American expression means exactly what it says.
Stop facing me in a way that causes trouble between us. Get away! Leave me alone! It
is usually said in anger with the understanding that if the other person doesn't stop
talking and move away fast, he or she will suffer consequences.

name: get real
meanings: [{"name":"face reality; think and act in a serious fashion; stop fantasizing","examples":["Jane isn't going to believe that weird excuse you gave her. Get real.","Get real! He's never going to give you the money.","“Stop daydreaming, my dear,” Mike said to his sister. “You'll never win the lottery. Get real—you need a job!”"],"media":[]}]
origin:
In just two words, this strong, modern African-American expression is an order
to give up illusions and white lies. Stop pretending and confront the real world.

name: get something off your chest
meanings: [{"name":"to tell someone about something that has been worrying or upsetting you or making you feel guilty for a long time","examples":["Something is bothering me, and I want to get it off my chest. Please don't smoke here.","You've been a little cold to me lately. Is there something you'd like to get off your chest?","I had spent two months worrying about it and I was glad to get it off my chest.","You look very troubled about something. Why don't\nyou talk about it and get it off your chest?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Your heart is in your chest, and the heart “feels” emotions such as love and
fear. So if some worry, criticism, or secret has been troubling you and you finally tell
someone, you're getting it “off your chest” (out of your heart) at last.

name: get the green light
meanings: [{"name":"get permission to go ahead with a project","examples":["Mrs. Smith hoped to get the green light from the principal to redesign her science lab.","His boss finally gave him the green light to start the new project."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The world's first traffic light was installed in London in the horse-and-buggy
days of 1868. A revolving gas lantern with red and green panels told drivers when to
stop (red) and proceed (green). It was a good idea until it exploded a year later. When
motorcars became popular on the streets of America in the early 1900s, traffic signals
kept the flow of cars and pedestrians moving safely. At first they were mechanical
signs, like those found at early railroad crossings, which said “stop” and “go.” The
first electric traffic light in America was installed in Detroit in 1920. When motorists or
pedestrians saw a green light, they knew they could move on. Today when you propose
a project to someone in authority (like your teacher, your parents, or your boss), you
hope to “get the green light,” the permission to go and do what you want to do.

name: get the lead out of your feet / get the lead out of one's pants
meanings: [{"name":"to get busy; to move or work more quickly","examples":["C'mon, you guys. Get moving. Get the lead out of your feet!","If you're going to sell cars, you're going to have to shake the lead out.","Come on, you guys. Get the lead out!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression, which was used a lot in the American armed forces during the
Second World War, suggested that if you were moving sluggishly or working slowly, it
was as if you had lead, a heavy metal, in your feet. If you got it out, you could speed
up your actions. Another version of this idiom is “Get the lead out of your pants.”

name: get the sack
meanings: [{"name":"to be fired","examples":["I had a great job at Heavenly Hamburgers, but the boss gave me the sack.","She got the sack for always being late.","Marie has two small children to support. You can't\njust give her the sack. What is she going to do for\nmoney?","John lost his job yesterday. He got the sack."],"media":[]}]
origin:
There are many expressions that mean to be dismissed from work, including
“get the ax,” “get a pink slip,” and “get your walking papers.” “Get the sack” might
go back as far as the 1500s. In those days workmen who traveled around from job to
job carried all their tools in a sack. If a man was fired, he was told to get his sack, pack
up his tools, and move on.

name: get this show on the road
meanings:
[{"name":"get going; move forward; get the work started; do it; to get started","examples":["Every morning, Dad shouts, “Let's get this show on the road. You don't want to be late for school.”","Everyone ready? OK, let's get this show on the road!","If we're going to be on time, we'd better get this show on the road.","We've been waiting for hours, and I'm ready to get
started. Let's get the show on the road.","I can't wait any longer. If we don't get the show on
the road, I'm going to have to schedule this meeting
for another day."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Centuries ago, ordinary people didn't have cars, buses, trains, or planes to
take them to faraway places, so things came to them. In those days, there were many
traveling shows that journeyed from town to town. Carnivals, circuses, fairs, itinerant
acting companies, medicine shows, even showboats would arrive at a place, set up
stages and tents, and put on performances. When it was time to travel on, the boss
might yell, “Let's get this show on the road!” which meant work quickly and pack up
because we've got to move on to the next place. Today you can say “get this show
on the road” to anyone you want to hurry up and get going, not just to a traveling
performer. A similar saying is “get the ball rolling.”

name: get to the bottom of something
meanings: [{"name":"to find out the real cause of something; to uncover the hidden reason for something","examples":["The principal vowed to get to the bottom of the graffiti on the walls.","Police are working furiously to get to the bottom of this recent string of break-ins.","The committee aimed to get to the bottom of the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the federal response to the outbreak."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Writers were using this expression in the late 1500s. The bottom is usually
the base or root. If you search and investigate enough, you'll get to the bottom of
something. Then you'll know how it got started.

name: get under your skin
meanings: [{"name":"to bother or upset someone;","examples":["It really gets under my skin when my parents clean up my room.","His constant boasting was beginning to get under my skin.","Jack really gets under my skin - he never buys anyone a drink."],"media":[]},{"name":"to affect someone positively even though he or she does not want or expect to be affected that way; grow to like something","examples":["I used to hate the city, but after a while it kind of got under my skin.","The actress accepted the role because the character really got under her skin."],"media":[]}]
origin:
If something irritating like a bug gets under your skin, it can cause a bad
rash and itching. In the same way, if a person does something that irritates or upsets
you, he's “getting under your skin.”

name: get up on the wrong side of the bed
meanings: [{"name":"to awake with a bad temper or mood, feeling cross or grouchy; to be in a bad mood throughout the day","examples":["Watch out! Mother got up on the wrong side of the bed.","Be careful when you talk to the boss. He got up on the wrong side of the bed this morning."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the time of the ancient Romans the left side of anything was considered
evil or menacing. In fact, the word “sinister” comes from the Latin word for “left.”
The ancient Romans thought bad luck would come to anyone who put his or her left
foot down first when getting out of bed. The expression began as “got up left foot
forward.” The superstition that left was bad continued for centuries and gave birth to
today's expression “get up on the wrong side of the bed.”

name: get one's feet wet
meanings: [{"name":"to get a little first-time experience with something; to begin doing a new job, activity, etc., in usually a slow and simple way in order to become more familiar with it","examples":["Masha had never been in a play, but she took a small part just to get her feet wet.","She got her feet wet at her new job by doing some simple filing tasks.","I worked as a substitute teacher for a while, just to get my feet wet.","I'm looking forward to learning to drive. I can't wait to get behind the steering wheel and get my feet wet."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression has been used for centuries, as far back as the 1500s. Imagine
a swimmer who is afraid of diving into the water. He tiptoes in slowly, just getting his
feet wet so he can get used to the water. Then he can plunge in when he's ready. In
the same way, we “get our feet wet” when we venture into new territory by having our
first experience with something.

name: get your goat
meanings: [{"name":"to annoy very badly; to make a person angry; to irritate someone","examples":["It really got his goat when he cooked for three hours and no one ate the meal.","That sort of attitude really gets my goat.","I'm sorry. I didn't mean to get your goat.","Jean got Sally's goat and Sally made quite a fuss about it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American expression dates from about 1900. It was a common practice to
put a goat in the stall of a nervous racehorse to be its friend and keep it calm. If people
wanted the horse to lose a race, they would sneak the goat out of the stall to upset the
horse. There are several expressions that also mean to disturb or annoy someone: “get
your dander up,” “get your back up,” and “get your hackles up.”

name: gift of gab
meanings: [{"name":"skill in talking, especially in an interesting and colorful way; the ability to talk glibly and persuasively","examples":["Uncle Frank really had the gift of gab.","Storyteller with a gift of gab and a whole lot of chutzpah.","She's got the gift of gab - she should work in sales and marketing.","I'm not much of a talker. I wasn't blessed with the\ngift of gab."],"media":[]}]
origin:
As early as the late 1600s and early 1700s, British writers and speakers were
using this phrase. There are a few theories about its origin. Middle Dutch was a
language used from the middle of the 12th century through the 15th, and the word
for foolish chatter was gabbelen. In the Gaelic language (spoken by some people in
Scotland and Ireland) the word for mouth is gob, and over the years it may have
changed to gab, the English word that today means to talk a lot about small matters.
So today, somehow, between gabbelen and gob, we get the “gift of gab.”

name: gild the lily
meanings: [{"name":"to spoil something that is already beautiful by adding something extra or not needed","examples":["Should I add a scarf to this jacket or would it be gilding the lily?","Ms. Kilmer really doesn't need all that makeup. That's like gilding the lily.","Your house has lovely brickwork. Don't paint it. That would be gilding the lily."],"media":[]}]
origin:
William Shakespeare used a similar expression in his play King John: “to gild
refined gold, to paint the lily .. . is wasteful and ridiculous excess.” Over the years
the saying got shortened to just “gild the lily.” “Gild” means to cover with a thin layer
of gold. Why did Shakespeare use “lily”? Because it is already a beautiful flower, and
covering it with gold to make it more beautiful would be unnecessary.

name: give me five
meanings: [{"name":"to slap a person's hand as a hearty greeting or a sign of solid agreement","examples":["My little cousin always yells, “Give me five!”","“Yo, Tom! Give me five!” shouted Henry, raising his hand.","Bob: Hey, man! Skin me! Bill: How you doing, Bob?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
“Five” in this 20th-century African-American expression refers. to fingers
on your hand. Giving someone your five fingers (and your palm, too) is a common
gesture when meeting. (A similar saying is “give me some skin.”) This way of saying
hello, showing harmony, or celebrating victory comes from a style of communication
used in West Africa.

name: give someone the shirt off your back
meanings:
[{"name":"to be extremely generous","examples":["Mr. Smith would give you the shirt off his back if you needed it.","She'd give me the shirt off her back if I ever needed help.","He's the kind of man who'd give you the shirt off his back.","The young woman's parents had denied themselves
luxuries and vacations to provide for her. They had
given her the shirts off their backs to give her a good
life."],"media":[]}]
origin:
First used in the 1770s, this idiom is almost self-explanatory. If you saw a
needy person in the street who was cold because he had no shirt, and you actually
took your own shirt off and gave it to him, it would be an act of great kindness. Today,
if you perform any act of self-sacrifice, we say it's like “giving the shirt off your back”
to someone.

name: give someone the third degree
meanings: [{"name":"use mental or physical pressure to get information or a confession from someone","examples":["The teacher gave the third degree to every student to find out who had glued his briefcase shut.","My mother put me through the third degree. Questions—questions—questions. She's driving me nuts!","I got the third degree when I got home last night."],"media":[]}]
origin:
If you've ever watched a TV crime show, you've seen a prisoner getting the
“third degree.” He's sitting in a small room. A bright light is in his eyes. The police are
asking him tough questions in loud voices. “Who did it?” “Where's the money?” “Who
drove the car?” Why is this kind of grueling interrogation called “the third degree”?
There is an international organization called the Freemasons that started centuries ago.
It has three levels of membership, called degrees. To get to the third, or highest, degree
a person must undergo strong questioning. By the late 1800s “third degree” came to
mean any kind of intense interrogation, and by the early 1900s it was being applied to
police “grilling” (as if the prisoner were a piece of barbecue meat). Note: Third-degree
burns, although also very painful, have nothing to do with this expression.

name: give up the ghost
meanings: [{"name":"to die; to stop running","examples":["On the way to the theater, Ernesto's old car just gave up the ghost.","Our old TV had finally given up the ghost.","The old man gave up the ghost."],"media":[]}]
origin:
“Ghost” in this idiom doesn't
mean a dead person. It means the soul, which is thought to leave the body when a
person dies. So if somebody “gives up the ghost,” he or she stops living; if something
“gives up the ghost,” it stops working.

name: give your eyeteeth for something
meanings: [{"name":"to want something very badly; to be willing to give up something valuable to get something else","examples":["I'd give my eyeteeth to own a motorcycle like that.","Most people would give their eyeteeth for hair like yours."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Some people think eyeteeth got their name in the 1500s because the nerves of
these teeth are close to the eyes. Eyeteeth are important because they're used for biting
and chewing. If you want something so much that you are willing to sacrifice your
eyeteeth for it, that thing must be extremely important to you. A similar expression is
“to give your right arm” for something.

name: go against the grain
meanings: [{"name":"to say or do something in an unconventional way that annoys people; to anger a person by going against his/her wishes or feelings","examples":["He really goes against her grain when he says that a woman can't be president.","It goes against his grain to question the boss's judgment.","These days it goes against the grain to show too much respect for authority."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying has been in common use since at least the 17th century. William
Shakespeare popularized it in one of his plays. The parallel fibers in wood grow in a
certain direction. That's the wood's natural grain. When you work with wood, it's easier
to saw or plane in the direction of the grain. If you went against the grain, you'd probably
rough the wood up, not smooth it down. You might get splinters. Applied to life, not just
carpentry, “going against the grain” means doing or saying things in a way that upsets
or angers people. A similar saying is “rub someone the wrong way”

name: go along for the ride
meanings: [{"name":"to watch but not take part in an activity; to keep someone company","examples":["Harriet swore that she didn't trash any lawns. She just went along for the ride.","He wasn't interested in buying anything; he was just along for the ride.","He just came/went along for the ride.","My wife is speaking at the dinner and I'm just going along for the ride."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This idiom was born in the late 1890s, at the beginning of the automobile age.
Originally, it meant exactly what it said. If you had nothing better to do, you might go
along with people for a ride in their car. The driver was doing something (driving the
car) for a purpose (to get somewhere). You weren't doing anything, just sitting there in
the car, looking out the window. Today we say that you're “going along for the ride” if
you're joining an activity just to have something to do or just to be with other people.

name: go bananas / go insane
meanings: [{"name":"to be or go crazy","examples":["Come quick! Your brother has gone bananas.","Sorry, I just went bananas for a minute.","The crowd went bananas.","I thought he was going to go bananas.","You cracked it. Mom's gonna go insane!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying comes from 20th-century America. Bananas are the food most
associated with monkeys. When people think of monkeys (“monkey business,” “more
fun than a barrelful of monkeys,” etc.), they think of silly, uncontrolled behavior. If a
person is in a weird mood because he or she feels frustrated or bored with a situation,
he or she might “go bananas” and start acting like a monkey.

name: go fly a kite
meanings: [{"name":"go away; leave; stop bothering me","examples":["When he asked for her help, she told him to go fly a kite.","Bill: Dad, can I have ten bucks? Father: Go climb a tree!","Fred: Stop pestering me, John. Go jump in the lake! John: What did I do?","Bob: Well, Bill, don't you owe me some money? Bill: Go fly a kite!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Imagine you're trying to do homework, and someone is really annoying you.
There are a lot of expressions that you could shout at him that are similar to “Go fly
a kite!”: “Go jump in a lake!” “Go climb a tree!” “Go fry an egg!” You're telling
the kid that he is a pest, and you're commanding him to go away and do something
else. Flying a kite is an activity that should keep him busy so that you can get your
work done.

name: go for broke
meanings: [{"name":"to risk everything on one big goal or effort; to try as hard as possible","examples":["Instead of applying to several colleges, he went for broke and applied only to his first choice.","Okay, this is my last chance. I'm going for broke.","Look at Mary starting to move in the final hundred yards of the race! She is really going for broke."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Since the 17th century “broke” has meant “without money.” Two hundred
years later, this idiom was created at the gambling tables. When a gambler “went for
broke,” he risked all his money at once in a wager. If he won, he was rich. If he lost,
he was broke. Today, people who “go for broke” try as hard as possible to achieve a
single goal.

name: go over like a lead balloon
meanings: [{"name":"to fail miserably; to go over badly","examples":["Your joke went over like a lead balloon.","If that play was supposed to be a comedy, it went over like a lead balloon.","Her suggestion went over like a lead balloon."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This is a fairly recent expression. The writer who first used it imagined what
would happen if you tried to float a balloon filled with lead. It would never get off
the ground. In the same way, any project or attempt that fails miserably is like a lead
balloon that doesn't go over a blade of grass, let alone a treetop. This expression is
often applied to a joke that gets no laughs.

name: go over with a fine-tooth comb
meanings: [{"name":"to search through something very carefully; to examine something very closely","examples":["She went over the lawn with a fine-tooth comb, oe she couldn't find her contact lens.","The police are going over the evidence with a fine-tooth comb."," I can't find my calculus book. I went over the whole place with a fine-tooth comb.","I searched this place with a fine-tooth comb and didn't find my ring."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A fine-tooth comb has teeth spaced very closely together. It is often used to
help find and comb lice, which are very tiny, out of people's hair. Figuratively speaking,
if you search an area with a fine-tooth comb, you're examining and inspecting it with
great care so you won't miss a thing, no matter how small. A related idiom is “leave no
stone unturned”

name: go to bat for someone
meanings: [{"name":"to help someone out; to defend someone","examples":["Ivan went to bat for his friend when he defended him in front of the investigations committee.","Senators will go to bat for companies that pay lots of taxes.","I tried to go to bat for Bill, but he said he didn't want any help.","I heard them gossiping about Sally, so I went to bat for her."],"media":[]}]
origin:
There are a number of sports, like baseball or cricket, that you play with
a bat. That's where this expression comes from. When a baseball player can't play
because he's sick or injured, a pinch hitter helps him out by taking his place in the
game and literally “going to bat” for him. Off the playing fields, if you support people
in time of need, especially by defending them when they're in trouble, you're “going
to bat” for them, even though you might have nothing at all in your hands.

name: go to the dogs
meanings: [{"name":"to decline in looks or health; to be ruined or destroyed; to ruin oneself; to become much worse in quality or character","examples":["Our favorite restaurant has gone to the dogs lately.","He used to be a handsome movie star, but now he's gone to the dogs.","After Joe retired, the business went to the dogs."],"media":[]}]
origin:
As far back as the 1500s, food that was not thought suitable for human
consumption was thrown to the dogs. The expression caught on and expanded to
include any person or thing that came to a bad end, was ruined, or looked terrible.
For a similar phrase, see “gone to pot”

name: gone to pot
meanings: [{"name":"become ruined; to get worse and worse; to fail","examples":["This was once a beautiful park, but now it's all gone to pot.","Their business is going to pot.","Our old neighborhood has gone to pot."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This idiom from the 1500s originally referred to old or weak animals that
couldn't breed, lay eggs, give milk, or pull wagons. They were more useful on the
dinner plate than in the barnyard, so they were slaughtered and cooked in a pot. Now
we describe anyone or anything as having “gone to pot” if the person or thing has
worn out, is in bad shape, or can't do its job properly. Other similar expressions are
“go to wrack and ruin” and “go to the dogs.”

name: goody Two-shoes
meanings: [{"name":"a person who thinks he or she is perfect and tries to be","examples":["Tamika is such a Goody Two~shoes that everyone hates her.","She's a real goody-goody – I hate her!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the middle 1700s there was a nursery tale called “The History of Little Good
Two-Shoes.” In it, a little girl who owned only one shoe was given another one. She
went all over, showing off her pair of shoes, saying, “Two shoes.” Today a person who
thinks he or she is perfect is sarcastically described as a “Goody Two-shoes,” after the
title character of that book. A similar phrase is “goody-goody.”

name: gravy train
meanings:
[{"name":" job that pays well for little work; a much exploited source of easy money; a life of luxury","examples":["The kid was already asleep when he went to babysit. What a gravy train.","Conferences are seen as a gravy train by many organisers who charge exorbitant rates for poor services.","The public should know which senators are on the corporate gravy train.","Scott got himself a job where he won't have to work
very hard. He's really riding the gravy train.","They made some very wise and profitable
investments, and now they can retire and live off the
interest. They're on the gravy train.","If I had a million dollars, I sure could ride the gravy train. "],"media":[]}]
origin:
This bit of American slang originated in the 1920s, when “gravy” was a slang
word for easy money often gotten by illegal means. People who worked on railroad
trains made up the phrase “gravy train.” It referred to a good-paying job that
was easy.

name: grease someone's palm
meanings: [{"name":"to bribe someone; to pay someone in the hope that he'll do something for you in return","examples":["If you want to get something done around here, you have to grease someone's palm.","You may have to grease his palm to get the usher to give you the best seats for the concert.","I'd never oil a police officer's palm. That's illegal."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Grease is a lubricant. It makes machinery operate smoothly and wheels roll
quickly. In this expression, when you “grease someone's palm,” you don't actually
smear it with a thick oily substance. Money is the “grease” that gets things moving.
Some people think that in order to get the best table at a restaurant you have to grease
the headwaiter's palm, and to get the repairman to come on a Sunday, you have to
grease his palm. You have to give the person some money, often secretly, sometimes
illegally, to get what you want. The ancient Romans used a similar expression in Latin,
so there must have been some bribery going on back then, too.

name: greek to someone
meanings: [{"name":"too difficult to understand; unknown","examples":["The computer saleswoman explained how to install the DVD burner, but it was Greek to me.","I don't understand this. It's all Greek to me.","She said it was Greek to her, and that it made no sense at all."],"media":[]}]
origin:
William Shakespeare used this phrase in one of his plays, Julius Caesar. In
the play, which takes place in 44 B.c., a Roman who spoke only Latin said that he had
heard another man speaking Greek, but he could not understand what he was saying.
It was “Greek to him.” The expression caught on. Today, if you don't understand
something you've heard or read because it is so complicated or technical, then it's
“Greek to you.”

name: green thumb
meanings: [{"name":"having a special talent for making flowers and green plants grow well; natural ability to grow plants","examples":["My uncle has a green thumb. You should see his roses.","My sister has a green thumb, but I kill most plants that I buy.","Amy really has a green thumb. Everything she plants\nin her garden grows so well.","You must have quite a green thumb. Your flowers are\nalways so beautiful and healthy-looking."],"media":[]}]
origin:
If you rubbed green plant leaves or parts between your fingers, you'd
probably get chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants, on them. If a person loves
gardening and has great ability to make plants grow, it's easy to see why people
would say that he or she has a “green thumb.”

name: green with envy
meanings: [{"name":"extremely jealous","examples":["My new car made my neighbor green with envy. ","Bill was green with envy that I won first place.","When he heard about my new job he was green with envy."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Colors often take on descriptive meanings. Red sometimes means angry. Blue
describes sad and lonely feelings. And since about 1600, thanks to William Shakespeare,
green has been associated with jealousy and desire. He referred to jealousy as “the
green sickness” in his play Antony and Cleopatra.

name: grit your teeth
meanings: [{"name":"to show courage and determination when dealing with problems or challenges; to bear pain courageously","examples":["I have to remove this splinter from your finger, so just grit your teeth.","Starting your own business can be very tough, but you just have to grit your teeth and keep working at it.","We had to grit our teeth and agree with their conditions because we wanted the contract.","I hate going to the gym, but I just grit my teeth and try to get through it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In 18th-century America this expression was becoming popular. The ancient
Greeks had used a similar expression that translated as “set your teeth.” One of the
definitions of the verb “grit” is to clamp your teeth together tightly. When people are
faced with a tough or painful job that demands a lot of physical or emotional strength,
they may grit their teeth in determination. Related sayings are “bite the bullet” and “face the music”

name: gum up the works
meanings: [{"name":"to prevent something from working or flowing  or opening properly; to ruin someone's plans","examples":["I had set my alarm clock to wake me up on time, but my little cousin gummed up the works.","Some dirt got inside the gears and gummed up the works.","When I woke up this morning my eyes were all gummed up.","Please, Bill, be careful and don't gum up the works.","Tom sure gummed up the whole plan."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression was first used in the 1800s, when a lot of new machines were
being invented. Most machinery had to be oiled well to work properly. Sometimes
the oil got so thick and gummy that, instead of helping the machine run smoothly,
it actually interfered with — or even stopped — the working of the machine. Today
anyone or anything that “gums up the works” ruins someone's plans or spoils any
kind of undertaking.

name: handle with kid gloves
meanings: [{"name":"to treat gently and carefully; to be very careful with a touchy person","examples":["When you're speaking to Courtney, handle the subject of summer vacation with kid gloves.","Bill has become so sensitive. You really have to handle him with kid gloves.","You don't have to handle me with kid gloves. I can take it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Kid gloves are made from the smooth hide of a young goat and are gentle
to the touch. If you handle anything (like a fragile sculpture) or anyone (like your
grumpy uncle) “with kid gloves,” you're being careful and gentle. The last thing you
want to do is break the sculpture or anger your uncle. You're making every attempt to
avoid all possible problems.

name: hand-to-mouth existence / hand to mouth
meanings: [{"name":"to spend your salary as fast as it's earned without saving any for the future; to live in poor circumstances","examples":["He lives a hand-to-mouth existence doing odd jobs around town.","Both dropped out of college and essentially lived hand-to-mouth in order to pursue their musical dreams.","Low wages mean a hand-to-mouth existence for many people.","We can't handle another kid. We're living hand to mouth as it is."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Writers were using this saying in the 16th century. Imagine a starving person
who is given food. If he could, he'd save some for later, but because he's so hungry, he
gobbles it all down. Every morsel goes directly from his hands into his mouth. Today
we say that a person lives a “hand-to-mouth existence” (or “from hand to mouth”)
when he or she lives from day to day, spending every dollar earned without being able
to put aside any savings for the future.

name: hands are tied
meanings: [{"name":"not able to act; held back from doing what you want to do; powerless to do anything","examples":["I'd like to help you with your homework, but the teacher said we had to work alone, so my hands are tied.","The judge says her hands are tied because the law requires a harsh sentence in such cases.","I'd like to raise people's salaries but my hands are tied."],"media":[]}]
origin:
People started using this expression in the 1600s. It calls up the image of a
person whose hands are actually tied together. Can she paint a picture? No. Can she
change the tires on a car? No. Can she do anything meaningful with her hands tied?
No. Today this saying has nothing to do with your hands actually being tied up. If you
want to do something but are prevented or forbidden by forces or people beyond your
control, your “hands are tied,” figuratively speaking.

name: (hand)writing on the wall
meanings: [{"name":"a sign that something bad is going to happen; a warning of danger or trouble; an omen","examples":["When the police questioned him, Phil saw the handwriting on the wall and confessed.","No one told him he was going to be fired, but he could see the writing on the wall. [=he could see that he was going to be fired soon]","I can see the writing on the wall that this company is doomed."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This idiom originated in the Old Testament. The King of Babylonia
had a vision in which he saw a mysterious message written on the palace wall, “Mene,
mene, tekel, upharsin.” Daniel was sent for to explain the meaning of the strange
words. When he arrived, he told the king that it was a warning that his kingdom would
be conquered. In time the prophecy came true. Today we say that you can read or see
the “handwriting on the wall” when you can see signs that misfortune is coming.

name: hang in there
meanings: [{"name":"to continue without giving up; to not lose faith or courage; be patient","examples":["My brother kept calling, “Hang in there, you can do it!” And I did!","Hang in there – exams are almost over.","Bob: Everything is in such a mess. I can't seem to get things done right. Jane: Hang in there, Bob. Things will work out.","Mary: Sometimes I just don't think I can go on. Sue: Hang in there, Mary. Things will work out."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American slang expression probably came from boxing. A fighter who's
exhausted but doesn't want to give up might hang on the arms of his opponent or on
the ropes around the ring. That way he'll stop getting punched and be able to rest
for a few seconds so he can get himself back up and continue the fight. By using this
expression, you don't actually have to be hanging onto something physical in order
to make it through a tough situation or a difficult project.

name: hang out your shingle
meanings: [{"name":"to open a private office, especially a doctor's or lawyer's office, by putting a sign over the door","examples":["After many years of training, she hung out her shingle, “Samantha Fox, Animal Doctor.”","She graduated from law school and hung out her shingle.","Some people hang their own shingle when they are tired of the corporate 9 to 5."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In 19th-century America, when professional people opened private offices,
they hung out signs that were often painted on a shingle, a thin piece of wood used
to cover the roof or sides of a building. Today we use the phrase “hang out your
shingle” to refer to the whole process of opening up your own office: renting the
space, filling it with furniture, hiring help, and hanging up the sign that announces
you're in business.

name: hanging by a thread
meanings: [{"name":"to be in a dangerous or unsafe position; to depend on something very small to save you; to be very close to death, failure, etc.","examples":["You are not quite failing, but you are hanging by a thread.","The patient's life was hanging by a thread.","John isn't failing geometry, but his passing grade is just hanging by a hair.","Your whole argument is hanging by a thread."],"media":[]}]
origin:
There's a myth that tells of a king in the 5th century B.c. who grew tired of
being told how wonderful he was by a flatterer named Damocles. The king threw a
magnificent banquet for Damocles, who was having a grand time until he looked at
the ceiling. He was shocked to see a large, sharp sword hanging by a single, thin hair,
and pointing straight down at his head! He quickly learned his lesson: Power and
happiness are not secure and usually depend on the will or favor of someone else.
Today, when people are in risky situations, we say they're “hanging by a thread.”

name: hat in hand
meanings: [{"name":"to behave in a humble and sorry way; to beg or plead for a favor or a pardon","examples":["Hat in hand, I went to the judge pleading for mercy."],"media":[]}]
origin:
For centuries people have begged for money in public by holding out a
container to passersby. Often it was a hat. Taking off your hat in the presence of others
is an act of respect. So a person, even one without a hat, who is begging for favors
or forgiveness is a person with his or her “hat in hand.” A related saying is “pass the
hat”

name: have a bone to pick with you
meanings: [{"name":"to have a disagreement to discuss with someone; to have something to argue about with someone","examples":["My new boss said she had a bone to pick with me and called me into her office.","Hey, Bill. I've got a bone to pick with you. Where is the money you owe me?","I had a bone to pick with her, but she was so sweet that I forgot about it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying goes back to the early 16th century, and is based on the image of
people arguing over fine points like dogs picking over bones to get every last bit of
meat. Others think it may have originated in the 19th century from the idea that two
people can argue the way two dogs can fight over a bone. In either case, if someone
has “a bone to pick” with you, it means he or she has a complaint about something
you said or did.

name: have a screw loose
meanings: [{"name":"to behave or look in a strange or foolish manner; to be odd and not ordinary; to seem crazy","examples":["That substitute gym teacher must have a screw loose.","Her brother definitely has a screw loose – I don't really trust him.","Yes, he has a screw loose somewhere. He wears a heavy jacket in the middle of summer."],"media":[]}]
origin:
During the machine age beginning around 1860, many contraptions were
held together by nuts, bolts, and screws. If a screw came loose, the machine would
not operate as it was supposed to. It might start to do all sorts of bizarre things.
People aren't held together with screws, of course, but if they start acting weirdly, this
expression might fit them perfectly.

name: have your cake and eat it too
meanings: [{"name":"to spend or use something up but still have it; to have two things when you must choose one; to have or enjoy the good parts of something without having or dealing with the bad parts","examples":["You can either go to a movie or get pizza, but you can't have your cake and eat it too.","I worked at home so I could raise my family and still earn money – I guess I wanted to have my cake and eat it too.","Don't buy a car if you want to walk and stay healthy. You can't eat your cake and have it too.","They seem to think they can have their cake and eat it too by having excellent schools for their son without paying high taxes."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying started sometime in the 1540s. Once you ve eaten a piece of cake,
you don't have it anymore. So you have to make a decision to eat it or save it. In
the same way, money that you've spent is money that you no longer have in your
pocket. You have to choose what to do with what you have. The original version of this
expression is “you can't eat your cake and have it too.”

name: half-baked
meanings: [{"name":"not planned or considered carefully enough; foolish, silly","examples":["A half-baked idea.","Opening up a store which sells only tape will not be successful. It is a half baked idea.","It was a half-baked scheme for getting rich."],"media":[]}]

name: hand it to someone
meanings: [{"name":"to recognize that someone deserves respect for what the person did; give credit, acknowledge","examples":["I've got to hand it to you. Your idea to open a store in this location was great.","You've got to hand it to her, she built that cabin herself.","I have to hand it to him. He did a wonderful job.","I mean you've got to hand it to her, she's brought up those three children all on her own."],"media":[]}]

name: hand over fist
meanings: [{"name":"[for money and merchandise to be exchanged] very rapidly, quickly and in large amounts","examples":["What a busy day. We took in money hand over fist.","They were buying things hand over f ist.","Business was good and we were making money hand over fist.","Warners and CBS Studios made money hand over fist.","Paul's candy was such a success at the fair, his stall\nwas always busy with buyers. He was taking in\nmoney hand over fist, faster than he could count it."],"media":[]}]
origin: This phrase has a nautical history. It relates to the practice of climbing a rope hand over hand. This soon became known as hand over fist, with the fist being the hand gripping the rope. The term hand over fist soon evolved from making progress up a rope to making progress generally. Today, it relates only to financial gain.

name: hand something to someone on a (silver) platter
meanings: [{"name":"to allow someone to get something very easily, without having to work for it","examples":["His father is president of the university and his education was handed to him on a silver platter.","If you sell your share in the company now, you're handing the ownership to him on a silver platter."],"media":[]}]

name: handful
meanings: [{"name":"difficult person; as much as one can manage (often used for a person, often a child, who is difficult to control)","examples":["Her older son is fine but the little one is a bit of a handful.","My three year old runs around the house and often breaks things. He's a real handful.","She straightened that out, and I give her credit, but she is still a handful.","The kids are quite a handful.","I know I can be a bit of a handful.","Bob: Sara can be a real handful these days. \nJane: Well, I admit it's been a while since I looked after a toddler."],"media":[]},{"name":"a very few, esp. when compared to a larger group; a small quantity or number","examples":["A handful of professional athletes make millions, but most do not do so well.","She invited all her friends to her party, but only a handful of them turned up.","There were only a handful of guests at the reception.","He only knows a handful of different recipes.","The centre is staffed by a handful of volunteers."],"media":[]},{"name":"as much or as many as the hand will grasp; an amount of something that can be held in one hand","examples":["He pulled out a handful of coins from his pocket.","I use two handfuls of pasta per person.","Add a large handful of chopped herbs.","He scooped up a handful of soil and examined it carefully."],"media":[]}]

name: hard feelings
meanings: [{"name":"anger or resentment; feelings of dislike or anger toward someone that you think has mistreated you","examples":["I know we had our differences, but let's not have any hard feelings.","She felt/had no hard feelings towards him.","I'm sorry it didn't work out, but no hard feelings."],"media":[]}]

name: hard up (for something)
meanings: [{"name":"short of money; not having enough of something important or valuable","examples":["Everyone comes to her desk and takes supplies. I know she's hard up for pencils.","We're a bit hard up at the moment so we're not thinking about holidays.","If you're so hard up for friends, why don't you join a club?","You cannot be that hard up."],"media":[]}]

name: harp on
meanings: [{"name":"complain about something many times; to talk about (a subject) constantly or repeatedly in an annoying way","examples":["I know losing your job was awful, but don't harp on it. You are only making yourself more depressed.","She's always harping on the importance of a good diet.","He seems to enjoy harping on my shortcomings.","He's always harping on our lack of discipline."],"media":[]}]

name: has-been
meanings: [{"name":"a person who in the past was famous, important, admired, or good at something, but is no longer in public favor","examples":["Since the movie star was found guilty of a crime, I haven't seen him in any motion pictures. He's a has-been.","She's a has-been TV star."],"media":[]}]

name: have a ball
meanings: [{"name":"to have fun; to spend time in a very enjoyable way","examples":["Everyone had a ball at the party.","So how was the party last night? Oh, it was great - we had a ball!","Bill: Well, we're off to the party. Jane: Okay. Have a ball! ","“Have a ball!” said Mary as her roommate went out the door."],"media":[]}]

name: have a fit / throw a fit
meanings: [{"name":"become upset; express extreme anger","examples":["She'll have a fit if she finds out you broke her watch.","My mother threw a fit when she saw the mess we made.","Don't have a fit if it doesn't turn out as you want.","If I so much as moved a chair, Mom would throw a fit.","Oh, my God. Bob's gonna have a fit.","Jane would have a fit if she knew you were accompanying me to this party."],"media":[]}]

name: have a good head on your shoulders
meanings: [{"name":"be smart or sensible; to have common sense","examples":["You have a good head on your shoulders and I'm sure you'll do fine in college.","Mary doesn't do well in school, but she's got a good head on her shoulders.","John has a good head on his shoulders and can A be depended on to give good advice."],"media":[]}]

name: have a mind of one's own
meanings: [{"name":"be able to think independently; to have one's own ideas and make one's own choices about what should be done","examples":["Although we all voted one way, she voted in a completely opposite direction. She's really got a mind of her own.","Her parents want her to go to college, but she has a mind of her own and insists on trying to become an actress."],"media":[]}]

name: have been around
meanings: [{"name":"have a lot of experience; become worldly-wise","examples":["She knows all about office politics. She has been around for awhile.","He knows what he's talking about - he's been around."],"media":[]}]

name: what's coming to one
meanings: [{"name":"what one deserves; deserve a punishment","examples":["I didn't study for the exam and I failed. I had it coming.","He's a dirty cheat, and I'm going to see that he gets what's coming to him.","If you cheat, you'll get in trouble. You'll get what's coming to you.","They gave Billy what was coming to him."],"media":[]}]
origin: (*Typically: get ~; have ~; give one ~.)

name: have/got it made
meanings: [{"name":"to be in a very good position or situation; be sure of success, have everything often without much effort","examples":["My brother has it made with a good job, a beautiful wife, and a big house with a pool.","With his father at the head of the firm, he's got it made.","Everyone thinks if you're in a hit movie, you've got it made.","You're taking all the easy classes this semester – you've got it made!"],"media":[]}]

name: have it out with someone
meanings: [{"name":"discuss a conflict or misunderstanding with the other person involved","examples":["My friend and I had a big fight last week. This morning I had it out with him and now everything is okay.","She'd been late for work every morning and I thought I'd better have it out with her."],"media":[]}]

name: have your heart in your mouth
meanings: [{"name":"to be extremely frightened about something; to be very excited or nervous about something anticipated","examples":["My heart was in my mouth when | reached the top of the roller coaster.","My heart was in my mouth when I opened the letter.","He waited for her arrival with his heart in his mouth.","You sure don't seem relaxed—in fact, it seems like your heart is in your mouth."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Homer used this expression thousands of years ago in his famous epic poem
The Iliad. When you are terrified, your heart starts pounding violently and there's a
choking feeling in your throat. Homer referred to that feeling as having “your heart in
your mouth.” For centuries that's the way many people have described the feeling of
extreme terror or dread.

name: have one's heart set on (something)
meanings: [{"name":"want something very much","examples":["She has her heart set on a new bicycle.","She's got her heart set on ballet lessons.","I had my heart set on that teddy bear."],"media":[]}]

name: head and shoulders above someone
meanings: [{"name":"far superior; much better than","examples":["When it comes to catching fish, Lew is head and shoulders above everyone else.","There's no competition - they're head and shoulders above the rest.","They are/stand head and shoulders above the competition."],"media":[]}]
origin:
When it was first used in the 1800s, this saying referred to height: a very tall
person towers over a very short one. But over the years the meaning has been stretched
to include any skill one has that is better than someone else's. So a five-foot person
may be head and shoulders above a six-foot person in math, tap dancing, and writing
stories.

name: head honcho
meanings: [{"name":"the person in charge; the chief, boss, leader","examples":["Do what the head honcho tells you if you want to keep your job.","The head honcho is hard to reach because he is too busy."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The Japanese word hanchu means “squad leader” (han=squad, chu=chief).
During the Korean War (1950-53), American soldiers changed the spelling to honcho,
and added “head,” probably because head honcho made a catchy phrase. Today
a head honcho is the principal of a school, the owner of a business, or anyone in
charge.

name: head in the clouds
meanings: [{"name":"absentminded; daydreaming; lost in thought","examples":["My report card said that I should pay more attention in class — that my head was usually in the clouds.","Since he met Sara, he's been walking around (with his head) in the clouds.","From then on, my head was permanently in the clouds."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the mid-1600s the idea was first written that if you weren't aware of what
was going on, if your mind was ina dreamy state, then your head was in the air. Later
“air” was changed to “clouds” because air goes all the way down to the ground but
clouds are usually high up. When your “head is in the clouds,” it means your mind is
definitely somewhere else.

name: hear a pin drop
meanings: [{"name":"so silent you can hear very soft things happening; without sound; noiseless","examples":["During study period, the teacher wanted the room so quiet she could hear a pin drop.","After he announced that he was leaving, you could hear a pin drop in the office.","When she rose to speak, there was pin-drop silence."],"media":[]}]
origin:
If a lamp fell and smashed to the floor, you'd hear it from another room. But
if a pin dropped, you might not hear it land, even if you were standing right there. In
the early 1800s when this expression was first used, women sewed most of their own
clothing. Pins and needles were expensive and sometimes hard to come by, so if a pin
dropped, you'd hope that the room was silent enough so that you could hear it hit the
floor. Then you could find it more easily. A room so quiet that you could “hear a pin
drop” would be a very quiet room indeed. Nowadays we can use this phrase for any
very hushed place, with or without dropping pins.

name: heart of gold
meanings: [{"name":"an extremely kind, generous, humane, and forgiving nature","examples":["Lynda has a heart of gold, and everyone loves her for it.","A woman with a heart of gold gives us lodging for the night.","He plays the part of a tough cop on TV who really has a heart of gold."],"media":[]}]
origin:
William Shakespeare used this expression, which comes from the 1500s.
Your heart couldn't pump blood if it were made of something hard like gold. But
“heart” has always stood for more than just an organ in your body. In poetry and
song it means your basic character, your ability to feel affection and love, and the
place where your deepest feelings are. Gold has always had a special meaning in our
language, too. Expressions like “good as gold,” “the gold standard,” and “worth your
weight in gold” suggest that gold is highly desirable. So when you say that someone
has a “heart of gold,” it means that the person is lovely, thoughtful, compassionate,
considerate, concerned, kind, generous, forgiving, caring, unselfish, helpful, and
magnanimous. That's a nice person!

name: heart's in the right place
meanings: [{"name":"someone only has good intentions; to have good intentions even though mistakes occur","examples":["Kevin messes up sometimes, but his heart's in the right place.","She's not too smart, but at least her heart is in the right place.","He's an odd man but his heart is in the right place.","He is very strict with his students, but his heart is in the right place."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Everyone's heart is right in the middle of the chest. Since the heart is often
considered the center of one's emotions and feelings, this expression means that even
if what you try to do comes out wrong, your intentions are right.

name: heavens to Betsy
meanings: [{"name":"an expression of astonishment, amazement, and disbelief","examples":["A 100-year-old woman just flew a plane by herself from New York to California. Heavens to Betsy!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression is a real mystery. We know what it means, and we think it
originated in the United States in the late 1890s. But nobody today is 100 percent
certain where it came from. Why “heavens”? Who was “Betsy”? Even the word expert
who titled his book of curious sayings Heavens to Betsy! couldn't name the source.

name: hide or hair
