meanings: [{"name":"to understand how something works; to figure something out","examples":["Dad couldn't make heads or tails out of the instructions for assembling the new IKEA furniture.","I couldn't make heads or tails of her reaction.","His handwriting was so bad that we couldn't make heads or tails out of it.","We couldn't make heads or tails of your directions."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Cicero, a Roman statesman and public speaker of the first century B.c., used
a similar expression, “neither head nor feet.” The current English saying comes from
the 1600s. The head is the front or top of something. The tail is the end or bottom. So if
you can make heads or tails out of something, you can understand it from beginning
to end, from top to bottom. This expression is usually used in the negative (“They
can't make. ..”) because there are a lot of things in this world that are difficult to
understand.

name: make no bones about something
meanings: [{"name":"to speak directly, plainly, honestly, and without hesitation or doubt; to be very sure and definite about (something)","examples":["The class teacher made no bones about not liking hats worn in class.","This is the greatest cake I've ever eaten. Make no bones about it. ","Make no bones about it, Dhruthi is a great singer.","He made no bones about his plans to cut expenses.","Make no bones about it—we will win."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The origin of this old idiom, first used in print in 1548, is not clear. Some word
experts have suggested that it came from the fact that if there are no bones in your
soup, you can just swallow it without worrying about choking. That's like speaking
plainly without worrying.

name: make your mouth water
meanings: [{"name":"to look so attractive and desirable that it makes you want to have it very much; to want to eat or drink something that looks or smells delicious","examples":["Seeing those posters of Hawaii made my mouth water for a vacation on a beach.","That beautiful salad makes my mouth water. ","Talking about food makes my mouth water."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression was used as early as the mid-1500s, but since time began,
people have known that the sight, smell, or even thought of food can make a person's
salivary glands start up, causing the mouth to water. Though this saying is often
used in connection with food or drink, it can really be used when looking forward to
something that you want a lot.

name: march to (the beat of) a different drummer
meanings: [{"name":"be an individual; do your own thing; don't do what everybody else does; be original and creative","examples":["Bob, with his outlandish clothes and weird hairdo, marches to the beat of a different drummer.","His strange behavior was no surprise—he had always marched to (the beat of) a different drummer.","Her friends went to college, but she heard a different drummer and moved to the city to be an actor.","Since Sally started marching to the beat of a different drummer, she has had a lot of great new ideas."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Members of a marching band keep step to the beat of a drum. In life, not
in a parade, those who dress, behave, or think differently are out of step with most
other people and march to the tune of their own drummer. They live according
to their own rules. This expression was made popular by Henry David Thoreau, a
writer and naturalist of the mid-1800s. Thoreau strongly believed in individual
rights. He lived for two years in a one-room cottage by the shores of Walden Pond
in Massachusetts to get closer to nature. In his famous book Walden, published in
1854, Thoreau wrote: “If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it
is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music he hears.”

name: mess with someone or something
meanings: [{"name":"to annoy, argue with, hassle, or otherwise anger and irritate a person","examples":["Don't even think of messing with the new teacher. She's tough.","I wouldn't want to mess with him.","I wouldn't want to mess with him.","You'd better not be messing with me."],"media":[]},{"name":"to deal with or be involved with (something that causes or that could cause trouble)","examples":["The company doesn't want to mess with small distributors."],"media":[]},{"name":"to handle or play with (something) in a careless way; to mess around with (something)","examples":["Don't mess with the camera.","He was messing with his bike and then he couldn't fit the parts back together."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This modern African-American expression is similar in meaning to “bug
someone”. “To mess” is to butt into other people's business or interfere
with other people's lives.

name: midas touch
meanings: [{"name":"to make a lot of money at whatever you do","examples":["Darren has the Midas touch and is making millions in the fashion design business.","Bob is a merchant banker and really has the Midas touch.","The poverty-stricken boy turned out to have the Midas touch and was a millionaire by the time he was twenty-five."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Midas was a legendary king of Phrygia (in modern-day Turkey). In return for a good deed, he was granted one wish by the god Dionysus, and asked for the power to turn everything he touched into gold. When he discovered to his horror that his touch had turned his food and drink—and even his daughter—to gold, he begged Dionysus to take back the gift, and Dionysus agreed to do so. When "Midas touch" is used today, the moral of this tale of greed is usually ignored. Today anyone who is able to make lots of money
at whatever he or she does is said to have the “Midas touch.”

name: mince words
meanings: [{"name":"not to come right to the point; to be less than 100% honest; to use mild or vague words so as not to offend or hurt someone","examples":["Please don't mince words. Tell me exactly what you think of my painting.","A frank person never minces words.","He doesn't mince words when it comes to giving his opinion about the new law.","The report does not mince words, describing the situation as extremely serious."],"media":[]}]
origin:
William Shakespeare used this expression in some of his plays in the late
15008, but it might have been in use before that. Originally “mince” meant to soften
or lessen the force of certain words in order to be polite. Today, if you mince words or
mince matters, you are not being honest and open.

name: mind over matter
meanings: [{"name":"the power of your mind is stronger than the body","examples":["His ability to keep going even when he is tired is a simple question of mind over matter.","He announced what he called \"the ultimate test of mind over matter\" - a woman walking over hot coals.","You need to concentrate harder. Pay no attention to your surroundings. This is a case of mind over matter."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Virgil, a Roman poet who was born in 70 B.c., used this expression in his
famous poem, The Aeneid. “Mind” means brain, thoughts, and willpower. “Matter”
means a physical object, and it can also mean trouble or difficulty. Notice also that
“mind” and “matter” both begin with “m,” and alliteration helps make a saying more
popular.

name: mind your p's and q's
meanings: [{"name":"to behave properly; to display good manners; mind your manners","examples":["Please try to mind your p's and q's when the princess visits the school.","When you children go to visit Aunt Mary, you'll have to mind your p's and q's; not like at home, where I let you do as you please.","I have to mind my p's and q's when I'm with my grandmother.","We'd better mind our p's and q's for this new teacher; I hear she's very strict."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This term was beginning to be used in the 1600s, and by the late 1700s it was
very popular. The letters “p” and “q” can often be confused, so children learning
to read and printers selecting type have to be careful with these letters. Another
possibility comes from old English pubs where a list of the pints (“p's”) and quarts
(“q's”) a drinker consumed were written on a blackboard to be paid for later. Finally,
pieds and queues are dance steps that a French dancing instructor would teach
his students to perform with care. There's no proof as to where this catchy saying
originated, though.

name: miss the boat
meanings: [{"name":"to lose an opportunity; to arrive too late and miss out on something","examples":["If you're late to the interview, you'll miss the boat for the job.","There were tickets available last week, but he missed the boat by waiting till today to try to buy some.","I decided not to go to college, but watching all my friends go off made me feel like I'd missed the boat.","Pay attention, John, or you'll miss the boat and not learn algebra.","Tom really missed the boat when it came to making friends."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression has been used by many people since about 1900, when there
were no airplanes and many people traveled to far-off places by boat. If you arrived
at the dock after the boat had sailed because you lost track of time, overslept, or were
delayed, then you missed out.

name: money burns a hole in your pocket
meanings: [{"name":"can't stop yourself from spending whatever money you have","examples":["Howard is broke again because money burns a hole in his pocket.","Sally can't seem to save anything. Money burns a hole in her pocket. ","If money burns a hole in your pocket, you never have any for emergencies."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Naturally, you'd want to get something like a lit candle out of your pocket if
you thought it could really burn a hole in it. This saying calls up an image of money
setting fire to your pants pocket if you don't find something to buy with it fast. Some
people feel that they have to spend whatever coins or bills are in their pockets at the
moment, sometimes on something totally frivolous, just to spend them. This expression
goes back to the 1500s because there have always been people who have difficulty
saving their money. Don't confuse this idiom with “having money to burn,” which
means being so rich that you can burn some of your money and still have plenty left.

name: monkey business
meanings: [{"name":"silliness or fooling around; dishonest or illegal activities; idiotic pranks; shenanigan","examples":["That's enough monkey business. Now, settle down.","Our teacher warned us not to try any monkey business while she was out of the room.","Stop the funny business. This is serious!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression has two meanings. One concerns comical behavior like that
of a playful monkey. The other refers to sneaky, unlawful actions. So a student could
be sent to the principal's office for monkey business, and a politician can be sent to
jail for monkey business. This idiom, from 2oth-century America, is like many other
expressions that relate human behavior to animal behavior ("sly as a fox,” “wise as
an owl,” and so on), and probably comes from an older expression, “monkeyshines,”
which dates from the 1820s.

name: more (to something) than meets the eye
meanings: [{"name":"there are hidden facts that can't be seen or understood right away","examples":["There is more to this proposal than meets the eye.","There is more to that problem than meets the eye.","What makes you think that there is more than meets the eye?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This British cliché from the 1800s says that often things have deeper levels of
meaning and importance than you can see at first. The full truth of a situation has to
be thoroughly investigated. You might have to use a microscope to research skills to
uncover the real facts of something.

name: more than one way to skin a cat
meanings: [{"name":"there are several different ways of reaching the same goal","examples":["Scott tried every solution to the puzzle he could think of because he knew there was more than one way to skin a cat.","Jill: How will we fix the sink without a wrench? Jane: There's more than one way to skin a cat. ","Our first approach didn't work, but we'll figure out some other way. There's more than one way to skin a cat."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American idiom has been in use since the mid-1800s, when removing
animals' pelts was more common than it is today. Each person who skinned a cat or
animal had his or her own particular way of doing it. Over the years the saying took on
broader meaning, and now it can refer to the many methods of accomplishing goals.
The original British expression was “there are more ways of killing a cat than choking
it with cream.”

name: mum's the word
meanings: [{"name":"you must keep silent; don't tell anyone the secret","examples":["Don't tell anyone about the surprise for Mr. Edward. Remember, mum's the word.","We want her birthday party to be a surprise, so mum's the word.","“Mum's the word,” said Jane to ease Mary's mind about her secret."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Since at least 1350 “mum” has meant silent. The word itself sounds like a
person trying to talk with her lips shut tight. “Mum's the word” has been a popular
expression since about 1700.

name: name is mud
meanings: [{"name":"the person is in trouble, possibly doomed, and worthless; people do not like or trust someone","examples":["Everyone knows that it was Tiger who started the fight during the game. Now that we're disqualified, his name is mud.","The scandal ruined his reputation and now his name is mud.","If he doesn't turn up tonight, his name will be mud.","If I can't get this contract signed, my name will be mud.","His name is mud ever since he broke the crystal vase."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1700s “mud” was a slang word for “fool” or “stupid person” in England.
Starting in the early 1800s, the saying “His name is mud” was used in the British
Parliament to point out any member of Parliament who had disgraced himself.

name: necessity is the mother of invention
meanings: [{"name":"inventiveness or creativity stimulated by need or difficulty","examples":["He created shoes with stilts so he could reach the ceiling. Necessity is the mother of invention."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A phrase similar to this was used by people in ancient Greece, and today it
is a proverb in Italian, French, German, and some other languages. The first use of it
in English was in a British play in 1672. It's very popular all over the world, probably
because it states a universal truth. If you urgently need something that you don't have,
you will discover or invent it by using your imagination and skill. In this expression,
“mother” means the creative source that gives birth to the invention.

name: need something like a hole in the head
meanings: [{"name":"not at all; to have no need for something at all;","examples":["She already has too many shoes. She needs another pair like a hole in the head.","In the earliest days of medicine, people needed a trip to the doctor like a hole in the head.","Extra work? I need that like I need a hole in the head."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This bit of American slang comes from the 1940s. It is similar to older sayings
that used the idea of not needing something that is totally unnecessary such as “I
need this like I need a disease... a cough...a toad....” and so on. The words
“hole in the head” come from a Yiddish expression, Joch in kop.

name: needle in a haystack
meanings: [{"name":"something hard or impossible to find; anything hopeless (in a search)","examples":["Searching for your earring at the park will be like looking for a needle in a haystack.","Finding the piece of paper I need in this huge pile of documents is like looking for/trying to find a needle in a haystack","Trying to find a white glove in the snow is like looking for a needle in a haystack.","I tried to find my lost contact lens on the beach, but it was like looking for a needle in a haystack."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Since the early 1500s there have been similar expressions to describe things
difficult to find: “like finding a needle in a meadow of hay” and “like finding a pin's
head in a cartload of hay.” In the mid-1800s the expression became “needle in a
haystack.” Sayings like these are popular in other languages, too. Finding anything in
a haystack is hard, but finding a needle in one is nearly impossible.

name: nickel-and-dime
meanings: [{"name":"unimportant, small-time, trivial, petty","examples":["He said he worked for a big corporation, but it was really only a nickel-and-dime company.","The break-in at a Philadelphia parking lot wasn't a nickel-and-dime case.","It was a nickel-and-dime dispute."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In this 2oth-century African-American saying, “nickel-and-dime” refers to
two of the smallest units of United States money. Anything that's “nickel-and-dime'” is
the opposite of “big bucks.” Note: This expression can also be used as a verb meaning
to act in a cheap manner, as in “He never takes her to fancy restaurants. He always
nickels and dimes her.”

name: nitty-gritty
meanings: [{"name":"what is essential and basic; specific practical details; the basic facts of a situation","examples":["Let's get down to the nitty-gritty - how much will it cost?","When you write your report, stick to the nitty-gritty.","Stop messing around and get down to the nitty-gritty."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Grit means tiny, rough granules of stone or sand. Imagine you're trying to
examine or explain something. Instead of wasting time on unimportant subjects,
you concentrate on the grit, the small but basic and necessary points. “Nitty-gritty,”
a 20th-century African-American phrase, is a rhyming extension of the word “grit.”
“Grit” was stretched to “gritty” and was rhymed with “nitty” to make a colorful,
fun phrase.

name: no dice
meanings: [{"name":"refused; no! absolutely not!; not possible; It's not going to happen","examples":["I asked my father for a raise in my allowance, but he said, “No dice!”","When I asked about a loan, he said, “No dice.”","No. It can't be done, no dice.","He said no dice to my request.","I asked if we could go to the party, but Mom said no dice."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This 20th-century American saying must come from gambling games that
use dice, but no one is sure about the original meaning. If there are no dice, there's no
game, which should explain how this phrase came to mean “no!”

name: no skin off your nose / no skin off someone's teeth
meanings: [{"name":"used to say that someone does not care or does not have a strong opinion about something","examples":["He doesn't care if | make the football team or not. It's no skin off his nose.","Go if you like—it's no skin off my nose.","It's no skin off my nose if you don't take my advice.","She said it was no skin off her teeth if we wanted to sell the house.","It's no skin off my nose if she wants to act that way. "],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American idiom dates to the 1920s. Originally, the expression was
“no skin off my back.” “Nose” is more suitable because if you stick your nose into
somebody's business, you can get it hurt.

name: no spring chicken
meanings: [{"name":"not young anymore","examples":["Grandma can't run and play ball the way she used to. She's no spring chicken.","That actress is no spring chicken, but she does a pretty good job of playing a twenty-year-old girl.","Jane: How old do you think Robert is? Jill: Well, he's certainly no spring chicken.","At 63 she's still a spring chicken compared to the other residents.","Getting fit takes time and commitment and if you're no spring chicken, you have to take it easy along the way."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying has been around since the early 1800s, and it almost always
applied to women, although there's no reason it couldn't refer to men, too. A spring
chicken is a really young chick, like a baby. The expression began as “now past a
chicken,” and the saying today is a variation of the original.

name: get one's nose out of joint
meanings: [{"name":"angry, jealous, or annoyed at someone;  to resent that one has been slighted, neglected, or insulted","examples":["When Alice's scarf didn't win first prize in the knitting contest, her nose was out of joint for a week.","John's nose was really put out of joint when Jane was promoted and he wasn't.","You get your nose out of joint too easily about stuff like that.","Now, don't get your nose out of joint. She didn't mean it.","Come on, we are kidding. Don't get your nose out of joint."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The peculiar thing about this expression is that your nose doesn't have a
joint. People in England knew that in the 1580s when this saying
was first used, but they used it anyway. It means to be angry because your plans are
spoiled or because somebody has taken something away from you or done something
you don't like. Maybe another person got the part you wanted in the play, or stole
away your best friend, or got a higher grade on the final exam. That might hurt a lot,
almost as much as if someone had punched you in your nose and put it out of joint (if
it had a joint, which it doesn't).

name: not your cup of tea
meanings: [{"name":"not one's choice or preference; not something that someone likes or is good at","examples":["Please show me another hat. This one's not my cup of tea.","Thanks for inviting me, but ballet isn't really my cup of tea.","You three visit the museum without me. Looking at fussy old paintings is not my cup of tea.","The man JoAnn met at the party was nice, but he\nwasn't her cup of tea."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In Britain, tea has been an extremely popular drink since the mid-1700s. Even
now many English people have a cup of tea every mid-afternoon, and there are many
different flavors to choose from. In the late 1800s, people in England started saying
that something they liked was their “cup of tea.” Later, probably in the 1920s, the
expression took on its present meaning.

name: nothing new under the sun
meanings: [{"name":"everything is just a little different but pretty much the same as an earlier invention","examples":["This expensive pasta is really just macaroni. There's nothing new under the sun.","Jill: The newspaper today is shocking. Three prominent politicians have been convicted of fraud. Jane: That's not shocking. It only proves that there's nothing new under the sun."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying
can be used when you see something that's supposed to be new but is really
a variation of something old. Advertisers try to convince us that their products are
different from earlier items. But if you look closely, you may discover that in some
cases there's “nothing new under the sun.”

name: nothing to sneeze at
meanings: [{"name":"not small or unimportant; something to be taken seriously","examples":["He won the silver medal, not the gold, but that's still nothing to sneeze at.","An extra two thousand bucks a year is nothing to sneeze at.","It's not a lot of money, but it's nothing to sneeze at.","Our house isn't a mansion, but it's nothing to sneeze at."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the early 1800s people were already using this saying. Perhaps it comes
from the idea of turning your nose up at something or someone to express scorn or
contempt. Since sneezes come from your nose, something that's “not to be sneezed
at” should be treated as important and worthy.

name: nothing ventured, nothing gained
meanings: [{"name":"If you don't try to do something, you'll never accomplish it","examples":["C'mon, try making that dive. Nothing ventured, nothing gained.","Bill: Should I ask my boss for a promotion? Jane: Nothing ventured, nothing gained.","I think I'll audition for a part in that play. Nothing ventured, nothing gained."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This old proverb states a commonsense truth: If you don't make an
effort — even though you may be risking failure — you will never reach your goal.
Nothing risked or dared (“ventured”), nothing attained (“gained”).

name: nutty as a fruitcake
meanings: [{"name":"crazy or extremely strange in behavior or dress","examples":["I was convinced that Bill's uncle was as nutty as a fruitcake","Don't pay any attention to John; he's nutty as a fruitcake.","Mary's schemes for making money are nuttier than a fruitcake."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This widely used saying originated in America in the late 1920s. “Nutty” was
slang for crazy; a “nut” was an eccentric person who seemed abnormal in the way he
or she appeared or dressed. Fruitcakes are made with plenty of nuts, so if a person is
as “nutty as a fruitcake,” he or she is really strange.

name: off the beaten path (track)
meanings: [{"name":"in a remote place rarely visited by people;  not known or popular with many people","examples":["That restaurant's really off the beaten track but worth the trip.","We found a nice little Italian restaurant off the beaten track.","We wanted to find a camping site that was a little bit off the beaten path.","The store is truly located off the beaten path, in an industrial park tucked away on a quiet road."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1600s, when this idiom was first used, there were many dirt roads. As
people walked or rode over them, the paths were beaten down by feet, horses' hooves,
and wagon wheels. They looked well used. But if something was “off the beaten track”
(or “path”), then few people traveled that way. We now use this expression to describe
anything unusual, not often used, or not seen by many people.

name: off the top of your head
meanings: [{"name":"stating something quickly and without thinking hard about it; in an impromptu manner","examples":["Right off the top of his head he listed all the state capitals in alphabetical order.","\"What's the capital of USA?\" \"I don't know off the top of my head, but I could go and look it up.\"","Mary: How much do you think this car would be worth on a trade? Fred: Well, right off the top of my head, I'd say about a thousand.","Tom: What time does the morning train come in? Bill: Off the top of my head, I don't know."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the middle of the zoth century, Americans started using this expression.
Thoughts come from your brain, which is in the top of your head. So if you blurt out
facts quickly without having to think about them, then you're talking “off the top of
your head,” as if right out of your brain.

name: off-the-wall / off the wall
meanings: [{"name":"shocking; highly unusual; bizarre; odd; silly","examples":["That new talk-show host is definitely off-the-wall.","Teenagers love his off-the-wall comedy.","Why are you so off-the-wall today?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
In handball, racquetball, and squash, a player hits the ball against the wall.
When it comes off the wall, you don't always know where it's headed or what it's
going to do. Some word experts think that's how this new expression, which describes
unpredictable people or odd behavior, may have been thought up.

name: off your rocker
meanings: [{"name":"crazy; silly; foolish; not thinking correctly","examples":["My boss is off his rocker. He wants me to be at work early the morning after the dance.","Sometimes, Bob, I think you're off your rocker."],"media":[]}]
origin:
People have been using this phrase since the mid-1800s. “Rocker” in this
idiom refers to a rocking chair, and there are at least two theories about how being
“off your rocker” came to mean “crazy.” If you fell off your rocking chair, it was a sign
of being mentally unstable. “Rockers” are also the two curved pieces upon which the
chair rocks. A rocking chair with a missing rocker moves strangely, like a person whose
thinking is mixed-up. Other expressions with similar meanings are “off your nut” and
“off your trolley.”

name: old hat
meanings: [{"name":"out-of-date; not new; too familiar; uninteresting","examples":["Let's try a new place for our next vacation. Dooley's Dude Ranch is so old hat.","Hardly anybody uses typewriters anymore. That's just old hat.","He may be old hat among the trendy younger generation, but his shows draw more viewers than any other comedian."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when this phrase became popular,
men and women wore hats much more than they do today. Most people wanted to
keep up with the latest styles, and an old hat was no longer fashionable.

name: old wives' tale
meanings: [{"name":" superstition; a belief or practice not based on fact","examples":["Wearing garlic around your neck won't scare off evil. That's just an old wives' tale.","The old wives' tale about the full moon causing people to act crazy.","You really don't believe that stuff about starving a cold do you? It's just an old wives' tale."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This idiom has a long history. Plato, a famous Greek philosopher who lived
around 300 B.C., first used this phrase. In the 1300s it appeared in English. Then
Erasmus, a Dutch scholar, put it in his writings in the 1500s. The “old wives” in this
idiom refer to people during the olden days who gave advice based on superstitions.
Some examples of these “tales” are “feed a cold and starve a fever,” “don't touch a
frog or you'll get warts,” and “it's bad luck to walk under a ladder.”

name: on a shoestring
meanings: [{"name":"on a strict budget; with or using very little money","examples":["They tried to start a school band on a shoestring.","She started her business on a small/tight/shoestring budget and could not afford to overspend.","The film was made on a shoestring."],"media":[]}]
origin:
No one today is quite sure about the origin of this idiom, although we know
it started in America in the late 1800s. A “shoestring” is what we call a shoelace today.
Perhaps the writer who first used this expression was comparing a tiny amount of
money to a piece of string like a shoelace.

name: on cloud nine
meanings: [{"name":"blissfully happy; joyous","examples":["Liz is on cloud nine since being named Junior Scientist of the Year.","\"Was Helen pleased about getting that job?\" \"Pleased? She was on cloud nine!\"","When I got my promotion, I was on cloud nine. ","When the check came, I was on cloud nine for days."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Though this saying comes from the late 19th century, nine has been a
mystical number for thousands of years, back to the time of the ancient Greeks. The
saying originally was “on cloud seven,” probably coming from “seventh heaven,”
the highest of the heavens in Jewish religious literature. Nine was then substituted,
perhaps because it is a sacred Christian number. This is because three is a trinity and
represents perfect unity, and nine is a trinity of trinities (3 x 3). Other idioms that
express great joy also suggest being up high: “on top of the world”, “walking on air”, and so on.

name: on pins and needles
meanings: [{"name":"waiting anxiously for something; extremely nervous","examples":["I was on pins and needles until I got the phone call that the plane had landed safely.","Don't keep Mom on pins and needles – give her a call.","I've been on pins and needles all day, waiting for you to call with the news."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying was first used in the late 1800s. When you're waiting nervously
for something to happen, you sometimes feel as if you can't sit still — like needles or
pins are sticking you. A writer once said it was like being “on pins and needles,” and
the phrase stuck. Other expressions of nervousness are “butterflies in the stomach” and “on tenterhooks”

name: on someone's case
meanings: [{"name":"to nag, find fault with, badger or scold someone constantly about his or her business, situation, circumstances","examples":["His wife was on his case because he started smoking again.","Her brother is always on her case about the clothes she wears.","I just don't want him getting on my case for being late for work.","I'll get on Tom's case about being late so much.","I'm sorry, I won't get on your case anymore."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In this popular African-American idiom, “case” means your business or
current situation in life. You often hear or read this expression either as a complaint
that someone is on your case about something, or as a demand that someone get off
your case about something.

name: on tenterhooks
meanings: [{"name":"uncertain, anxious, very tense; in painful suspense about how something will turn out","examples":["Tommy waited on tenterhooks to see if he would win the award.","We were on tenterhooks all morning waiting for the phone to ring.","Don't keep me on tenterhooks! Tell me your news! ","We were all kept on tenterhooks waiting to find out what happened."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the mid-1700s, when this saying originated, a tenter was a frame for
stretching newly woven cloth. The “tenterhook” was a hook or bent nail that held
the cloth to the tenter. At that time a person who was worried sick not knowing the
outcome of a situation was said to be “on tenters,” meaning that their emotions were
stretched out tensely. Later the phrase became “on tenterhooks,” which expressed
even sharper and more intense feeling.

name: on the ball
meanings: [{"name":"alert; effective; skillful; knowledgeable","examples":["Mr. Smith hired me because he thinks I'm really on the ball.","if the teacher has something on the ball, the pupils won't squirm much.","I didn't sleep well last night and I'm not really on the ball today.","We need someone who's really on the ball to answer questions from the press."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying originated with British football — what we call soccer. It could
also be said that a person is “on top of things.” Also, in the all-American sport of
baseball, a pitcher who was able to get something “on the ball” (like great speed)
would be more likely to win the game. As ball games, including basketball, became
more popular, so did this expression.

name: on the cuff
meanings: [{"name":"on credit; to be paid later","examples":["Cosmo couldn't pay his bill, so he asked the owner to put it on the cuff.","I'll take two of those, and please put them on the cuff.","I'm sorry, Tom. We can't put anything more on the cuff."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression probably came from the days when bartenders in old saloons
wore stiff cuffs that detached from the end of their shirtsleeves. When customers
wanted to pay for their drinks at a later date, the bartender often wrote the charges
down on his cuffs. There is another, similar idiom, “off the cuff,” that has a totally
different meaning: to speak about or do something freely without thinking about
it first.

name: on the double
meanings: [{"name":"very quickly; right away; at a fast pace; twice as fast as normal","examples":["The coach told the players to get onto the field on the double.","Get over here right now—on the double! ","She wants to see you in her office on the double."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This is an old army command. When the person in charge wanted the soldiers
to march twice as fast as normal, he'd holler, “On the double!” which meant to double
the speed. Today, anyone can use this expression when he or she wants someone to
hurry up.

name: on the fence
meanings: [{"name":"neutral; undecided; not choosing one way or the other","examples":["Are you for or against the new honor code, or are you still on the fence?","Many consumers are still on the fence, waiting for a less expensive computer to come along.","Todd's still sitting on the fence, trying to decide which school he wants to go to.","Ann is on the fence about going to Mexico.","I wouldn't be on the fence. I'd love to go."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This popular expression from the early 1800s makes you think of a person
actually sitting on a fence, body right in the middle, not completely on one side or the
other, with one leg dangling over each side. In the same way, if a person straddles an
issue without committing himself or herself, that's a person “on the fence.”

name: on the fly
meanings: [{"name":"in a hurry and often without preparation; HASTILY, SPONTANEOUSLY; simultaneously with another task","examples":["This new rule seems to have been created on the fly.","I'll try to capture the data on the fly.","Please try to buy some aspirin somewhere on the fly today.","He had written a program that could translate from Japanese on the fly."],"media":[]}]
origin: If you do something on the fly, you do it quickly, often while you are doing something else, without preparing and without thinking too much about how it should be done

name: on the fritz / on the blink
meanings: [{"name":"broken; out of order; not working; not working correctly","examples":["We can't watch the game at my house because my TV is on the fritz.","The fridge is on the fritz.","This vacuum cleaner is on the fritz. Let's get it fixed.","How long has it been on the blink?","The clock in the office has been on the blink for\nmonths. I don't think they'll ever get it fixed."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Though this expression is a recent one (the early 1900s), nobody today is quite
sure how it got started. One word expert gave the following possible explanation.
During World War I, a degrading term for a German soldier was “Fritz,” a common
German name (short for Friedrich). Something not working or ruined could be
compared to the defeated Germans.

name: on the horns of a dilemma
meanings: [{"name":"having to choose between two undesirable courses of action or unpleasant things","examples":["Mary found herself on the horns of a dilemma. She didn't know which to choose.","I make up my mind easily. I'm not on the horns of a  dilemma very often."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A bull can be a fierce animal, and nobody wants to be stuck on the sharp
points of a bull's horns. But you feel that you're in that position if you are forced
to decide between two possibly dangerous choices. A similar saying was used by
people in the Middle Ages and by the Dutch scholar Erasmus around the year 1500.
In medieval times a “dilemma” was a way of arguing in which one of two statements
must be proved to be true.

name: on the hot seat (in the hot seat)
meanings: [{"name":"in a  difficult or uncomfortable position and subject to a lot of Unpe questions and personal attacks","examples":["Fran was caught eating a candy bar at the weight loss class — Now she's really on the hot seat.","When the company ran into financial trouble, it was the accountant who found herself in the hot seat.","I was really in the hot seat for a while.","Now that John is on the hot seat, no one is paying any attention to what I do."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The “hot seat” in this expression refers to the electric chair. But you can be
on — or in — the hot seat in a freezing cold room if you've been accused of doing
something bad, or you've been caught in an embarrassing situation and people are
questioning and criticizing you.

name: on the rocks
meanings: [{"name":"financially ruined or wrecked; near disaster; finished","examples":["I need a loan because my dog-walking business is on the rocks.","I think their marriage is on the rocks.","That bank is on the rocks. Don't put your money in it.","My finances are on the rocks just now."],"media":[]}]
origin:
An unfortunate ship that has run aground and is on the rocks will eventually
sink. In the 1800s the phrase “on the rocks” (meaning headed for disaster) was
expanded to describe many areas of life, not just ships at sea. Note: There's also a
totally different meaning for this saying. A person can order a drink “on the rocks.” In
this case, “rocks” means ice cubes.

name: on the ropes
meanings: [{"name":"almost failing; on the verge of collapse; nearly ruined","examples":["Last summer, my ice cream store did a lot of business, but now, in the middle of winter, it's on the ropes.","For a while, our business was on the ropes."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This phrase was first used in the 1800s and referred to boxers who were almost
knocked out. They hung onto the ropes around the boxing ring so they wouldn't
totally collapse. Later the saying was expanded to include any person, business, or
situation that was in great difficulty or nearly ruined.

name: on the spur of the moment
meanings: [{"name":"suddenly; acting without thinking about it first, impulsively","examples":["On the spur of the moment, I rode my bike fifteen miles for a slice of my favorite pecan pie.","We hadn't planned to go away - it was one of those spur-of-the-moment decisions.","We just jumped in a car on the spur of the moment and drove to the seaside.","On the spur of the moment, we decided to go to the beach.","I had to leave town on the spur of the moment."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the early 1800s, when this idiom was first being used, many people rode
horses to get where they were going. Riders often wore short, spiked wheels, called
spurs, on the heels of their boots. When they wanted to urge a horse to go faster, they
pressed the spurs against its body. If an opportunity is like a spur that gets a person
to do something impulsively without waiting, you can easily see how “on the spur of
the moment” originated. Now, of course, it relates to any sudden decision to act and
has nothing to do with horses.

name: on the tip of your tongue
meanings: [{"name":"temporarily forgotten but at the point where one can almost say it; ready to say something but unable to remember it precisely","examples":["The name of the song was on the tip of her tongue, but Jeannie couldn't remember it fast enough to win the contest.","I know her - her name is on the tip of my tongue, but it won't come to me.","I have his name right on the tip of my tongue. I'll think of it in a second.","John had the answer on the tip of his tongue, but Anne said it first."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying was first used in a British novel (Moll Flanders by Daniel Defoe)
in the early 1700s, and it became very popular by the mid-1800s. Where do spoken
words come from? First from your brain, then to your mouth, and just before they
emerge from your lips they pass over the tip of your tongue. Sometimes, when you just
can't remember something like a name, place, or date but you know you know it, and
you can almost utter it, you say that the words are stuck “on (or ‘at') the tip of your
tongue.” They can't get through your lips to the waiting world.

name: on the warpath
meanings: [{"name":"in a very angry mood; infuriated","examples":["Mr. Ozawa is on the warpath because his car broke down again.","The boss is on the warpath today because the project is behind schedule.","I told my friends to watch out because my mother was on the warpath.","Her supporters went on the warpath in response to her opponent's accusations."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This phrase is from the mid-1800s and originally referred to Native Americans
who were often at war with settlers or other nations about land rights. The expression
meant “going to war.” By the end of the 19th century, the meaning had grown to mean
being in a rage about something.

name: on top of the world
meanings: [{"name":"feeling extremely happy; glorious; ecstatic","examples":["She was feeling on top of the world after winning the tennis tournament.","Since he got a new job, he's on top of the world."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Many writers have used this famous expression since the early 1900s with the
verb “sitting.” “Down” has always suggested downhearted feelings such as sadness
and depression (see “down in the dumps,”). But being “up” or “on top” has
meant emotions such as delight and joy (see “walking on air,” and “on
cloud nine,”). “The world” represents everything, such as your life, your job,
and your family. So, if you're sitting “on top of the world,” you're overjoyed because
of good health, success, and so on.

name: once in a blue moon
meanings: [{"name":"almost never; very seldom; hardly ever","examples":["The teacher is tough, but once in a blue moon she doesn't give us homework.","My sister lives in Alaska, so I only see her once in a blue moon.","Once in a blue moon he'd call, but for months at a time we heard nothing.","Once in a blue moon, I buy a fashion magazine, just to see what people are wearing."],"media":[]}]
origin:
On some nights when the bright part of the moon is a crescent, some people
say the other part has a bluish color to it. This “blue moon” is rare. A similar expression
was first used in the early 1500s and has been popular ever since.

name: one good turn deserves another
meanings: [{"name":"If someone does you a favor, you should do a favor for that person in return","examples":["I helped Lin fix her flat tire, and she gave mea ride. One good turn deserves another.","Jill: Thanks for the ride. Jane: It's the least I can do after you helped me wash the car last week. One good turn deserves another.","Child: I don't want to help Grandma go shopping. Father: But she helped you with your homework yesterday. And one good turn deserves another."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This is an adage, a general truth that people have come to accept over many
years. It dates as far back as the early 1400s and means that if you receive help from
someone, it's only fair and proper that you help that person in return. The meaning of
“turn” here is a deed or action. The same idea, but in a negative sense, appears in the
idiom “eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth”

name: one-horse town
meanings: [{"name":"a place with few comforts and activities; a dull rural town","examples":["They got fed up with the noisy, crowded city, so they moved to a one-horse town out West.","I refuse to spend a whole week in that one- horse town! ","I grew up in a one-horse town, and I liked it very much."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression was first used in the 1850s when there were more horses than
people in some American towns. If a town had only one horse, it must have been really
small, with very little happening. This exaggerated saying became popular even
though it is insulting. Now it can describe any business or project that's considered
rather minor or dull.

name: one-track mind
meanings: [{"name":"always thinking about only one subject","examples":["Paul has a one-track mind. All he ever thinks about is football, football, football.","Bob has a one-track mind. He can only talk about tennis."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Most railroads have at least two tracks so trains can go in different directions
without crashing into one another. However, on a single-track railroad line, train
traffic can move in only one direction at a time.

name: open a can of worms
meanings: [{"name":"to cause trouble; to set unpleasant events in motion; to cause set of problems, an array of difficulties.","examples":["If you mention my report card to my mother, you'll open a can of worms.","Our boss is reluctant to change the policy now because she doesn't want to open a can of worms."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A can of worms might be fine to open if you are by the banks of a river on a
summer's day getting ready to fish. But you wouldn't want to open it anywhere else;
the situation might cause a lot of trouble! In this expression, “worms” are difficult or
delicate issues. A related idiom is “let sleeping dogs lie”

name: other side of the coin
meanings: [{"name":"a different way of looking at or thinking about a situation","examples":["The new building is wonderful, but on the other side of the coin, it cost $10 million.","I like having a white car, but the other side of the coin is that it soon gets dirty.","The economy is improving, but the other side of the coin is that inflation is becoming a bigger problem."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This metaphor has been around since the beginning of the zoth century and
is widely used. Every coin has two sides, but you can see only one side at a time. Like a
coin, every issue has more than one side to it. You have to know the “other side of the
coin” to get the full story.

name: out in left field
meanings: [{"name":"unusual; crazy; totally wrong; eccentric","examples":["Mary's suggestion, a “dress as your favorite vegetable” party, was way out in left field.","I wouldn't vote for him – his ideas are way out in left field.","People need to feel free to speak up and share new ideas, even if those ideas are coming from way out in left field.","Sally is a lot of fun, but she's sort of out in left field. ","What a strange idea. It's really out in left field."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Baseball became a popular sport in the United States in the 2oth century,
and this expression is based on one of the field positions. Left field is a long way
from home plate and is one of the farthest outfield positions to which fewer balls are
hit. If home plate is called “home” because it's a safe place where a player starts out
from and hopes to come back to, then “left field” means something far from what's
considered normal. It's really weird!

name: out in the boondocks / in the boonies
meanings: [{"name":"in remote places; in rural regions; in sparsely populated areas","examples":["She lives way out in the boondocks.","Penny lives out in the boonies with her parents."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Tagalogs are native Filipinos who live in or near Manila, the capital city of
the Philippines. In the Tagalog language, bundok means “mountain.” The United
States military forces stationed in the area of the Philippines in the first half of the
2oth century extended the meaning of the word from mountain to any place that is
far from heavily populated centers. Today, the saying is sometimes shortened to “in
the boonies.”

name: out like a light / out cold
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. unconscious (often suddenly)","examples":["I fell and hit my head. I was out cold for about a minute.","Tom fainted! He's out like a light! ","Jane: That kid looks passed out, Kate.\nKate: Yeah, he's out cold."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. intoxicated","examples":["I'm sorry, but you've been out cold for ten hours and we need to talk.","I laced it with sleeping pills. He's gonna be out like a light in two minutes.","He's not sleeping. He's out cold. Why did you give him sleeping pills?"],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. sound asleep; fast asleep","examples":["As soon as my head hit the pillow, I was out like a light.","After a few minutes of tossing and turning, she was out like a light.","I just tucked her in, and she is out like a light."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In America in the 20th century, when the wonders of electricity spread across
the land, people could turn on and shut off lights with just a flick of a switch. By the
middle of the century, “out like a light” was a way of saying that a person had fallen
asleep very quickly or had been knocked out or drugged into unconsciousness in a
matter of seconds.

name: out of here
meanings: [{"name":"good-bye; I'm going; I'm leaving","examples":["Just one more slice of cake and I'm out of here. ","It's five o'clock, so I'm out of here.","In three minutes I'm outa here","I'm out of here. Bye."],"media":[]}]
origin: This catchy, modern African-American saying means just what it says.

name: out of sight, out of mind
meanings: [{"name":"if you don't see someone or something for a long time, you'll eventually stop thinking about someone or somethng","examples":["Ever since I moved, none of my old friends have gotten in touch with me. It's out of sight, out of mind with them, evidently.","My electric bill somehow got moved to the bottom of the stack on my desk, and I forgot all about paying it. Out of sight, out of mind.","Problems in remote places can be out of sight, out of mind for many people."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Homer, an ancient Greek poet, used this proverb in his famous epic The
Odyssey in about 850 B.c. A similar saying was popular in English as early as the
1200s. The image is clear: What is missing from your view will soon be missing from
your thoughts. The expression “absence makes the heart grow fonder” states the
opposite idea.

name: out of the blue / out of the clear blue sky
meanings: [{"name":"suddenly and without any warning; totally unexpectedly","examples":["The job offer came out of the blue.","One day, out of the blue, she announced that she was leaving.","Then, out of a clear blue sky, he told me he was leaving.","My sister Mary appeared on my doorstep out of the blue, after years with no word from her."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This late 19th-century expression is related to another saying, “a bolt from
the blue”. A bolt of lightning or sudden shower from a clear blue sky
would be unexpected. Sometimes this idiom is shortened to “out of the blue.”

name: out of the frying pan and into the fire
meanings: [{"name":"from a bad or difficult situation to one that is even worse","examples":["First, you were late. Now, you spilled glue all over the teacher's desk. You've jumped out of the frying pan and into the fire.","Many kids who try to run away from unhappy homes discover that they've jumped out of the frying pan into the fire when they try to live on their own."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This proverb, popular in many languages, was used in English in the early
1500s. A piece of food being fried in a pan is hot enough, but falling out of the frying
pan and into the fire is even worse!

name: out of the mouths of babes
meanings: [{"name":"children can unexpectedly say very intelligent things","examples":["The four-year-old said, “Aunt Roslyn, your dress is as pretty as a garden.” Out of the mouths of babes, you know.","Child: Don't eat so much candy, Mommy. Candy is bad for your teeth. Mother: Out of the mouths of babes."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The full version of this saying is something like “out of the mouths of babes
come smart ideas,” but you don't have to say the whole thing for people to get the
idea.

name: out of the woods
meanings: [{"name":"safe from trouble or danger","examples":["The doctor says Bruce's condition has improved slightly, but he's not out of the woods yet.","When the patient got out of the woods, everyone relaxed."],"media":[]}]
origin:
For centuries, at least back to ancient Roman times, people thought of the
woods as a dark, mysterious, possibly dangerous place. If you were stuck in the
woods, you could be in trouble. But if you got “out of the woods,” you were safe.
This expression can be used to mean being past any kind of critical phase in a risky
situation or getting free of danger or trouble.

name: out on a limb
meanings: [{"name":"taking a chance; in a dangerous position from which it is hard to withdraw or change; at risk","examples":["She's going out on a limb in criticizing her own party leadership.","The mayor went out on a limb when he opposed the new sports center.","By speaking up against her boss, she is putting herself\nout on a limb."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This American saying dates from the late 1800s, when hunting animals in the
woods was a more common activity than it is today. It probably referred to a hunted
animal that climbed a tree and got itself stranded out on a limb where it could easily
be shot. Later the idiom grew to describe any person who takes a risk that might lead
to trouble.

name: over a barrel
meanings: [{"name":"helpless; in someone's power; at a disadvantage; out of one's control; in a dilemma","examples":["Jack is really over a barrel since he lost the only copy of the book he needed for his report.","He got me over a barrel, and I had to do what he said.","Ann will do exactly what I say. I've got her over a barrel.","He saw me cash my\npaycheck and then asked me for a loan. I could not refuse. He had me\nover a barrel."],"media":[]}]
origin:
There are a couple of possible explanations for this idiom. One is that a person
rescued from drowning was often laid over a barrel to help empty his or her lungs of
water. The other is that a person about to be flogged, or whipped for a crime, was often
tied over a barrel to hold him down.

name: over the hill
meanings: [{"name":"past one's prime; unable to function as one used to; too old","examples":["A ninety-two-year-old man finished the marathon and proved he wasn't over the hill yet.","I don't think of myself as being over the hill yet.","You're only fifty! You're not over-the-hill yet.","Some people seem over-the-hill at thirty."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Since at least the middle of the 2oth century, writers have made comparisons
between living your life and climbing a hill or mountain. When you're young and full
of energy, you climb up the hill and head for the top. After that, as you come upon
middle age and old age, your body slows and you go down the hill, no longer able
to do all the things you could do before. You're “over (the top of) the hill.” But some
old-timers would say, “I'd rather be over the hill than under it.”

name: over your head
meanings:
[{"name":"too difficult for someone to understand; beyond one's capability","examples":["Most of that lecture was over my head.","Calculus is very hard for me. I'm in over my head.","Tim can't compete with these people. They are much
more capable in their field than he is. He's in way
over his head.","Be careful how much work you take on. Don't
promise to do more than you can handle. Don't get in
over your head."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This widely used expression has two meanings. One is that if you invest more
money than you can afford in a risky business venture, then you're in “over your
head” and probably on the road to financial disaster. In this case, you should try to
“keep your head above water”. The other meaning is that if a person
tells a joke or makes a remark that you don't understand, it goes “over your head”
rather than into your brain.

name: par for the course
meanings: [{"name":"what should be expected because of past experience; typical; not unusual","examples":["Mr. Humdinger gave me a “C.” The way he's been grading lately, that's about par for the course.","It's par for the course that she's late to the meeting.","The school budget is going to be cut again this year, but then that's par for the course.","So he went off and left you? Well that's about par for the course. He's no friend.","I worked for days on this proposal, but it was rejected. That's par for the course around here."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1920s this expression, which came from golf, was broadened to include
other activities in life. In golf, “par” is the number of golf strokes it usually takes for
a golf expert to play a course. That's how “par for the course” came to mean a typical
or expected result. It usually has a slightly negative tone to it: “It took me three hours
to get home in this blizzard, about par for the course.” Related expressions are “up to
par” (satisfactory) and “below par” (unsatisfactory).

name: pass the buck
meanings: [{"name":"to shift a responsibility to someone else; to blame someone or make them responsible for a problem that you should deal with","examples":["Stop trying to pass the buck and take responsibility for what you did.","She's always trying to pass the buck and I'm sick of it!","Don't try to pass the buck - this is your responsibility, not mine.","Don't try to pass the buck! It's your fault, and everybody knows it.","Some people try to pass the buck whenever they can."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In a 19th-century American poker game, “buck” was a piece of buckshot
(a shotgun pellet) or a pocketknife with a buckhorn handle. It was passed to you if
you were the next dealer. By 1900, “passing the buck” meant shifting responsibility
for something to another person. In 1949 President Harry Truman put a sign on his
desk that read “The Buck Stops Here.” That meant that he was accepting personal
responsibility for all decisions that needed to be made and all actions that needed to
be taken. He wasn't going to direct his problems to anybody else.

name: pass the hat
meanings: [{"name":"to collect donations of money from people.; to beg","examples":["I need money for the amusement park. I may just have to pass the hat.","They're passing the hat around the company to get money for charity.","They passed the hat for families affected by the disaster","Jerry passed the hat around to all the other workers.","He passed around the hat to everyone."],"media":[]}]
origin:
At one time, hats were passed around at entertainment events by people
asking for money. The custom might have originated with street minstrels who
entertained people and then requested payment. And a hat is an excellent container
in which to collect money. A related expression is “hat in hand”

name: pay through the nose
meanings: [{"name":"to pay too much money for something; to pay exorbitantly or dearly","examples":["In that restaurant, you'll pay through the nose for a meal.","I found the perfect dress, but I had to pay through the nose for it.","We paid through the nose to get the car fixed.","Why should you pay through the nose?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Here's an idiom from the 1600s. “Rhino” was once a slang word for money,
but originally it was the Greek word for nose. The two words are similar in sound and
their meanings might have come together to make this expression. Another possibility
comes from Danish authorities charging Irish people a poll tax in the 9th century and
cutting off or slitting the noses of those who failed to pay their taxes. There's also
a gambling origin tied to “bleeding” a player — duping him to lose all his money.
Now, if you “pay through the nose,” you'd be paying an extremely expensive price for
something. A related body part idiom is “pay an arm and a leg.”

name: pen is mightier than the sword
meanings: [{"name":"writing is more powerful than fighting; Eloquent writing persuades people better than military force","examples":["I'd rather be a writer than a general because the pen is mightier than the sword.","Believing that the pen is mightier than the sword, the rebels began publishing an underground newspaper.","Alan: Why do you want to become a journalist? Bill: The pen is mightier than the sword."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This famous saying was first used in the 1600s. It started out as “the pen is
worse than the sword.” A pen and a sword have certain characteristics in common.
Both are thin, pointed, and handheld. But history has shown that writers and statesmen
using their pens have often had a greater effect on the course of events than military
leaders and conquerors wielding swords. Think of the Magna Carta, the Declaration of
Independence, and other important writings that have changed the course of history
more than wars have.

name: penny for your thoughts
meanings: [{"name":"What are you thinking? Tell me what is on your mind.","examples":["You seem so serious. A penny for your thoughts.","\"A penny for your thoughts?\" \"Oh, I'm just thinking about what I want to do over the weekend.\"","You haven't said very much – a penny for your thoughts.","Noticing that Janet looked pensive, Bill said, “A penny for your thoughts!”","Noticing that Janet looked pensive, Bill said, “A penny for your thoughts!”","You seem very pleased with yourself today. A penny for your thoughts!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Early in the 1500s, when people first started using this expression, a penny
was worth more than it is today. So if you offered a penny to a person who was either
thinking or daydreaming, you'd be offering a lot to know what was going on in his
or her mind.

name: penny-wise and pound-foolish
meanings: [{"name":"careful in small matters but careless about important things; saving small amounts of money while wasting large amounts","examples":["That was penny-wise and pound-foolish. You saved a dollar in car fare when you walked all the way home, but now you need new sneakers.","The plans to cut funding are penny-wise and pound-foolish.","Sam: If we drive to six different grocery stores, we'll get the best bargains on everything we buy. Alan: But with gasoline so expensive, that's penny-wise and pound-foolish."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This was a well-known proverb by the early 1600s in England, where a
pound is a unit of money. A penny was always worth much less than a pound. So the
expression meant you were smart about things that were small and careless about
things that were big.

name: people who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones
meanings: [{"name":"you should not criticize others if you are just as bad as they are","examples":["He complained about her driving, but he's already had two accidents. People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.","Jill: Richard sure was drinking a lot at the office party. Jane: I noticed you had quite a few cocktails yourself. People who\nlive in glass houses shouldn't throw stones."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying became popular in the 1300s during the time of the English poet
Geoffrey Chaucer, who used it in one of his books. If you lived in a glass house, you'd
better hope that no one would throw stones at it! You should not judge other people if
you have the same faults as they do.

name: pie in the sky
meanings: [{"name":"something not possible; an unrealistic hope","examples":["Martha thinks that if she goes to Washington, she'll meet the president and tell him her ideas. What a pie~in-the-sky idea!","Don't hold out for pie in the sky. Get realistic.","What these pie-in-the-sky people really want is money.","Get rid of your pie-in-the-sky ideas!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
In 1906 an American union organizer wrote a song called “The Preacher and
the Slave” that had the words:
Work and pray,
Live on the hay,
You'll get a pie in the sky when you die!
(That's a lie.)
“Pie” meant decent working conditions and good wages. Union workers wanted those
things while they were alive, not after they died. The song was popular, and the phrase
“pie in the sky” came to mean promised pleasures that probably won't come true, or
rewards that are given after you die.

name: piece of cake
meanings: [{"name":"something easily done; CINCH, BREEZE","examples":["Don't worry. Skateboarding down this hill is a piece of cake.","The exam was a piece of cake.","For him, taking tests is a piece of cake.","Glad to help. It was a piece of cake.","Rescuing frightened cats is my specialty. Piece of cake!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This phrase could have come from an African-American dance contest in the
mid-19th century. Contestants made up complex strutting movements, usually with
high steps, and the winner won a cake. The dance was called the cakewalk, and the
expression “that takes the cake” came from it. A related expression is “easy as pie”

name: play both ends (against the middle)
meanings: [{"name":"to try to get opposing people or groups to fight or disagree so that you will get an advantage from the situation","examples":["Evan got the other two candidates to call each other names, and he got elected. How's that for playing both ends against the middle.","If you try to play both ends, you're likely to get in trouble with both sides."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In the 1800s there was a popular card game in America called faro, in which
the dealer allowed a double bet by a player. The phrase was later applied to dishonestly using two opposing sides for one's selfish purposes.

name: play cat and mouse
meanings: [{"name":"to tease or fool someone; to be coy and evasive with someone.","examples":["She plays cat and mouse with her little brother, pretending to hand him a lollipop, then taking it away when he reaches for it.","The governor has been playing (a game of) cat and mouse with the media, refusing to say definitely whether he will run for reelection.","I know what you are up to. Don't play cat and mouse with me!","I wish that they wouldn't play cat and mouse with me!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
If you're in a room with both a cat and a mouse, you might observe the way
the sneaky cat treats the poor little rodent. The cat tricks the mouse into thinking
it's safe, then catches it, lets it go, then catches it again. It's a game of capture and
release. Today, anyone who toys with a helpless victim is playing “cat and mouse”
with him or her. This expression became popular in 1913 in England when suffragettes
(women fighting for the right to vote) were arrested for their civil disobedience and
went on hunger strikes in jail. Parliament passed a law releasing prisoners who refused
to eat. When a suffragette got healthy, she was arrested again. People called the law
the “Cat and Mouse Act.”

name: play fast and loose
meanings: [{"name":"to behave in a clever and dishonest way; to act carelessly, thoughtlessly, and irresponsibly","examples":["You told Linda you'd help her, but then you didn't show up. You shouldn't play fast and loose with your friends.","I'm tired of your playing fast and loose with me. Leave me alone.","Bob got fired for playing fast and loose with the company's money."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying might have come from a 14th-century game in which tricksters
cheated people at country fairs by challenging them to perform impossible tricks
and then taking their money when they couldn't. The game involved loops in a piece
of string or folds in a belt. In the late 1500s William Shakespeare used this phrase in
some of his plays. People who “play fast and loose” promise to do one thing and then
do another.

name: play it by ear
meanings: [{"name":"to figure out what you're going to do as you go along instead of beforehand; to do something without special preparation","examples":["The toga costumes aren't ready, and the performance is tonight, so we'll just have to play it by ear. Use the bedsheets for togas because the show must go on.","If we go into the meeting unprepared, we'll have to play everything by ear.","He never prepared his presentations. He always played things by ear."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Ever since the 1600s people have been using this expression to mean playing
a song by remembering the melody, not by reading the sheet music. You hear the song
in your head, and you don't need to look at the notes to perform it. But 300 years later,
the saying took on an additional meaning: to improvise what to do without planning
ahead. Suppose you decide to go to a new place without learning about it. Then you
have to “play it by ear” when you get there and decide where you're going to stay and
what you're going to do without knowing what to expect in advance. In emergency
situations, people often have to “play it by ear.”

name: play second fiddle (to someone)
meanings: [{"name":"to be in a subordinate position to someone.; to be in an inferior position","examples":["I'm not prepared to play second fiddle to Christina any more - I'm looking for another job!","I'm tired of playing second fiddle to John.","I'm better trained than he, and I have more experience. I shouldn't always play second fiddle."],"media":[]}]
origin:
In an orchestra, there are the roles of first violin (or fiddle) and second fiddle.
The person who plays “first violin” is supposed to be the most important musician
in an orchestra. So, since at least the middle 1700s, when this saying was first used,
“playing second fiddle” has meant to act the smaller part or be in a lower position
rather than to be the leader.

name: play with fire
meanings: [{"name":"to do something risky or dangerous; to do something that could cause you trouble later","examples":["Threatening the bully in the neighborhood is really playing with fire.","You're playing with fire if you try to cheat on the test.","Be careful with that knife! You are playing with fire! ","If you mess with Max, you are S playing with fire."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression has been commonly used for hundreds of years, at least since
the late 1500s. The metaphor is clear: If you're being irresponsible about something
dangerous and inviting disaster, it's like playing with fire. You're taking a big risk.

name: point of no return
meanings: [{"name":"a critical point at which turning back or reversal is not possible","examples":["We can't cancel the show now. We've reserved the theater and sold tickets. We've reached the point of no return.","Scientists fear that global warming has gone beyond the point of no return.","Once the contract is signed, we've reached the point of no return."],"media":[]}]
origin:
During World War II, pilots knew that they had only enough fuel to fly a
certain number of miles. The point when they would reach the crucial mark was called
the point of no return. If they continued to fly on, they would not have enough fuel to return to their home base.

name: pot calling the kettle black
meanings: [{"name":"You should not criticize someone for a fault that you have too.","examples":["Elliott accused me of being selfish. Talk about the pot calling the kettle black!","Bill told Barbara she was sloppy, but Bill never cleans up after himself, either. That's the pot calling the kettle black.","My sister says I dress funny, but if you've seen some of the clothes she wears, you know it's a case of the pot calling the kettle black."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The theory about the origin of this idiom goes back to the early 1600s. It
suggests that a pot and a kettle both got black from standing too long over an open
fire. The pot couldn't fault the kettle for being blackened by smoke because the pot
was the same color. In the same way, you can't criticize a person for something if the
fault is one of yours, too. A similar idea is contained in the saying “People who live in
glass houses shouldn't throw stones”

name: pour oil on troubled waters
meanings: [{"name":"to try to make peace between people who are arguing","examples":["My brothers were having a terrible fight in the car, but my mother poured oil on troubled waters by saying they were both right.","My husband's always arguing with my father, and I'm the one who has to pour oil on troubled waters."," Don can calm things down. He's good at pouring oil on troubled waters.","Alice is very good at pouring oil on troubled water."],"media":[]}]
origin:
As early as A.D. 731 this expression referred to the belief that if you poured
oil on rough, stormy ocean waves, it would calm them. Now it means to smooth over a
stormy or disturbed situation of any kind on land or sea.

name: power behind the throne
meanings: [{"name":"the person who actually controls the person who is apparently in charge","examples":["The president's wife had so much influence on him that people knew she was the real power behind the throne.","Mr. Smith appears to run the shop, but his brother is the power behind the throne.","They say that the vice president is the power behind the throne."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying was being used in England by the 1770s. “Throne” does not
always stand for a royal position. It could mean the office of any leader. If someone
else is telling the leader what to do, he or she could be called the “power behind
the throne.”

name: proof of the pudding is in the eating
meanings: [{"name":"success is measured by the final result; You don't know the quality of something until you have tried it or experienced it.","examples":["The car looks gorgeous, but the only way to know how it runs is to test-drive it. The proof of the pudding is in the eating.","Theory says that this material will produce a superior widget, but the proof of the pudding is in the eating."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This proverb has been enormously popular since at least the 1600s, especially
with British writers. The only way to know if a pudding is good and has turned out
right is to taste it.

name: pull a fast one
meanings: [{"name":"to deceive; to mastermind a trick or deception; ","examples":["My sister pulled a fast one. She asked me to hold the brush. Then she left, and I had to finish painting the room.","You paid too much - I think he pulled a fast one on you.","I don't think he was being truthful – I think he was just trying to pull a fast one.","She was pulling a fast one when she said she had a headache and went home.","Don't try to pull a fast one with me! I know what you're doing."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression originated in the English sport of cricket and meant to bowl
a fast ball. It probably became popular in the United States either in reference to a
fast shuffle of cards or to the fastball in baseball, which usually comes when you're
not expecting it.

name: pull a rabbit out of a hat
meanings: [{"name":"to produce something that is needed as if by magic; to unexpectedly find a solution to a problem","examples":["We were very hungry, and suddenly Mr. Mooser took some cookies out of his pocket. It was like pulling a rabbit out of a hat.","The company's in real trouble, and they don't seem to have any rabbits to pull out of the hat.","Where am I going to get the money? I can't just pull it out of a hat!","I don't know where she found the book. She pulled it out of thin air, I guess."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The magician's trick of pulling a live rabbit out of an empty top hat is very
old, but this expression is relatively new (from about the 1930s). The meaning has been
transferred from the specific (a magic trick) to the general (producing by surprise the
answer to a difficulty). Sometimes this idiom is shortened, as in, “We didn't think we
had a jack to fix the flat tire, but he just pulled one out of a hat.”

name: pull no punches
meanings: [{"name":"to hit as hard as possible; to attack with full force; to be perfectly honest; to not hold back","examples":["Tell me what you thought of my acting. Don't pull any punches.","She doesn't pull her punches when talking about lazy people.","My father is very direct and pulls no punches."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying came originally from the sport of boxing. If a fighter pulled back
on a punch, he held back, didn't hit as hard as he could, and landed a soft blow. By
the 1930s this expression was being used about all sorts of activities. If you pulled your
punches, you were careful not to hurt anybody. If you pulled no punches, you were
completely honest, even if it might hurt someone's feelings.

name: pull out all the stops
meanings: [{"name":"to do everything you can to make something successful; to do something as enthusiastically as you can","examples":["They pulled out all the stops for their daughter's wedding.","The kids pulled out all the stops and organized a really great party.","The company pulled out all the stops to advertise their new product.","When he throws a party, he really pulls out all the stops.","The mayor decided to pull out all the stops and campaign in every district."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This saying comes from the second half of the 19th century and refers to the
workings of big organs. Church organs had many pipes that an organist played by
pulling out knobs called stops. If you pulled out all the stops, you got the fullest,
loudest, most ear-filling sound possible. That idea was carried over to other activities
in life where one goes all out to succeed or enjoy an activity.

name: pull strings
meanings: [{"name":"to exert behind-the-scenes influence; to secretly control others from a distance as if they were puppets","examples":["The movie is sold out, but since your uncle runs the theater, maybe you could pull strings and get us tickets.","I may be able to pull a few strings if you need the document urgently."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Marionettes (string puppets) have been used to entertain people for
centuries. A puppeteer, out of sight of the audience, pulls the strings that make the
puppets move.

name: pull the rug out from under you
meanings: [{"name":"to unexpectedly withdraw support; to suddenly place somebody at a disadvantage; to ruin someone's plans, hopes, or dreams","examples":["I asked Arnold to be my campaign manager, but he decided to support someone else and pulled the rug right out from under me.","When they pulled the carpet out from under her, she was devastated.","Do you sometimes just have the feeling that someone is trying to pull the rug from under your feet?","I was close to getting the contract until Don came along and pulled out the rug."],"media":[]}]
origin:
