meanings: [{"name":"Fig. [for a fact] to become apparent to someone; [for something] to be suddenly realized by someone","examples":["It suddenly dawned on me that I hadn't eaten all day.","On the way home, it dawned on me that I had never returned your call, so when I got home I called immediately.","The solution finally dawned on him.","It began to dawn on her that she was lost.","It finally dawned on him that she'd been joking.","I was about to pay for the shopping when it suddenly dawned on me that I'd left my wallet at home."],"media":[]}]
origin: The expression suggests that the dawn reveals a situation. See the light simply means to understand, whereas dawn on someone suggests that one has been blind or slow to understand.

name: dig up something
meanings: [{"name":"to discover information about someone, esp. damaging information","examples":["The firm hired a private detective to dig up information on the former supervisor.","Have you dug up any information on the new employee?"],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to take something out of the ground by digging; to break the ground or to make a hole in it with a tool, machine, etc.","examples":["It's time we dug up those potatoes.","They're digging up the road outside to fix a faulty water main.","Why is that bush there? You were supposed to dig it up."],"media":[]}]

name: dish out something
meanings: [{"name":"Lit. to serve up food to people","examples":["I'll dish it out, and you take it to the table.","Careful how you dish out the mashed potatoes. There may not be enough.","Jon, could you dish the carrots out for me, please?"],"media":[]},{"name":"to give something, or to tell something such as information, news or your opinions","examples":["The company dishes out propaganda on a regular basis.","NBC dished out more than $790 million to broadcast the Athens Games to U.S. audiences.","Dolly Parton is dishing out all her family recipes.","His collaborators are dishing out misinformation."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to give out trouble, scoldings, criticism, etc","examples":["The boss was dishing criticism out this morning, and I really got it.","The teacher dished out a scolding to each one who was involved in the prank.","Sometimes he's nasty and insulting. He can really dish out.","She is dishing out gifts.","He's mad at me for teasing him – he can dish it out, but he can't take it!"],"media":[]}]

name: do the trick
meanings: [{"name":"to achieve or produce the desired result; to do exactly what is needed","examples":["The recipe needs a little help. I think salt may do the trick.","I need something to put these papers in – this folder should do the trick.","This new paint scraper really does the trick.","This sauce needs more flavour - I know, some lemon juice should to do the trick.","Is this envelope large enough to do the trick?"],"media":[]}]

name: do without (someone or something)
meanings: [{"name":"to manage, work, or perform successfully without having someone or something present","examples":["When the television broke, I knew that I could do without it for a week or two.","Thank you, Kate, we can do without language like that (= we don't want to hear your offensive language).","We can't afford to fix the car this month, so I guess we'll need to do without it for a few weeks.","I guess I will have to do without dinner.  Yes, you'll do without.","The country cannot do without foreign investment.","There are a great number of things that he can easily do without."],"media":[]}]

name: doctor up
meanings: [{"name":"to give someone medical treatment, especially first aid","examples":["Give me a minute to doctor Fred up, and then we can continue our walk.","Mary doctored her ailing husband."],"media":[]},{"name":"to restore to good condition; repair; fix","examples":["The hem on the dress ripped. I doctored it up with some tape.","She doctored up an old clock."],"media":[]}]

name: double-cross someone
meanings: [{"name":"to betray someone","examples":["Don't even think about double-crossing me! ","Richard double-crossed Mr. Big a few years back.","I cannot double-cross my best friend."],"media":[]}]
origin: Originally a more complicated switching of sides in a conspiracy wherein the double-crosser sides with the victim of the conspiracy—against the original conspirator.

name: dough
meanings: [{"name":"money","examples":["I didn't have to spend a lot of dough for a new stereo.","He says he can make a lot of dough.","I don't have much dough."],"media":[]}]

name: down-and-out / down and out
meanings: [{"name":"having no luck, no money, and no opportunities","examples":["There are many young people down-and-out in the city.","Nobody loves you when you're down and out.","John gambled away all his fortune and is now completely down-and-out."],"media":[]},{"name":"someone who is impoverished","examples":["There were a couple of down-and-outs sleeping under the railway bridge.","The down-and-out touched Martin for a fiver."],"media":[]}]

name: down and dirty
meanings: [{"name":"crude and carelessly done; made or done hastily; not revised or polished","examples":["The last time he painted the kitchen, it was a down and dirty job because he thought we were moving.","a down and dirty solution."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. coarse; mean-spirited; marked by or given to fierce often unscrupulous competition","examples":["The campaign for governor really got down and dirty in the final week.","a down-and-dirty political campaign."],"media":[]}]

name: down in the mouth
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. sad-faced; depressed and unsmiling.","examples":["Since her dog died, Barbara has been down in the mouth. ","Bob has been down in the mouth since he was laid off from his job."],"media":[]}]

name: dribs and drabs
meanings: [{"name":"small amounts that come or happen over a period of time; little by little, small quantities; bit by bit","examples":["They received donations in dribs and drabs.","She told us the story in dribs and drabs.","I'll have to pay you what I owe you in dribs and drabs.","The whole story is being revealed in dribs and drabs."],"media":[]}]

name: in droves
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. in large numbers; a large group, especially of people, moving towards a place or doing something together as a group","examples":["The settlers arrived on the prairie in droves.","People came in droves to hear her sing.","Donors showed up in droves to give blood.","In July and August these gardens attract droves of visitors.","Doctors and nurses have been leaving the profession in droves.","Every summer droves of sightseers crowd the city."],"media":[]}]

name: drive at something
meanings: [{"name":"to try to explain or say something; to be making a point; to be hinting at something; to work up to making a point","examples":["I couldn't understand what she was driving at.","What are you driving at? What's the point?","I could tell Mary was driving at something, but I didn't know what it was.","What were you driving at when you said that insulting comment?"],"media":[]}]

name: drive someone up the wall
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. to annoy or irritate someone; make someone crazy","examples":["Stop whistling that tune. You're driving me up the wall.","All his talk about moving to California nearly drove me up the wall.","My son is driving me up the wall!","Your constant tapping is driving me up the wall!"],"media":[]}]

name: dwell on
meanings: [{"name":"to think or talk about (someone or something) for a long time especially something bad or unpleasant","examples":["Let's not dwell on the past,\" she said.","Don't dwell upon your mistakes."," There is no need to dwell on Sarah further."],"media":[]}]

name: call (someone) on the carpet
meanings: [{"name":"to criticize or reprimand(someone) for doing something wrong; (of a person or organization in authority) to make someone answer questions about something they have done wrong or may have done wrong","examples":["One more error like that and the big boss will call you on the carpet.","He was/got called on the carpet for missing the deadline.","How do you react when your boss calls you on the carpet?","Documenting all conversations can help if you are later called onto the carpet to defend yourself.","I'm sorry it went wrong. I really hope the regional manager doesn't call me on the carpet again."],"media":[]}]

name: damn with faint praise
meanings: [{"name":"to criticize in such a way that one appears to be praising when in fact one is condemning or disapproving (In this idiom the word ‘faint' means weak or feeble.)","examples":["The critic did not say that he disliked the play, but he damned it with faint praise. ","Mrs. Brown is very proud of her son's achievements, but damns her daughter's with faint praise.","Of course, to say a restaurant isn't as bad as you thought it would be is to damn with faint praise.","He appeared in his interview to damn his colleague with faint praise.","Jeff told me that the diet I was trying was showing results, and he asked how much more weight I had to lose. \nHe was really telling me that I'm still too fat. He was damning me with faint praise.","Alicia told me that she was never able to make her old shoes last more than a few years the way I could.\nShe was really trying to point out that my shoes were old and that hers are not. She damned me with faint praise."],"media":[]}]

name: days are numbered
meanings: [{"name":"used to say that someone or something will die, fail, or end soon; there is only a short time before something ends","examples":["Judy always comes to work late, and I think the boss is going to fire her soon. Her days are numbered.","Your old car's days are numbered. It's only a matter of time before you have to get a new one.","He knew that his days as the team's coach were numbered.","The doctors have told her that her days are numbered."],"media":[]}]
origin: The expression suggests that the number of days associated with a situation is not indefinite. It is of ten used about someone facing death or dismissal.

name: dead to the world
meanings: [{"name":"sound asleep.","examples":["After all that exercise, he's dead to the world.","He's dead to the world, and I can't rouse him.","Crystal tried to wake her sons to get them on their way to school, but they had stayed out until well past midnight and now they were dead to the world. Nothing could rouse them.","I was barely aware that my telephone was ringing in the middle of the night because I was dead to the world. I couldn't drag myself out of bed in time to answer it."],"media":[]}]

name: deal someone in
meanings: [{"name":"to include someone in something, especially a card game; to pass out cards to someone, making that person a player in a card game.","examples":["If you'll excuse me for a moment; I'm going to make a phone call. But I want to play this round of cards, so you can deal me in.","Can you deal me into this hand? ","Deal in anyone who wants to play.","Do you want to play cards with us? Sure, deal me in."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to permit someone to take part in something.","examples":["Let's deal him into this project. Yes, deal in this guy.","Should we deal her in?","Mary thought their business venture was promising, but she didn't have a lot of money, so she told them to deal her out."],"media":[]}]
origin: The expression originates from the idea of being included or excluded from a hand of cards in a card game like poker, and is still in reference to card games. It is also used figuratively in business ventures and other group activities.

name: deal someone out
meanings: [{"name":"Lit. to skip someone when dealing a hand of cards.","examples":["Please deal me out of the next hand. I have to go make a telephone call.","They dealt out the old lady because she would not pay attention to the game."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to remove someone from participation in something.","examples":["They dealt me out at the last minute. They dealt out Fred, too.","Mary thought their business venture was promising, but she didn't have a lot of money, so she told them to deal her out."],"media":[]}]
origin: The expression originates from the idea of being included or excluded from a hand of cards in a card game like poker, and is still in reference to card games. It is also used figuratively in business ventures and other group activities.

name: deal in something
meanings: [{"name":"to buy and sell something.","examples":["My uncle is a stockbroker. He deals in stocks and bonds.","My aunt deals in antiques.","He is chief operating officer for a company that deals in medical technology."],"media":[]}]

name: deal something out to someone
meanings: [{"name":"to pass something out piece by piece, giving everyone equal shares; to give out (something) to appropriate individuals","examples":["Aid workers dealt out a packet of emergency supplies to each earthquake victim.","The manager dealt the proposals out, giving each person an equal number to read.","We have only a small amount of food and clothing to deal out to each refugee.","She dealt out a card to everyone in the room."],"media":[]}]

name: deal with someone or something
meanings: [{"name":"to manage someone or something","examples":["This is not a big problem. I think I can deal with it.","I am sure I can deal with Jill.","I'll deal with you later.","We weren't able/equipped/prepared to deal with such a large crowd of people."],"media":[]},{"name":"to make business agreements with (someone)","examples":["He deals fairly with all his customers.","Their salespeople are very easy to deal with.","We'll continue to deal with the suppliers."],"media":[]},{"name":"to be about (something); to have (something) as a subject; cover, be concerned with","examples":["Her speech dealt with health care and the nation's economy.","Her newspaper articles often dealt with problems at work.","The guidelines deal with topics such as diet and exercise."],"media":[]},{"name":"to accept or try to accept (something that is true and cannot be changed); stop making excuses and do something to change a situation","examples":["The weather is bad, but we'll just have to deal with it.","Just deal with it!"],"media":[]}]

name: draw a blank
meanings: [{"name":"to fail to remember something","examples":["He said we'd met before, but I just drew a blank (= I did not remember him).","I always draw a blank when I run into people I don't know very well. I never quite sure I have met them before.","Charles drew a blank when he tried to remember the date of his wedding anniversary. He had to ask his wife when it was.","He asked me for my phone number and I drew a blank - I just couldn't remember it."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to get no response; to find nothing","examples":["I asked him about Tom's financial problems, and I just drew a blank.","We looked in the files for an hour, but we drew a blank."],"media":[]}]
origin: Used at least since the 16th century, this idiom originally referred to lottery tickets. One who drew a blank had a ticket worth nothing.

name: cut and dried / cut and dry
meanings: [{"name":"fixed; determined beforehand; usual and uninteresting; routine","examples":["I find your writing quite boring. It's too cut and dried.","The lecture was, as usual, cut and dried.","Most fire investigations are pretty cut and dried, but this one has left more questions than answers.","Unfortunately, there is no cut-and-dried answer to the problem of immigration.","Everything's not all cut and dry."],"media":[]}]
origin: The phrase originally alludes to the dried herbs that you could purchase from a shop. They lacked freshness and spontaneity, which differs from the fresh herbs that you could grow yourself. It is also rumoured to date back to the time when wood was cut and dried in order to make fire with it. It was very rigid and inflexible. In most cases the phrase has a negative connotation.

name: cut corners
meanings: [{"name":"to do things poorly or incompletely in order to save money; to take shortcuts; to save money or effort by finding cheaper or easier ways to do something","examples":["I don't like to cut corners when I have company for dinner.","Will speeding up nurses' training lead to improved patient care, or is it simply cutting corners?","The dictionary took nearly 70 years to complete because its makers refused to cut corners.","It doesn't pay to cut corners by buying cheap tires for your car. You'll only have to buy new ones much sooner, and the cheap ones may cause you to have an accident.","Don't cut any corners when you write that report. Spend as much time as you need on it and do a good job. It will be important when the boss decides who gets the next promotion."],"media":[]}]

name: cut from the same cloth / made from the same mold
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. sharing a lot of similarities; seeming to have been created, reared, or fashioned in the same way","examples":["She and her brother are cut from the same cloth. They both tell lies all the time.","Father and son are made from the same mold and even sound alike on the telephone.","We're cut from the same cloth, you and I."],"media":[]}]

name: call a spade a spade
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. to call something by its right name; to speak frankly about something, even if it is unpleasant. (Considered offensive by some. Use only with discretion.) ","examples":["Well, I believe it's time to call a spade a spade. We are just avoiding the issue."," Let's call a spade a spade. The man is a liar.","Some people say Ben is generous with his money, but I call a spade a spade. He's not generous, he's foolish.","It's polite of you to refer to them as “lively” children, but let's call a spade a spade. They are actually very naughty."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is usually used when something is described
more favorably than it deserves. Call a spade a spade is a
request for a more realistic description. The phrase dates
back to ancient Greece, where the words for “spade,” “boat,”
and “bowl” were very similar; the original translation my have
been ‘call a boat a boat.'

name: catch someone's eye
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. to establish eye contact with someone; to attract someone's attention","examples":["This necklace just caught my eye and I couldn't resist buying it.","When Tom had her eye, he smiled at her.","I was walking past some stores when a beautiful red dress in one of the windows caught my eye.","When the girls met their mother in front of the post office, they could see her walking towards them in the crowd, but couldn't catch her eye.","One of the books on the top shelf caught my eye, and I took it down to look at it."],"media":[]}]

name: catch someone's fancy
meanings: [{"name":"to appeal to someone very much; to seem interesting or pleasing to someone","examples":["Something about the movie really caught their fancy.","Before you decide that you don't want anything for your birthday, let's go to the jewelry store. You might see something there that catches your fancy.","She has enough money to buy anything that catches her fancy."],"media":[]}]
origin: This similar to tickle/strike (someone's) fancy

name: change horses in midstream
meanings: [{"name":"to change plans or leaders in the middle of some action or event; ","examples":["The president told the people that if they wanted the country to continue to move forward, they should reelect him. He said that to elect his opponent would be like changing horses in midstream.","The chairman of the board died suddenly before he could complete his plans for the company. The stockholders were forced to change horses in midstream and elect someone new.","I'm already baking a cherry pie. I can't bake an apple pie. It's too late to change horses in the middle of the stream.","The house is half-built. It's too late to hire a different architect. You can't change horses in midstream.","Jane: I've written a rough draft of my research paper, but the topic doesn't interest me as much as I thought. Maybe I ought to pick a different one. Jill: Don't change horses in midstream."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression connotes that trying to change horses in the
middle of a stream is not a wise thing to do—it would be better
to wait until one is on land. This expression is same as: change horses in  the middle of the stream

name: change of heart
meanings: [{"name":"to change one's attitude or decision, usually from a negative to a positive position","examples":["Karen told her boss that she planned to leave the company, but after the boss offered her a pay raise, she had a change of heart and agreed to stay.","The girl's parents said no at first, but then they had a change of heart and let her go to the dance.","But just as construction was about to begin in 2023, the couple had a change of heart.","She was going to sell her house but had a change of heart at the last minute.","I had a change of heart at the last minute and gave the beggar some money. "],"media":[]}]
origin: The expression is usually applied to an emotional attitude.

name: lead/live a charmed life
meanings: [{"name":"to be lucky or avoid danger; a life unusually unaffected by dangers and difficulties; ","examples":["Despite all her wealth, Harris hardly led a charmed life.","That boy leads a charmed life. He always manages to avoid getting into trouble.","Monica leads a charmed life—she'll never have to work a day in her life.","She was a popular society girl, leading a charmed life."],"media":[]}]
origin: a life protected as if by magic charms

name: checkered past
meanings: [{"name":"a past history of having done bad things or been in trouble; a personal history that includes both successes and failures, or ethical and unethical behavior","examples":["Larry has quite a checkered past, but things are getting better. He has a new job and is saving for a new apartment.","The personnel director of the company refused to consider Mr. Dupont's application for employment because of his checkered past.","The senator has a checkered past."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the alternating black and white
(opposite colors) of a checker board. It is generally used in
a negative sense, focusing more on failures and unethical
behavior than on successes and ethical behavior.

name: chew over something
meanings: [{"name":"to think slowly and carefully about something","examples":["I've been chewing the problem over since last week.","I know the idea doesn't seem appealing at first, but why don't you chew it over for a few days before you decide?","Janice is not sure she is going on vacation in August. She's chewing it over."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The idiom probably originates from another expression, chew
the cud, referring to the fact that a cow chews slowly and
regurgitates its food to chew it a second time.

name: clean slate (wipe the slate clean)
meanings: [{"name":"a person's record (as from a school or a job) that shows no evidence of any problems, broken rules, etc; a new beginning, usually achieved by removing any record of previous bad deeds or debts","examples":["Everyone who comes to this school starts with a clean slate.","The man had done some terrible things in the past, but he moved to a new town and changed his name. He was trying to make a new life with a clean slate.","If you pay me what you owe me, you'll have wiped the slate clean"],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the idea of a slate, the
forerunner to the blackboard, which can be wiped clean to
allow for new writing.

name: clean out someone/something
meanings: [{"name":"to get or use up all of someone's money; to take or steal everything someone has","examples":["The robbers broke into the bank at night and cleaned the place out.","We needed to go to the grocery store after the party. Our guests really cleaned us out!","The bill for supper cleaned me out, and we couldn't go to the flick.","The robbers cleaned out all the bank's cash."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to empty someone's bowels","examples":["That medicine I took really cleaned me out.","Whatever was in that stew cleaned out every kid in the entire scout camp."],"media":[]},{"name":"to remove dirt or unwanted things from the inside of something(a room, closet, garage, etc.)","examples":["Someone has to clean the garage out. ","I'll clean out my closet tonight.","We spent the weekend cleaning out the garage.","I got a call when I was cleaning out the fridge this morning."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression is sometimes used to describe stealing, but
can also be used to describe legal situations where everything
is taken.

name: clear the air
meanings: [{"name":"to resolve hidden resentment or uncover hidden thoughts; to get rid of doubts or hard feelings","examples":["All right, let's discuss this frankly. It'll be better if we clear the air.","I must have done something to offend Louise—she's been so unfriendly to me. I told her I wanted to clear the air, but she just turned and walked away from me.","The boss called a meeting because there were lots of rumors flying around the office. He said he wanted to clear the air."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the idea that when there is
smoke or fog in the air, it is difficult to see.

name: closed minded
meanings: [{"name":"not willing to consider different ideas or opinions; ","examples":["I encourage you to try new things. Don't be so closed-minded!","Anyone who wants to make the world a better place will eventually have to contend with closed-minded people.","He's becoming increasingly closed-minded in his old age."],"media":[]}]

name: clown around
meanings: [{"name":"act silly; engage in attention-getting playful or boisterous behavior","examples":["As a youngster he was always clowning around in the classroom.","The teacher asked the students to stop being silly. She told them to stop clowning around.","Jerry likes to clown around and is always playing practical jokes on everyone.","The boys were clowning around with each other.","The kids are having fun clowning around.","Will you stop clowning around and look?","Look, you skipped, clowned around to every lecture I ever gave. As far as I'm concerned, your chemistry education is over."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Synonyms",["monkey around","fool around","horse around"]]]

name: cock-and-bull story
meanings: [{"name":"an incredible story told as true; a hard-to-believe, made-up story; a story that is a lie","examples":["You want me to believe some cock-and-bull story that you're late getting home because you got lost and then ran out of gas?","The driver tried to explain his way out of getting a speeding ticket by inventing a cock-and-bull story.","He gave me some cock-and-bull story about having to be at his cousin's engagement party.","Don't give me that cock-and-bull story.","I asked for an explanation, and all I got was your ridiculous cock-and-bull story!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: song and dance; snow job. 
The expression originates from an English fable in which a
cock and a bull had an unbelievable conversation.

name: come full circle
meanings: [{"name":"to return (figuratively) to a point where one has been before; to return to the original position or state of affairs","examples":["Things have come full circle now that long skirts are back in fashion.","Bruce practiced law in a small law firm, then taught law at a university, then gave up teaching and is practicing law again. He has come full circle.","We started with a small, two-bedroom house, but as the family grew, so did the size of the houses we moved into over the years. Now that the children are grown and have left home, we've come full circle and are moving back into a small house.","The family sold the house generations ago, but things have come full circle and one of their descendants lives there now."],"media":[]}]

name: come home to roost
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. [for a problem] to return to cause trouble [for someone]; If a past action, mistake, etc. comes home to roost, it causes problems at a later date","examples":["As I feared, all my problems came home to roost.","All his earlier mistakes are coming home to roost.","He's been cheating people for years but now the/his chickens are (finally) coming home to roost.","Her bad decisions are coming home to roost.","If you tell a lie, you may get caught up in it and find that it comes home to roost.","Dorothy is convinced that she is ill and dying because her unhealthy lifestyle has come home to roost."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. [for a fowl or other bird] to return to its home, as for a night's rest","examples":["The chickens come home to roost in the evening."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from the idea of a bird
leaving and then returning to its roost, the perch on which
a bird rests. It is usually used to refer to something bad
happening to someone who has demonstrated some bad
behavior in the past.

name: Come off it!
meanings: [{"name":"Inf. Stop acting arrogantly!; a behavior that must be stoped","examples":["Come off it, Tiff. You're not the Queen of England.","First you ask for juice and then change your mind and say you want milk. I get it for you, and now you beg for water. Come off it!"],"media":[]},{"name":"a response to a statement that cannot be believed; Give up your incorrect point of view!","examples":["Come off it! You're wrong, and you know it!","Come off it, Pete – you know that's not true!","Ask Simon to cook the meal? Come off it, he can hardly boil an egg!","You expect me to believe that you don't know how that dent in the car fender got there? Oh, come off it!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is always used as an expletive in the command
form. It is very informal and would normally only be used by
parents with their children, or between equals.

name: cook up something
meanings: [{"name":"to invent (something, such as an idea, excuse, etc.) to deal with a particular situation","examples":["When Paul's friends planned his surprise party, they had to cook up a good excuse to get him to the restaurant without his suspecting a thing.","The prison inmates cooked up a scheme to break out of jail.","They cooked up a scheme to fool their neighbor.","You'll have to cook an excuse up quickly. I don't have a plan right now, but I think I can cook one up.","Fred cooked up a scheme that was supposed to earn him a lot of money."],"media":[]},{"name":"to prepare (food) for eating especially quickly","examples":["He cooked this whole meal up in less than 30 minutes.","I can cook up some hamburgers.","He cooked up some food for dinner."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression connotes scheming, but is not necessarily
negative.

name: cornered
meanings: [{"name":"trapped with no means of escape","examples":["The dogs chased the rabbit into the barn. It was cornered where it could not escape until the dogs' owner called them away.","When the police followed the thief into the back of the market, the thief tried to open the back door but found it locked. The police called out to the thief, “Come out now. There's no way to escape. We've got you cornered.”"],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: back to the wall

name: cross one's fingers (keep one's fingers crossed)
meanings: [{"name":"to wish for luck for someone or something, sometimes by actually crossing one's fingers; to hope for a good outcome for someone or something","examples":["I hope you win the race Saturday. I'm keeping my fingers crossed for you.","I'm trying out for a play. Keep your fingers crossed!","Owners are crossing their fingers that relief might be on the way.","I sure hope we haven't missed the plane. There isn't another one for a week. Cross your fingers.","We're hoping that the operation is a success. We have our fingers crossed."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from a superstition that
bad luck can be prevented by crossing one's fingers. The
expression refers to crossing one's middle finger over the
knuckle of the index finger.

name: back to the wall
meanings: [{"name":"to be in a difficult or desperate situation; ","examples":["Gary lost his job over a month ago and he has spent all his savings paying his bills. Now he doesn't have any more money, and his back is to the wall.","My back was to the wall. civilization.

origin: Though this expression has been used in English since the early 1800s, it actually comes from an older Spanish saying. Old, aristocratic Spanish families used to boast that their skin was fairly light because they had not intermarried with the darker-skinned Moors. The Spaniards' veins showed through their skin as visibly blue in color. If their skin was darker because they had intermarried, the blood would not appear so blue. “Blue blood” is a translation of the Spanish words sangre azul. Today anyone can be called a blue blood if he or she is of noble birth, a member of high society, and so on. A related phrase is “upper crust”

[{"name":"by being told by another person; by speaking rather than writing","examples":[" Walter heard about it from one of the company's
employees even though it had not been advertised
in the newspaper. He got the information by word of
mouth.","Jane and Sarah will be very hurt if they aren't invited
to your party. You won't be able to keep it a secret.
They are sure to hear about it by word of mouth.","I learned about it by word of mouth.","I need it in writing. I don't trust things I hear about by word of mouth."],"media":[]}]

name: ace in the hole
meanings:
[{"name":"a hidden but effective means of winning a conflict; an effective and decisive argument or resource held in reserve","examples":["The other team thinks they can win this basketball
game, but that's only because we haven't put our
best player in yet. He's our ace in the hole.","It looked like the politician would lose the debate
until he brought up his ace in the hole, an argument
that nobody could refute.","The twenty-dollar bill I keep in my shoe is my ace in the hole."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from some forms of the card game
poker, in which players have both community cards and
private (“hole”) cards in their hands. To have an ace in one's
private hand means that one can win the game without others
suspecting ahead of time.

name: acid test
meanings:
[{"name":"the most crucial or important test","examples":["The new team faced its first acid test when it played the national champions.","Parents might be willing to buy this new toy for their
children but the real acid test is whether or not the
children themselves like it.","The acid test for laundry soap is not how well it cleans
in hot water, but how well it cleans in cold water.","The senator doesn't look too popular just now, but the acid test will be if he gets reelected."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the use of nitric acid on gold
to determine whether the gold was genuine.

name: across the board
meanings:
[{"name":"Fig. [distributed] equally for everyone or everything","examples":["The school board raised the pay of all the teachers across the board.","The boss made some people angry. He gave 5% pay
raises across the board but some people thought they
should have gotten more than others.","The car dealership was cutting prices across the
board. Every car was on sale, not just a few."],"media":[]}]

name: actions speak louder than words
meanings:
[{"name":"the things that people do (actions) are more important than the things they say (words)","examples":["She's promised to be nicer to her sister from now on,
but actions speak louder than words.","Every politician will claim that he or she cares about
the problems of the average person, but actions
speak louder than words.","You keep saying that you'll do your fair share of the housework. Remember that actions speak louder than words.","Team USA is not expected to win, but they believe actions speak louder than words."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression implies that we can learn about a person's
true intentions by looking at what they do rather than what
they say.

name: joking aside / kidding aside
meanings: [{"name":"used to introduce a serious statement that follows a humorous statement; speaking seriously","examples":["I know I laugh at him but, joking aside, he's a very clever scientist.","I know I threatened to leave and go round the world, but, joking aside, I do need a vacation.","It looks like this is a job for Superman! But joking aside, this is a serious problem and we're going to need help.","That was a good joke, but all kidding aside, we have\nto get to work now.","What you're telling me sounds unbelievable. All\nkidding aside, are you serious?"],"media":[]}]

name: all wet
meanings: [{"name":"completely wrong; mistaken; wrongheaded; on the wrong track","examples":["He's all wet if he thinks I'm going to believe his lies.","Don't listen to Maria. She doesn't know what she's\ntalking about. She's all wet.","That's not the correct answer, John. You're all wet. ","If you think that prices will come down, you're all wet."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. completely wet","examples":["I fell in and got all wet."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: not know beans about (something); out to lunch;
for the birds; talk through (one's) hat

name: armed to the teeth
meanings: [{"name":"well-equipped with weapons; carrying many weapons; heavily armed with deadly weapons","examples":["The police won't enter the bank where the thief is.\nHe's armed to the teeth.","The invading soldiers were armed to the teeth. There\nwas no way the defenders could hope to win.","There are too many guns around. The entire country is armed to the teeth.","The bank robber was armed to the teeth when he was caught."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests having weapons (arms) from one's
toes to one's teeth.

name: at loggerheads
meanings:
[{"name":"in strong disagreement, in a quarrel; in conflict with someone; having reached an impasse (about something)","examples":["They have been arguing all day about what to do.
They really are at loggerheads.","John and Richard are at loggerheads about what
would be a fair price for the car. John thinks
Richard's price is far too low.","Tom is at loggerheads with Bill.","We are at loggerheads with each other.","The twins were at loggerheads over who should take the larger room."],"media":[]}]

name: at one's wits' end
meanings:
[{"name":"at a loss about what to do next; in a state of frustration; at the limits of one's mental resources.","examples":["She was at her wits' end trying to figure out how to control her 14-year-old son.","I'm at my wit's end with this problem. I cannot figure it out.","Tom could do no more. He was at his wit's end.","When the woman looked around and couldn't find
her little daughter, she looked up and down every
aisle in the store until she was at her wits' end. She
was almost hysterical when another customer in the
store suggested that she notify the store's security
officer.","We can't seem to persuade our son to stay in school.
We have tried every argument we can think of, but
nothing seems to help. We don't know what to do,
and we're at our wits' end."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: at the end of (one's) rope
Compare to: keep (one's) wits about (oneself); use (one's) wits;
scared out of (one's) wits
The word wits means mental abilities.

name: chicken out
meanings:
[{"name":"to become too frightened to do something; to lose one's nerve","examples":["The girls wanted to ask the movie star for his
autograph, but they got scared and chickened out.","You said you wanted to try parachuting, so we came
up in this airplane. The door is open and it's time to
jump. Don't chicken out now."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonyms: cold feet

name: drum someone out of something
meanings:
[{"name":"to expel someone from a group or organization; to remove someone from a job, group, etc., because of something bad the person has done","examples":["The minister was drummed out of office when it was discovered that he had been taking bribes.","If I suggested to the boss that the company pay for
the Christmas party, he'd probably fire me. I'd get
drummed out of the corps.","When Henry recommended that the men's club
should admit women as members, they drummed him
out of the corps.","The chairman was drummed out of office."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from a military setting where, when
someone left the corps in disgrace, he or she was escorted out
with a drum roll. Its usage includes any group and carries with
it a sense of disgrace or rejection.

name: eager beaver
meanings:
[{"name":"a person who is extremely zealous about performing duties and volunteering for more; someone who is very enthusiastic; someone who works very hard","examples":["When she first started working she was a real eager beaver.","New volunteers are always eager beavers.","The young assistant gets to work very early. She's a real eager beaver."," Paul just discovered jogging as a form of exercise,
and he went out and bought new running shoes, a
new tracksuit, and all the other gear that goes along
with it. He's a real eager beaver about jogging.","Dieting must be done slowly and carefully. Don't be
such an eager beaver to lose weight that you harm
yourself by not eating anything."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests the image of an anxiously working
beaver, which is reputed to be an active, industrious animal.
It has a slightly negative connotation, as of someone eager
to impress others with his/her effort.

name: fair and square
meanings:
[{"name":"in an honest and fair manner; completely fair(ly); justly; within the rules","examples":["Some people believe Andrew cheated, but he won the
contest fair and square.","The working people didn't like the result of the
election, but the opposition's candidate won
honestly. The election was fair and square.","The division of the money should be fair and square."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: square deal
In this expression, “square” means “right,” or “not crooked.”

name: fair shake
meanings:
[{"name":"a fair chance or fair treatment; to give someone or something a chance to prove itself (*Typically: get ~ ; have ~ ; give someone ~ .)","examples":["He's unpleasant, but we have to give him a fair shake. ","He got a fair shake from us. Don't worry!","It's only right that all the candidates should be given a fair shake.","Don't dismiss this place so quickly; spend a little
time getting used to it. Give it a fair shake.","You accuse me of stealing money from the store, but
you don't give me a chance to tell you my side of the
story. You're not giving me a fair shake."],"media":[]}]

name: fair to middling
meanings:
[{"name":"just average; neither good nor bad","examples":["Don asked Melissa what she thought of the new
restaurant. She told him she had been to better ones,
but it wasn't bad. It was fair to middling.","The food was fair to middling.","Now that I'm beginning to get over my cold, I'm
feeling fair to middling. I feel better than I did last
week, but I still have a stuffy nose.","Tom: How are you feeling today? Bill: Fair to middlin'.","My sewing is excellent, but my cooking is only fair to middlin'."],"media":[]}]

name: drop by the wayside / fall by the wayside
meanings:
[{"name":"to no longer be active or successful; to drop out of the situation","examples":["I've seen a lot of bands split up and fall by the wayside.","When Greg had too many groceries to carry at once,
he decided to keep what he needed for dinner that
night and let the rest fall by the wayside.","Larry's parents told him to look to the future,
concentrate on his long-term goals, and let the
unimportant things fall by the wayside.","Those who fall by the wayside will find it hard to catch up.","Many of the students will drop by the way- side and never finish."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to leave a march or procession in exhaustion to recover beside the pathway","examples":["A few of the marchers dropped by the wayside in the intense heat."],"media":[]}]
origin: Wayside is a land adjacent to a road or path. If someone falls by the wayside, they fail to finish an activity, and if something falls by the wayside, people stop doing it, making it, or using it.

name: fall for something
meanings:
[{"name":"to be deceived or believe an unlikely story","examples":["He fell for the trick.","You want me to believe that you're late because you
ran out of gasoline? You must think I'm a fool if you
think I'm going to fall for that.","The judge said she didn't believe the thief's excuse
that he simply forgot to pay for the food. The judge
told him, “I'm not going to fall for that old story.”","She fell for the excuse I gave her about getting stuck in traffic."],"media":[]}]

name: fall on deaf ears
meanings:
[{"name":"to be heard but ignored, or to be heard but to have no effect; [for talk or ideas] to be ignored by the persons they were intended for","examples":["Her pleas for mercy fell on deaf ears; the judge gave her the maximum sentence.","All of Sally's good advice fell on deaf ears. Walter had made up his own mind.","Ashley went to the bank to beg for a loan because she
had no job, but no one would listen to her. Her pleas
fell on deaf ears.","The young husband tried to tell his wife why he was
late getting home, but his excuse fell on deaf ears."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: turn a deaf ear. 
The expression is used to describe spoken words. The listener
is not really deaf, but acts that way. This idiom is essentially
synonymous with turn a deaf ear, but whereas the request
falls on deaf ears, the person who ignores the request turns
a deaf ear.

name: far cry from something
meanings:
[{"name":"something notably different; a thing that is very different from something else; much less than what was expected or anticipated","examples":["What you did was a far cry from what you said you were going to do.","The song they played was
a far cry from what I call music.","The effects of the new law were a far cry from what was intended."," The bellboy took them to their hotel room. It was
small, dark, and dirty—a far cry from what they were
expecting.","Don't get your expectations up too high. What you
get may be a far cry from what you want."],"media":[]}]

name: feel something in one's bones / know something in one's bones
meanings:
[{"name":"sense very strongly; have a strong feeling about something; to sense something without being able to see, hear or feel it; to have a premonition","examples":["The train will be late. I feel it in my bones.","I failed the test. I know it in my bones.","The sky may be clear, but it's going to rain. I can feel
it in my bones.","Do you ever get the feeling that someone is watching
you, even though you can't see him or her? You get
this feeling in your bones.","He knew in his bones that he was wrong."],"media":[]}]

name: feel the pinch
meanings:
[{"name":"to experience the problems caused by not having enough money or by paying higher costs","examples":["The government raised taxes so much that even the
rich began to feel the pinch.","When we had to pay for the university education of
all three of our children at the same time, we really
felt the pinch.","We are starting to feel the pinch of high fuel costs."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: strapped for cash

name: filthy rich
meanings: [{"name":"extremely rich — used to imply that a person's wealth is excessive or offensive","examples":["I happen to know that the woman is filthy rich and can well afford to compensate you.","He started the leading software company in the\nworld. He's not just a little rich—he's filthy rich!"," Whenever I buy a lottery ticket, I dream about what I\nwould buy if I were filthy rich.","There are too many filthy rich people now.","The filthy rich can afford that kind of thing, but I can't. "],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: flat broke
This expression arose from the idea that money was “filthy,”
or dirty. For some people, the idiom still carries a negative
connotation. But for others, to be filthy rich is a dream.

name: fine kettle of fish
meanings:
[{"name":"Fig. a troublesome situation; a vexing problem; a terrible mess. (Usually appears in the expression, This is a fine kettle of fish!) ","examples":["You borrowed money from the bank without telling
me and we don't have enough to pay it back. This is a
fine kettle of fish you've gotten us into.","Lois told her boss she could work on Saturday, but
she forgot and promised her friend she would
help her move on Saturday. She had gotten herself
into a fine kettle of fish.","This is a fine kettle of fish. My husband is not here to meet me at the train station, and there's no phone here for me to call him. ","Alan: Oh, no! I've burned the roast. We don't have anything to serve our guests as a main dish. Jane: But they'll be here any minute! This is a fine kettle of fish."],"media":[]}]
origin: The word “fine” is meant ironically.

name: first-rate
meanings: [{"name":"extremely good; best quality","examples":["George did a first-rate job on these drawings. I've\nnever seen better.","Lynn's work is always the best. It's always first-rate.","It is a first-rate restaurant.","The country's universities are first-rate.","It is a first-rate performance."],"media":[]}]

name: fishy
meanings:
[{"name":"looking or sounding suspicious; questionable","examples":["They won't say where they got their computer. Their
story sounds fishy to me. I think they may have
stolen it.","Someone called on the telephone telling me I had
just won a free trip to Hawaii, but first I had to buy
his or her product. It sounded pretty fishy, so I hung
up.","something's fishy about the way he's acting.","Bob squinted a bit. Something smells fishy here, he thought.","Something about the deal smelled fishy—too good to be true."],"media":[]}]

name: fits and starts
meanings: [{"name":"in an impulsive and irregular manner; periods of activity mixed with periods when nothing happens; in short bursts of motion or effort","examples":["When you play the violin, you must move the bow\nacross the strings smoothly, not in fits and starts.","It took Sally a long time to finish her education. She\npursued it in fits and starts.","The construction proceeded by fits and starts.","The reform process has proceeded in fits and starts."],"media":[]}]

name: flat broke / dead broke / flat busted
meanings: [{"name":"have absolutely no money; not having any money at all","examples":["I'd gladly loan you the money, but I can't because\nI'm flat broke.","They lost all their money in the stock market crash,\nand now they're flat broke.","Sorry, I'm flat broke. Not a cent on me.","You may be flat broke, but you will find a way to pay your electricity bill or you will live in the dark. ","Mary was flat busted, and it was two more weeks before she was due to get paid.","How can I tell her I'm dead broke?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: filthy rich
Compare to: go broke

name: fly in the face/teeth of someone/something
meanings:
[{"name":"to go against someone or something; to challenge someone or something; to show disrespect for something or someone","examples":["John has decided not to go to college. It's a bad
decision on his part. It flies in the face of all common
sense."," If you marry someone your parents disapprove of so
much, it will fly in the face of everything they want
for you.","His explanation flies in the face of the evidence.","You had better not fly in the face of the committee.","This is an argument that seems to fly in the face of common sense."],"media":[]}]

name: follow in someone's footsteps
meanings:
[{"name":"to follow the same career or lifestyle as someone else","examples":["She followed in her father's footsteps and went into medicine.","James was a convicted thief who had spent years in
jail. He didn't want his son to follow in his footsteps.","The daughter had always admired her mother's
work helping the poor. From an early age she was
determined to follow in her mother's footsteps.","The vice president was following in the president's footsteps when he called for budget cuts. "],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: chip off the old block
The someone in the expression is traditionally, but not
necessarily, a parent.

name: fool around
meanings:
[{"name":"to play, or to not be serious about an activity; to waste time doing something unnecessary or doing something amateurishly","examples":["Stop fooling around and clean your room as I told you.","I wish you didn't spend so much time fooling around.","When it comes to safety, we don't fool around.","Later in the day, the three of us were fooling around, waiting for Mr. Michaels to get class started.","Don't worry about the boys playing in the back
yard—I can see them through the window. They're
just fooling around.","If you want to pass history class, you'll have to study
hard and not fool around."],"media":[]}]

name: fool's gold
meanings:
[{"name":"something that appears to have great value but is in fact a cheap imitation;","examples":["The scientists thought they had discovered a source
of cheap energy through their experiments, but it
later proved to be nothing but fool's gold.","Don't invest all your money in a fancy scheme that
seems too good to be true. All you'll end up with is
fool's gold.","This isn't the first time that a high-profile company has turned out to be a bit of fool's gold."],"media":[]}]

name: fool's paradise
meanings: [{"name":"a state of delusory happiness; a state of being happy for foolish or unfounded reasons","examples":["Fred is confident that he'll get a big raise this year, but I think he's living in a fool's paradise.","We are headed for economic trouble, and anyone who thinks otherwise is living in a fool's paradise."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The idiom comes from the definition of fool, meaning an ignorant person, and paradise, meaning a wonderful place of contentment.

For example, a man might find himself on a beautiful island with many tropical fruits, and be very happy to be there, as long as he didn't know there were man-eating tigers moments away from attacking him. Therefore, what seems like a paradise is actually not, due to a lack of knowledge about the situation, or false beliefs.

name: footloose and fancy-free
meanings:
[{"name":"able to go anywhere and do anything that one wants; carefree","examples":["My sister's married but I'm still footloose and fancy-free.","When she was 20, she was footloose and fancy-free, with no family or serious career to tie her down.","Michael didn't want to get married. He wanted to
remain footloose and fancy-free.","When they finished college, they spent a year
traveling though Europe with their backpacks and
sleeping bags. They just wanted some time to be
footloose and fancy-free."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression literally means one's foot is not tied down and
one can freely follow one's impulses (fancy).

name: force to be reckoned with
meanings:
[{"name":"a person or organization who has power and influence; something or someone whose influence or power must be considered; someone or something that is important and powerful and must not be ignored","examples":["He has become a force to be reckoned with in politics.","I underestimated the influence of Mr. Franklin in this
company. He certainly is a force to be reckoned with.","Catherine seemed to be a gentle person, but when
Roger angered her, she lashed out at him. He
discovered she was a force to be reckoned with.","Walter is a force to be reckoned with. Be pre- pared to deal with him."],"media":[]}]
origin: If an organization or a person is described as a force to be reckoned with, it means that they are powerful and have a lot of influence:

name: for crying out loud
meanings:
[{"name":"an expletive that means “This is ridiculous!” or “I've had enough!” It carries no literal meaning of its own, but expresses a strong degree of exasperation; used to show anger, annoyance, etc","examples":["All you do is complain. For crying out loud, can't you
give us some peace and quiet for a while?","The children were jumping around, chasing after
each other and running around their mother until
she couldn't stand it anymore. She said to them,
“Stop playing around, for crying out loud.”","Why won't they let me in? It's my house, for crying out loud!","Fred: For crying out loud! Answer the telephone! Bob: But it's always for you! ","John: Good grief! What am I going to do? This is the end! Sue: For crying in a bucket! What's wrong?"],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonyms: for goodness' sake!; for heaven's sake!

name: for good
meanings: [{"name":"forever; permanently.","examples":["I finally left home for good.","They tried to repair it many times before they fixed it for good.","She's gone for good."],"media":[]}]

name: for goodness' sake
meanings:
[{"name":"used to express surprise or annoyance","examples":["This traffic is making me crazy! For goodness' sake,
can't we go any faster?","For goodness' sake, why didn't we order movie tickets
ahead of time? The line is so long that we'll probably
miss the beginning!","For goodness' sake, don't tell anyone else about this!","Will you hurry up, for goodness' sake?","For God's sake, put it on the coaster."],"media":[]}]
origin: Same as: for God's, heaven's, etc. sake

name: for heaven's sake
meanings: [{"name":"used to make a statement or question more forceful or to express surprise, anger, etc.","examples":["For heaven's sake, turn down that music!","For heaven's sake, why are you up so early? Go back\nto bed, so I can sleep!","For heaven's sake, how can it be so hot outside? I\nwish we had air conditioning."],"media":[]}]

name: fourth-rate
meanings:
[{"name":"of inferior quality; not the best","examples":["The company introduced a new car model, but the
production quality is still fourth-rate, like all their
other cars.","My assessment is that he's a fourth-rate man with
a first-rate education. He's been well trained, but
I don't think he understands what our company's
about."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: first-rate
Synonyms: second-rate; third-rate
Expressions using rate generally go only as far as fourth-rate.
Second-, third-, and fourth-rate are synonymous. There are
no degrees of inferiority. They are all opposites of first-rate.

name: from day one / since day one
meanings: [{"name":"the very beginning; the very first day","examples":["Their new employee caused trouble from day one.\nThey fired him only a month after hiring him.","You haven't done anything right since day one! You're fired! ","She was unhappy with her new car from day one."],"media":[]}]

name: get a hold of oneself
meanings:
[{"name":"to get control of ones' thoughts and emotions and stop behaving in a foolish or uncontrolled way","examples":["Stop crying, Mary. Get a hold of yourself and calm
down.","The man narrowly missed hitting another car on the
highway. Afterward, he pulled off the road to try to
get hold of himself.","Get a hold of yourself and tell me what happened."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: get it/(one's) act together; go to pieces
The expression get (a) hold of oneself emphasizes emotional
control whereas get one's act together emphasizes mental or
physical control.

name: get a hold of someone
meanings:
[{"name":"to contact someone or communicate with someone, usually by telephone; [get/have] the location of someone ","examples":["The real estate agent couldn't get hold of them before
the house was sold to someone else. They never
answered their phone.","The ambulance brought the little boy to the hospital,
and the doctor got a hold of the boy's parents before
he operated.","Try to get ahold of a plumber, would you?","I got hold of her just as she was going out the door.","I was able to get a hold of the factory and cancel the order."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. [get/have] a grasp of someone","examples":["I got hold of him and dragged him back from the edge just in time.","I took ahold of his hand and held on tight."],"media":[]}]

name: get a hold of something
meanings: [{"name":"to acquire or obtain something","examples":["I was able to get hold of a copy of the magazine, but\nit was the last one.","Sarah was very lucky to get a hold of an extra ticket\nto the ballgame.","Where can I get hold of some stamps?","Where can I get hold of today's newspaper?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is used to describe something that is somewhat
difficult to acquire, perhaps because it is rare.

name: get a leg up on / have a leg up on
meanings: [{"name":"to have an advantage over others","examples":["The company has a leg up on the competition thanks to the recent publicity.","I'm going to get a leg up on next year's budget by\nplanning several months in advance.","I have a leg up on Walter when it comes to getting around town, since I have a car.","I want to practice indoors all winter and get a leg up on Ken, since he thinks he can beat me at tennis."],"media":[]}]

name: get a move on
meanings: [{"name":"hurry up; stop wasting time","examples":["Get a move on! Everyone is waiting for you.","Come on, you two, get a move on!","We need to get a move on if we're going to catch that train.","Mary! Get a move on! We can't wait all day."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782438046/phrases/v2eygmtnlho2l4qmnxx5.mp4","publicId":"phrases/v2eygmtnlho2l4qmnxx5","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["\"get a move on\" vs \"move on\"",["\"get a move on\" - Hurry up; Speed up; start moving faster.","\"move on\" - Emotional Progress / Topic Transition / Physical Departure / Career or Life Change"]]]

name: get a word in edgewise/edgeways
meanings:
[{"name":"to manage to say something when other people are talking and ignoring you; to insert a word or sentence into an otherwise one-sided conversation","examples":["It was such an exciting conversation that I could hardly get a word in edgewise","Mary talks so fast that nobody can get a word in edgeways.","Elizabeth talked on and on. No one else got a chance
to tell her what he or she thought because they
couldn't get a word in edgewise.","Jerry finally got a word in edgewise when Tony
stopped talking to take a drink.","I'll be lucky if I get a word in edgewise."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The word edgewise means to turn something to its narrowest
dimension. The expression suggests that one must put one's
words edgewise in order to squeeze them into a conversation
where words are run together very tightly. The expression is
usually used in the negative, can't get a word in edgewise,
meaning that one is unable to get into the conversation
because someone else is doing all the talking.

name: get by (on a small amount of money)
meanings: [{"name":"to survive with only a small amount of money","examples":["We're getting by now, but if we get an unexpected bill\nit would bankrupt us.","How can he get by on so little money?","I can't get by on that much money. ","That is a very small amount of money to live on. No one could get by.","When we were students we got by on very little money."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonyms: keep one's head above water; make ends meet

name: get by (someone or something)
meanings: [{"name":"to move past someone or something","examples":["I need to get by this intersection, and then I will stop and look at the tires.","Please let me get by.","He's the kind of guy who doesn't let a good opportunity get by him."],"media":[]}]

name: get by (with something)
meanings: [{"name":"to satisfy the minimum requirements","examples":["I was failing geometry, but managed to get by with a D.","I took the bar exam and just barely got by."],"media":[]}]

name: get by (without someone or something)
meanings: [{"name":"to survive without someone or something","examples":["I can't get by without you.","We can probably get by without two cars.","There is tremendous pressure on families trying to get by without health insurance."],"media":[]}]

name: get it in the neck

each other as the good fit of a hand in a glove.

name: hang-up
meanings: [{"name":"an obsession, problem, or concern about something; a permanent and unreasonable feeling of worry about a particular thing, especially about a particular feature of yourself","examples":["She claims the marriage failed due to his emotional hang-ups.","Everyone has their own hangups.","He went bald very young and has a terrible hang-up about it."],"media":[]},{"name":"a problem/difficulty that causes a delay","examples":["The doctor never got back to me with the test results – I guess there was some hang-up over the weekend.","It is best to fix hangups as soon as they occur.","The machines had only minor hang-ups, and those were resolved quickly."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is used to describe an obsession or concern
that may be regarded as somewhat eccentric, unreasonable
or illogical.

name: hanky-panky
meanings:
[{"name":"mischievous behavior or activity; suspicious activity; dishonest or immoral behavior; questionable or underhanded activity","examples":["The children's mother thought that the children were
just a little too quiet. She thought they must be up
to some hanky panky.","The manager in charge of the warehouse suspected
that someone was stealing some of the equipment
stored there. There was definitely some hanky panky
going on.","I warned them not to try any hanky-panky.","financial/political hanky-panky"],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: monkey business

name: happy-go-lucky
meanings:
[{"name":"carefree","examples":["Nothing depresses Charlie—he always sees the bright
side of life. He's really a happy-go-lucky guy.","Sometimes sad events happen, and you just have to
learn to deal with them along with the good times.
Life can't always be happy-go-lucky."],"media":[]}]

name: hard act to follow / tough act to follow
meanings:
[{"name":"someone or something that has been so successful that it is very difficult for the person or thing coming next to be as good","examples":["The last manager of this department was hard-
working and well-liked by everyone. I doubt anyone
else will be as good as she was—she will be a hard act
to follow."," My job here is fun, stimulating, and the pay is good.
If I ever leave, it will be a hard act to follow.","Yesterday's thrilling victory will be a tough act to follow.","Bill's speech was excellent. It was a tough act to follow, but my speech was good too.","In spite of the fact that I had a tough act to A follow, I did my best."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from the time of vaudeville
when a show consisted of several acts, each by different actors.
It was hard to succeed if one's act followed another that was
extremely popular, because the audience would compare the
two and expect the second act to measure up to the high
standard of the first.

name: hard/tough row to hoe
meanings:
[{"name":"a difficult task to carry out; heavy set of burdens","examples":["Going to medical school is not going to be easy. In
fact, it will be a tough row to hoe.","Life can be a hard row to hoe. You have to put a roof
over your head and food on the table, and it's not
easy for anyone.","Teachers have a tough row to hoe in today's schools.","It's a tough row to hoe, but hoe it you will.","This is not an easy task. This is a hard row to hoe."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that using a hoe (a garden tool) to
weed a row of plants can sometimes be a difficult task.

name: have/get the last laugh
meanings:
[{"name":"to outsmart or get revenge on someone who thinks he or she has been clever; to succeed when others thought you would not; succeed or win after being laughed at or doubted by others","examples":["The boys thought they had tricked the girls by
locking them in the kitchen, but the girls had the last
laugh when the boys got hungry and realized they
couldn't get in.","Mark was lazy and decided to let Roger do most of
the work. But Roger had the last laugh because, in
the end, Mark got none of the credit.","She was fired from the company last year, but she had the last laugh when she was hired by their main rival at twice the salary.","John laughed when I got a D on the final exam. I got the last laugh, though. He failed the course.","Mr. Smith said I was foolish when I bought an old building. I had the last laugh when
I sold it a month later for twice what I paid for it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: he who laughs last, laughs best; laugh all the way
to the bank

name: heart-to-heart
meanings:
[{"name":"sincere; frank; a serious conversation between two people, usually close friends, in which they talk honestly about their feelings","examples":["I have to talk to you about something that is serious
and very important to both of us. I want to have a
