never talk to me seriously about things that are
important. Don't you ever talk heart to heart with
anyone?","He called his father for a heart-to-heart talk.","You need to have a heart-to-heart with your husband and tell him how you're feeling.","We had a heart-to-heart over a cup of coffee."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is usually used to describe an important and
sincere talk between two people.

name: hell to pay
meanings:
[{"name":"serious trouble; dire consequences","examples":["If he's late there'll be hell to pay.","There'll be hell to pay if she doesn't get the money in time.","I don't know how the accident happened, but the car
fender is ruined. I'm going to have hell to pay when I
get home.","Your parents told you not to be late getting home
again. If you don't get home on time tonight, you'll
have hell to pay.","I came home after three in the morning and had hell to pay."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonyms: in Dutch; in hot water; in the doghouse

name: hem and haw
meanings: [{"name":"to pause a lot and avoid saying something directly; to say “ah” and “eh” when speaking— avoiding saying something meaningful; to be uncertain and take a long time deciding something","examples":["My sister hemmed and hawed and then finally admitted she'd worn my shoes.","You don't have to be afraid to tell me what happened.\nStop hemming and hawing and get to the point.","The question surprised her and she hemmed and hawed a bit before answering.","We hemmed and hawed for months before actually deciding to buy the house.","The city council hemmed and hawed for a year before deciding to build the new school."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: beat around the bush; stonewall
The expression probably originates from the sounds one might
make when clearing one's throat and trying to introduce a
delicate subject.

name: hit-or-miss
meanings:
[{"name":"unplanned or random; equally likely to succeed or fail","examples":["Sometimes Ann is at home when I drop by to visit
her, and sometimes she's not. It's hit or miss catching
her at home.","The repairman's work is hit or miss. Sometimes the
machine works when he's finished fixing it, and
sometimes it doesn't.","The service you get in these big stores can be hit-or-miss, depending on the salesperson you talk to.","There was no planning. It was just hit and miss.","We handed out the free tickets hit or miss. Some people got one. Others got five or six"],"media":[]}]

name: hit pay dirt / strike pay dirt
meanings: [{"name":"do, find, or get something that results in money or success","examples":["Technology is only a tool; the real pay dirt is the customer.","His third book was published in 2010 and struck pay dirt.","They invested their money in oil wells in Texas and\nthey hit pay dirt. Now they're the richest people I\nknow.","When investigators examined phone records, they hit pay dirt.","He finally struck pay dirt last year when he was appointed head of the company's sales division."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: strike it rich
Compare to: hit the jackpot
The expression originates from the mining and gold-rush days
when a person could become rich if he or she found dirt with
gold in it.

name: hitch/thumb a ride
meanings:
[{"name":"to get a ride in a passing vehicle","examples":["Her car broke down, so she had to hitch a ride with a passing truck.","He hitched a ride to and from work with one of his colleagues.","Julian had no car, but he needed to visit his mother
in the hospital in another town, so he hitched a ride.","The boys had no way to get to the beach, about 60
miles away. They decided to stand by the side of the
highway and thumb a ride.","We thumbed a ride to Las Vegas.","I've never thumbed a ride myself but I know a few people who have."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression thumb a ride denotes that the traveler solicits
the ride by standing on the side of the road and extending his
or her thumb toward passing cars.

name: hold one's breath
meanings:
[{"name":"to wait for something to happen, often feeling anxious; wait for something to happen because it probably won't happen soon, if at all","examples":["Shirley said she would come, but don't hold your
breath. She often doesn't show up, even when she
says she will.","I'm hoping they will decide to buy the house, but I'm
not holding my breath. So many things can go wrong
with the deal.","Fans held their breath waiting for the final whistle.","Now it's a case of holding our breath till we hear the final outcome.","I expect the mail to be delivered soon, but I'm
not holding my breath. It's often late."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to stop breathing for a short period, on purpose","examples":["Do you hold your breath when you
dive into the water?","I can't hold my breath for very long."],"media":[]}]

name: hold one's own
meanings:
[{"name":"to be able to withstand opposition or attack; to do just as well as other people; to maintain your position or condition despite difficulties","examples":["Sarah may be the smallest child in the class, but
when it comes to defending herself, she can hold her
own.","We didn't think Mark was very good at speaking, but
he really held his own in that debate.","She can hold her own in any argument.","He was very sick, but now he's holding his own.","I can hold my own in a footrace any day.","She was unable to hold her own, and she had to quit."],"media":[]}]

name: hold one's tongue
meanings:
[{"name":"to keep silent; to refrain from speaking; to refrain from saying something unpleasant; keep one's thoughts to oneself","examples":["Hold your tongue, John. You can't talk to me that way!","I'm going to have to learn to hold my tongue (= to not say things that upset people).","I felt like scolding her, but I held my tongue.","Ella wanted to talk to Bob immediately, but there
were too many people around, so she held her tongue
and waited until they were alone.","The young boy began shouting at his mother, and she
lost her temper and told him to hold his tongue. She
told him it was not polite to talk to anyone like that.","I've listened to you criticizing him and I've held my
tongue, but I can't any longer. Now I'm going to tell
you some of the positive sides of his character."],"media":[]}]

name: hold/keep (someone/something) at bay
meanings:
[{"name":"to prevent someone from moving closer; to control something and prevent it from causing you problems","examples":["I held the attacker at bay while Mary got away and called the police.","The doctors have been able to keep her illness at bay for several months.","The hen held the dog at bay while her baby chicks ran
for safety.","They held the soldiers at bay with their swords for
as long as they could, but in the end, they were
defeated.","She fought to keep her unhappiness at bay.","I have to keep the bill collectors at bay until I get my paycheck.","The dogs held the bear at bay while I got my gun loaded."],"media":[]}]

name: hold water
meanings:
[{"name":"to be credible or sound; to stand up to scrutiny; to make sense; If a reason, argument, or explanation holds water, it is true","examples":["The politician argued that they had to raise taxes,
but the reasons he gave didn't hold water.","Her alibi just didn't hold water.","Two scientists claimed that they had achieved fusion
at room temperature. Other scientists wanted to test
the theory to see if it would hold water.","The jury convicted her because her story just didn't hold water.","The police's theory will not hold water. The suspect has an ironclad alibi."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is used in reference to arguments or ideas
rather than people.

name: hook, line, and sinker
meanings:
[{"name":"completely; totally; without hesitation or reservation","examples":["The children made up such a believable story that
their mother fell for it hook, line and sinker.","The salesman was such a smooth talker, he could
make anyone believe his stories. People always
swallowed them hook, line and sinker.","I forged the note and the teacher fell for it hook, line, and sinker.","They believed every word hook, line, and sinker.","She fell for our story hook, line, and sinker."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression often used with FALL FOR/
SWALLOW (SOMETHING). 
The expression originates from fishing. One expects the fish to
bite only the hook, but in some cases the fish might be taken
in so completely and foolishly that it swallows not only the
hook but the fishing line and the sinker as well.

name: horse around
meanings:
[{"name":"to behave in a silly and noisy way; to engage in horseplay(rough or boisterous play)","examples":["He was horsing around in the kitchen and broke my favorite bowl.","This fellow at work keeps horsing around.","The boys were horsing around on the boat when one of them fell overboard.","Don't forget we're in a library, boys. People are trying
to read quietly and concentrate on their work. Stop
horsing around.","The children should not horse around in the garage.
There are too many dangerous tools in there.","We spent the entire afternoon just horsing around."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: clown around; monkey around; fool around
Horse around emphasizes the physical nature of the play
whereas clown around means to act silly, and monkey around
means to fiddle or tinker with something.

name: horse sense
meanings:
[{"name":"common sense; shrewdness; cleverness; practical thinking","examples":["You just don't have any horse sense when it comes
to looking after yourself. You stay up late, don't get
enough sleep and eat poorly.","I took my father along when I went to shop for a new
car. He has real horse sense and can spot a good deal.","Pure horse sense should tell you it's dangerous to play with matches.","His words of wisdom are tinged with wit and old-fashioned horse sense.","My bet is that Smith has that political horse sense.","Bob is no scholar but he has a lot of horse sense."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from the idea that a person
who knew what to look for in a horse (i.e., had a sense for
horses) could find the best horses to buy.

name: huff and puff
meanings: [{"name":"to breathe in a loud and heavy way because of physical effort; to breathe very hard; to pant as one exerts effort","examples":["John came up the stairs huffing and puffing.","He huffed and puffed and finally got up the steep hill.","He was huffing and puffing when he got to the top of the stairs.","All the runners were out of breath and were huffing\nand puffing by the end of the marathon."],"media":[]},{"name":"to show one is annoyed or angry; to complain loudly and express disapproval","examples":["She'll huff and puff for a while, but she'll calm down later.","They huffed and puffed about the price but eventually they paid up."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A huff is a feeling of displeasure or resentment. A puff is a
burst of breath.

name: if/when push comes to shove
meanings: [{"name":"if the situation becomes serious","examples":["If push comes to shove, we can always sell the car.","The president isn't a forceful woman, but if push\ncomes to shove, she stands firm and lets her feelings\nbe known.","When push comes to shove, you know I'll be on your side.","If push comes to shove at the meeting, the front office can back you up with some statistics."],"media":[]}]

name: in a bind / in a fix / in a jam
meanings:
[{"name":"in a tight or difficult situation; stuck on a problem; in trouble","examples":["Can I borrow $10 from you? I'm in a bind. The banks
have closed and I need to stop at the supermarket on
the way home.","I'm in a bind. I owe a lot of money.","Whenever I get into a jam, I ask my supervisor for help.","When things get busy around here, we get in a bind. We could use another helper.","I'm in a jam. I have a doctor's appointment at the
same time as I have to pick the children up from
school. Do you think you could get the children for
me?","John is in a fix because he lost his wallet."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: over a barrel; between the devil and the deep blue
sea; between a rock and a hard place.
In a bind is less dramatic than the later ones,
which would be used when a problem has no apparent solution.

name: in a pinch
meanings: [{"name":"in a bad situation when help is needed; in an emergency; if necessary; as a substitute","examples":["My car has only six seats but it can carry eight people\nin a pinch.","We would prefer one large double room at the hotel,\nbut two small ones will be all right in a pinch.","I can help out in a pinch if you need a babysitter.","In a pinch, you can substitute another ingredient in the recipe.","A piece of clothing can be used as a bandage in a pinch.","In a pinch, you can use folded paper to prop up the table leg so the table won't rock."],"media":[]}]

name: in a rut
meanings: [{"name":"in a boring routine; too fixed in one particular type of job, activity, method, etc., and needing to change","examples":["My life has gotten into a rut.","I try not to get into a rut.","I'm tired of this job. I do the same old thing day in\nand day out. I'm in a rut.","Don't let yourself get into a rut. Try something new\nfrom time to time, and you won't get bored."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: on a treadmill
Compare to: old hat

A rut is a groove or narrow track pressed into a dirt road that
catches the wheel of a vehicle and forces the vehicle to go
in a restricted path that the driver is unable to alter. The
expression connotes going in a direction or doing an activity
without being able to vary it.
(As when the wheels of a buggy travel in the ruts worn into
the ground by other buggies making it easiest to go exactly
the way all the other buggies have gone before. *Typically: D be ~; get ~.)

name: in black and white
meanings:
[{"name":"in written or printed form","examples":["You can't agree to buy or sell a house with just a
handshake. The agreement has to be in black and
white.","I didn't believe what you were telling me was true,
but here it is in the newspaper in black and white.","I have it in black and white that I'm entitled to three weeks of vacation each year.","I want to see it in black and white."],"media":[]},{"name":"in a way that involves a simple choice between two opposite things (such as good and bad or right and wrong); A black-and-white subject or situation is one in which it is easy to understand what is right and wrong","examples":["Disarmament isn't a black-and-white issue for me.","She sees everything in black and white."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the black and white colors
of ink on paper.

name: in dutch (with)
meanings: [{"name":"in trouble","examples":["My parents said I'd better get home on time or I'll be\nin Dutch.","The boys got in Dutch with the teacher when they\ndidn't turn in their homework.","I'm in Dutch with my parents for my low grades.","You're in Dutch quite often, it seems."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: in hot water, in the doghouse, hell to pay
In the doghouse is less serious and often light-hearted. To have
hell to pay is generally stronger and more serious.

name: in full swing / in high gear / into high gear
meanings:
[{"name":"at the peak of activity or intensity; moving fast or efficiently; used to say that something is or becomes very active, exciting, or productive","examples":["Julie arrived about 30 minutes late and the party was
already in full swing.","The meeting started at 4:00 p.m. It was still in full
swing when the assistant manager arrived a little
after 6:00.","In the summer months, things really get into full swing around here.","We go skiing in the mountains each winter. Things are in high gear there in November.","Fuel prices are expected to rise as the summer travel season kicks/moves into high gear.","Jane: Kate, I think it's time to kick this fight into high gear."],"media":[]}]

name: in one's element
meanings: [{"name":"in a place or situation where one is comfortable and does well; in one's most comfortable or favorite environment; in a natural or comfortable situation or environment","examples":["Diana is in her element when she's in the classroom.\nShe's a natural teacher.","I love being in the country. When I'm in the city, I'm\nlost. I'm out of my element.","Bob stood up to sing in front of his classmates, and you could see he was in his element.","Sally is in her element when she's working with algebra or calculus.","Dhruthi loves to work with color and texture. When he's painting, he's in his element."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: out of (one's) depth; fish out of water; in (way)
over one's head
Out of one's element describes being uncomfortable in an
environment, whereas out of one's depth describes being asked
to perform beyond one's capability.

name: in stitches
meanings:
[{"name":"in a state of uncontrollable laughter; laughing very hard","examples":["Charlie had us in stitches with all his jokes.","The movie sure was funny. I was in stitches!","The movie was hilarious. We couldn't stop laughing.
We were in stitches.","We hired a very funny clown to perform at the
company picnic. He had the children in stitches from
beginning to end."],"media":[]}]

name: in the black
meanings:
[{"name":"making a profit; profitable","examples":["I wish my accounts were in the black.","The company lost money the first four years but now
it's making money and is finally in the black.","The government hasn't been in the black for the last
20 years. It has been spending more money than it

black either. We're just breaking even.","Sally moved the company into the black.","We'd be in the black in 18 months."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: in the red
The expression originates from the color of ink that was used
on the credit side of a business ledger or account book.

name: in the chips/money
meanings: [{"name":"wealthy; having lots of money","examples":["I'm in the chips this month. Let's go squander it.","If I were in the chips, I'd buy a Rolls Royce.","I would quit work and spend the rest of my life\ntravelling around the world if I were in the chips."," You children are asking for so many Christmas\npresents, you'd think I was in the money.","If I am ever in the money, I'll be generous."],"media":[]},{"name":"in the winning position in a race or contest; among the top three finishers in a race (such as a horse race)","examples":["I knew when Jane came around the final turn that she was in the money.","The horses coming in first, second, and third are said to be in the money.","Whatever horse I bet on, it never finishes in the money."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from a game like poker in which
chips represent money.

name: the long run
meanings:
[{"name":"a long period of time after the beginning of something","examples":["She is investing for the long run.","Your solution may cause more problems over the long run.","This deal will cost you more in the long run."," Brian had his own car, but he chose to take the train
to work every day even though it took more time. It
was easier in the long run because he didn't have to
tolerate traffic jams, pay for gas, or look for parking."],"media":[]}]

name: in the loop
meanings:
[{"name":"informed; in the group of persons communicating regularly about a specific plan or project","examples":["I don't know what's going on with the Jones deal since I'm not in the loop.","Bob and Jean are in the loop. They can tell you what's happening.","Sharon had worked with the same team for nearly two years,
but she still didn't feel like she was in the loop. She still had
to ask for information from her colleagues.","I'd be happy to let you work on that project by yourself, but
I'd like to know how you're progressing. Remember to keep
me in the loop, please."],"media":[]}]

name: in the red
meanings:
[{"name":"losing money; not making a profit","examples":["Apparently the company had been in the red for some time before it went out of business.","Many governments operate year after year in the red.
They simply keep borrowing money against the taxes
they expect to collect in the future.","Some years my business makes a profit, but other
years I'm in the red.","What with all those car repairs, we're going to be in the
red this month."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: in the black
The expression originates from the color of ink that was used
on the debit (loss) side of a business ledger or account book.

name: in the mainstream (of something)
meanings:
[{"name":"following the current trends or styles that are popular or are considered normal","examples":["Bob is too old-fashioned to be in the mainstream of modern living.","Andy Warhol was a painter whose work is
representative of the Pop Art period. He was in the
mainstream of Pop Art painting.","That politician advocates very extreme views that are
entirely different from most of the other politicians.
He is out of the mainstream of current politics."],"media":[]}]

name: ivory tower
meanings:
[{"name":"an isolated environment where one is out of touch with everyday reality; a place of retreat where one concentrates on intellectual rather than everyday matters","examples":["Our governor advocates a land value tax system, which is neither commonly used, transparent, or easy to comprehend but is endorsed by ivory tower economists.","The boss felt that he couldn't consider Richard for
the difficult job of manager because Richard seemed
out of touch with the workers. He was isolated in his
ivory tower.","If you didn't spend so much time in your ivory tower, you'd know what people really think! "],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests an ivory (white) tower high above the
masses. An ivory tower is often associated with an academic
or university environment, which is said to be isolated from
the real world, e.g., business and politics.

name: John Hancock/Henry
meanings:
[{"name":"one's signature; an autograph signature","examples":[" If you'll just put your John Hancock on this line at
the bottom of the contract, you can drive the car
away right now.","They sent the check back because he forgot to put
his John Hancock on it.","Let me just scribble my John Hancock on the bottom of the form.","Just put your John Henry on this line, and we'll bring your new car around."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression refers to the signature of the first person to
sign the American Declaration of Independence in 1776. John
Hancock's signature was larger than the others and stood
out clearly.

name: jumping-off place/point
meanings:
[{"name":"a starting place or inspiration; a point or place from which to begin something","examples":[" Kelly used her mother's lasagna recipe as a jumping-
off point, but added her favorite ingredients to make
it the way she liked it.","Joe used sheet music as a jumping-off point for his
song. He played the tune as written, but added to it
as he went.","Tucked among redwood trees, the hut is an ideal jumping-off place for exploring the forested and grassy knolls of Sam McDonald Park.","The local library is a good jumping-off point for your research.","The office job in that company would be a good jumping-off place for a career in advertising."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression is usually used for discussions or creative
pursuits.

name: kangaroo court
meanings:
[{"name":"a mock court set up outside the regular legal system; staged trial where the outcome is set from the beginning","examples":["The rancher and his friends tried and convicted the
horse thieves in a kangaroo court rather than let the
sheriff take them to jail for a trial according to the
law.","The political protesters had been tried and found
guilty in a court of law, and when the verdict was
read, they claimed that the jury and judge had not
been impartial, and that they had been tried in a
kangaroo court.","Bunker said the ordeal felt like a kangaroo court and that the committee had made up their minds before the hearing even began.","Is this a staff meeting or a kangaroo court?","You have turned this interview into a kangaroo court."],"media":[]}]
origin:
A kangaroo court has never been a court by or for kangaroos. 
What is known is that the first kangaroo courts originated in the United States at approximately the time of the 1849 California Gold Rush, and the word saw its earliest use in the southwestern U.S. It first turned up in print in 1853 in a book about Texas.

name: keep one's cool/composure
meanings:
[{"name":"to remain calm; to not become upset or angry","examples":["He kept his cool even though it was clear that he was being unfairly treated.","The performers struggled to keep their composure after several interruptions from the crowd.","I know you're angry, but you've got to try to control
yourself. Keep your cool and don't lose your temper.","It's particularly important to keep your cool in a
traffic jam. It's so easy to get angry and have an
accident.","Relax, man! Just keep your cool. It's hard to keep your cool when you've been cheated."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: hold/lose (one's) temper
Antonym: lose (one's) cool, hot under the collar; see red

name: keep one's eyes open/peeled (for someone or something)
meanings:
[{"name":"to be on the alert; be watchful; to look very carefully for something or someone","examples":["I'm looking for a special edition of a book, and
I haven't found it anywhere. When you're in the
bookstore, please keep your eyes peeled for it, will
you?","They planned to meet Joe on a crowded corner at
lunchtime. He hadn't arrived yet, but as people
walked toward the corner, they kept their eyes peeled
for him.","I'm keeping my eyes open for a sale on winter coats.","Please keep your eyes peeled for Mary. She's due to arrive here any time. Okay. I'll keep my eyes open."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that one's eyelids are pulled back in
order to not miss seeing anything.

name: keep one's head above water
meanings:
[{"name":"to avoid financial failure while having money problems; to manage to survive, especially financially","examples":["We have so much debt that we're barely able to keep our heads above water.","We have so little money that we can hardly keep our heads above water.","Mrs. Robinson has three children to support and she

Compare to: on hold; on ice

Shylock, the Jewish money lender, promising to pay it back

have sunk at sea, Shylock demands payment in the form of
one pound of Antonio's f lesh.

name: pull oneself up by one's (own) bootstraps
meanings: [{"name":"to improve or become a success by one's own efforts","examples":["If Sam had a little encouragement, he could pull himself up by his bootstraps.","Given a chance, I'm sure I can pull myself up by my own bootstraps.","He left school at 15 and pulled himself up by his bootstraps to ultimately head up a company.","Don't expect other people to help you get ahead in\nlife. If you want to get somewhere, you'll have to pull\nyourself up by your bootstraps and do it for yourself."],"media":[]}]

name: pull rank
meanings:
[{"name":"to take advantage of one's superior position (one's rank); to assert one's rank, authority, or position over someone when making a request or giving an order.","examples":["Usually the boss lets all the workers take part in
making important decisions, but this time she pulled
rank and made the decision entirely by herself.","First the army officer tried to persuade his men
politely to his way of thinking. When they still
wouldn't see matters his way, he had to pull rank and
give them orders.","He's their boss, but he doesn't like to pull rank (on them) if he can avoid it.","Car campers may pay, but hikers just spread out a groundsheet and a sleeping bag, and the spot is theirs; only a bear can pull rank.","Don't pull rank on me! I don't have to do what you say! ","When she couldn't get her way politely, she pulled rank and really got some action."],"media":[]}]
origin:
This phrase is based on one of the meanings of the word pull,
specifically ‘to exert control.'

name: pull something off
meanings: [{"name":"to accomplish something that had appeared difficult to finish or achieve","examples":["Do you think you can pull off this deal? Yes, I can pull it off","It's an ambitious plan, so let's see if we can really pull it off. It takes skilled negotiators to pull off a deal like that.","The central bank has pulled off one of the biggest financial rescues of recent years.","The thieves didn't think they would succeed in\nstealing the jewels, but they managed to pull it off.","Do you think we can pull the deal off? It's going to\ntake a lot of late nights and hard work to do it."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to tug or drag something off someone or something else","examples":["Sam pulled the covers off the bed and fell into it, dead tired.","He pulled off his clothes and stepped into the shower."],"media":[]},{"name":"to steer or turn a vehicle off the road; If a vehicle pulls off, it starts moving","examples":["I pulled off the road and rested for a while."," I had to pull off and rest.","The car pulled off and sped up the road."],"media":[]}]

name: put the screws/heat/squeeze on/to (someone or something)
meanings:
[{"name":"to put pressure on someone/something (to do something); to coerce someone/something","examples":["The government is finally putting the screws to an industry that's been evading environmental laws for years.","The senator wanted his colleagues to vote for his
proposal. They owed him a favor, so he began to put
the screws on.","I'd better pay Jim back soon, or I'm afraid he's going
to put the screws to me.","John wouldn't talk, so the police were putting the heat on him to confess. The police know how to put the squeeze on.","When my boss puts
the screws on, he can be very unpleasant. "],"media":[]}]

name: rack one's brain(s)
meanings:
[{"name":"to think very hard in order to try to remember something, solve a problem, etc","examples":["I've been racking my brains, but I just can't remember
where I know that person from.","When John saw the exam questions, he knew he
wasn't prepared. He racked his brain for the answers,
but he couldn't come up with anything useful.","I've been racking my brain all day trying to remember her name.","I racked my brains all afternoon, but couldn't remember where I put the book.","Don't waste any more time racking your brain. Go borrow the book from the library."],"media":[]}]

name: rake/haul someone over the coals
meanings:
[{"name":"Fig. to give someone a severe scolding; to criticize (someone) very severely","examples":["The bank teller stood silently in the manager's office
while she raked him over the coals for the errors he
had made that day.","The principal discovered who was responsible for
the vandalism at the school. He called them into his
office and raked them over the coals.","My mother hauled me over the coals for coming in late last night.","The manager raked me over the coals for being late again."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: chew (someone) out; read (someone) the riot act
Compare to: call (someone) on the carpet; give someone a piece
of (one's) mind; lay down the law
Rake someone over the coals is more severe than call someone
on the carpet.

name: rank and file
meanings:
[{"name":"the non-management workers in a company or the non-leadership members of a political party","examples":["The union asked its rank-and-file members to vote
against the new contract that the company was
offering.","Ted is getting promoted from the rank and file to a
position in middle management. He hasn't had much
schooling, but his years among the workers have
taught him enough to work his way up.","The
rank and file will vote on the proposed contract tomorrow. The last contract was turned down by the rank and file
last year."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. regular soldiers, not the officers. ","examples":["I think there is low morale among the rank and file, sir.","The rank and file usually do exactly as they are told."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression comes from the military formation of soldiers
side by side (rank) and one behind the other (file) forming
large groups such as platoons. The expression has come to be
applied to the non-management workers in a union or company.

name: read something into something
meanings: [{"name":"to give your own meaning to something rather than what was intended","examples":["I think you're reading too much into his comments – he's not trying to trick anyone.","Don't read too much into her leaving so suddenly - she probably just had a train to catch.","This statement means exactly what it says. Don't try to read anything else into it. ","Am I reading too much into your comments?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: read between the lines
The expression suggests that one can see meaning in some
action or something said or written that is not actually there.

name: rhyme or reason
meanings:
[{"name":"good sense or reason; logic; explanation","examples":["The teacher said my report was disorganized. My paragraphs seemed to be without rhyme or reason.","I was walking quietly down the street when I saw this
dog sitting inside its yard. Then, with no rhyme or
reason, the dog jumped over the fence and bit me.","Government money was given out to some people and not to others, apparently without rhyme or reason.","Linda didn't understand why George had done what
he did, so she asked him if there was any rhyme or
reason for his behavior. There was no rhyme or reason to his behavior.","Flares come and go, often with little rhyme or reason."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: method in/to (one's) madness
The expression rhyme or reason, which is usually used in the
negative or in question form, emphasizes the total lack of
apparent rationale for some behavior.

name: roll/put/throw out the welcome mat
meanings: [{"name":"to welcome someone in a warm and friendly way","examples":["The family rolled out the welcome mat for the new guest."],"media":[]}]

name: roll out the red carpet
meanings:
[{"name":"to formally greet or welcome an important guest who has just arrived; to give someone the best treatment and show them the finest hospitality","examples":["The governor rolled out the red carpet for his dinner guests.","The businessmen were given the red-carpet treatment
by the small town in the hopes that they would
decide it was a good place to build a factory.","Please don't go to any trouble for us when we come
to visit. You don't need to roll out the red carpet.","Some people roll out the red carpet when Taylor Swift comes to town, while others give the singer the truly royal treatment."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the practice in which, when
famous or important people are received, a red carpet is often
laid for them to walk on from their carriage or car to the
building they will enter. When someone is given the red-carpet
treatment, he or she is treated like an extra-special person.

name: rule of thumb
meanings:
[{"name":"a rough guide; an unwritten or customary rule based on experience or practice","examples":["In this company there is no written rule about how
long we can take for our lunch break, but the rule of
thumb has been about one hour."," Sometimes it's hard to know how you are supposed to
address people you are meeting for the first time. A
good rule of thumb is to be formal and wait until they
invite you to call them by their first names.","As a rule of thumb, the ice on the lake should be at least two inches thick to support one person.","Going by a rule of thumb, we stop for gas every 200 miles when we are traveling."],"media":[]}]

name: run amok
meanings:
[{"name":"to run around in a frenzied or disorderly way","examples":["There were 50 little kids running amok at the snack bar.","I hope the class will walk in an orderly line as we go
to the other classroom. There's no need to run amok.","The boys startled the sheep, and the sheep pushed
down the gate to the pen and ran amok through the
farm."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the Malay word amuk, which
has a similar meaning.

name: run its course
meanings:
[{"name":"to develop and finish naturally","examples":["The doctor told the patient that there was no
medicine he could give her for her illness. He told
her that she would just have to let the fever run its
course.","The disease usually runs its course in a few days.","There wasn't much the police could do to stop the
demonstration. Since it was peaceful, they let the
demonstration run its course."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["The expression is most often used in terms of illness, but can also be used to describe other processes that have a predictable or established course of events."]]]

name: run-of-the-mill
meanings:
[{"name":"ordinary; average; typical; ordinary and not special or exciting in any way","examples":["He gave a fairly run-of-the-mill speech.","That restaurant serves lots of different dishes, but
none is outstanding or very much better than in any
other restaurant. It's run-of-the-mill.","Ricky was an average student who liked to play
sports as much as the next boy. He was your run-of-
the-mill student.","The restaurant we went to was nothing special—just run-of-the-mill.  The service was good, but the food was run-of-the-mill or worse."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression run-of-the-mill originates from the idea of a
product such as fabric, which was first mass-produced (the
run) in a mill, enabling it to be uniform.

name: run/drive something into the ground
meanings: [{"name":"to carry something too far;  to use something so much that it breaks or stops working","examples":["It was a good joke at first, Tom, but you've run it into the ground. Just because everyone laughed once, you don't have to drive it into the ground.","They decided to run the car into the ground instead of changing it.","I'm going to push this idea with the boss until he\naccepts it, even if I have to run it into the ground."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to pound or force something into the ground","examples":["Use a heavy mallet to drive the stakes into the ground."," Run this post into the ground and nail this sign to it."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: beat a dead horse
Beat a dead horse means to talk about a topic or idea that
cannot succeed (it's dead), whereas run something into the
ground means to talk about a topic or idea that may be viable,
but to do so to excess.

name: sacred cow
meanings:
[{"name":"an idea or thing that cannot be altered; something that people accept or believe to be good or necessary without ever questioning their belief","examples":["Don't suggest that the boss should get rid of one of
his secretaries so that we might hire another clerk.
The subject of his secretaries is a sacred cow.","Even though the country needed to raise more
money to pay for military and social programs, the
president refused to raise taxes. To him “no new
taxes” was a sacred cow that he was unwilling to
sacrifice.","A university education is a sacred cow in the Smith family. Fred is regarded as a failure because he quit school at 16.","Don't talk about eating meat to Pam. Vegetarianism is one of her sacred cows.","Defense spending is a sacred cow in Congress."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the Hindu belief that cows
are sacred and cannot be killed or eaten. The expression is
frequently used to describe an idea or thing that ought to
be changed or altered but cannot be because the authority
forbids it.

name: sales pitch
meanings:
[{"name":"a speech or presentation designed to persuade someone to buy or do something","examples":["We got the whole sales pitch from the car salesman.","I hate door-to-door salespeople. They interrupt
whatever you are doing and keep you standing at
the door with their sales pitch about how good their
product is.","No one knew how Ken had managed to persuade the
boss to give him a bigger office, but they all agreed
he must have had a very good sales pitch.","It's not clear if voters liked the governor's sales pitch enough to reelect her."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: (give someone a) snow job; (give someone a) song
and dance
The expression is usually used to describe a sales situation, but it can also be used figuratively.

name: salt away
meanings:
[{"name":"to store something; to place something in reserve; to save something, esp. money, to use at a later time","examples":["I don't know what Ann does with all the money she
earns, but I know she doesn't spend it on herself. She
must be salting it away for her retirement.","Sometimes we give food to the old man next door,
because we know that he doesn't have much money.
Whenever we do, we try to give him enough so that
he can salt some of it away for another day.","He salted away a fortune over the years and no one ever knew!","I will salt away some money for emergencies."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to store and preserve a food-stuff by salting it","examples":["The farmer's wife salted a lot of fish away for the winter. ","She salted away a lot of food."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: on ice; save (something) for a rainy day
The expression originates from the practice of using salt to
preserve food before storing it.

name: save face
meanings:
[{"name":"to avoid having other people lose respect for oneself; to preserve one's good standing, pride, or high position (after a failure)","examples":["The ambassador was more interested in saving his face than winning the argument. ","We said he left "to pursue other interests" to let him save face, but actually we fired him.","The father lost face when his son was expelled from
school. It was a poor reflection on the man's ability
to influence and control his family.","I knew that what I had done was wrong, but when I
was discovered, I pretended that I hadn't known it
was wrong. That way I was able to save face."],"media":[]}]

name: say a mouthful
meanings:
[{"name":"Fig. to say a lot; to say something very important or meaningful; used to say that what someone said was entirely correct and was worth saying","examples":["John pushed his way in to the party and confronted
Laura. He began to rant and rave and say things
everyone knew he would later regret. He said a
mouthful.","Everybody managed to keep the surprise party a
secret until the last minute, when Jennifer's younger
sister gave it away. She said a mouthful before she
remembered that the party was supposed to be a

origin:
Compare to: go off half-cocked
The expression is usually used to describe when someone says
a lot, not so much in terms of the number of words as in the
significance of the words.

name: scare/frighten out of one's wits/mind
meanings:
[{"name":"so afraid that one is unable to think clearly; frighten very badly","examples":["Don't shout like that! You scared me out of my wits.","Michelle's brother played a prank on her, but she

scared me out of my wits!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
This expression is usually used as an exaggeration to mean
“very frightened for a short time.”

name: scare someone to death
meanings: [{"name":"to scare someone very much","examples":["You nearly scared me to death.\n","The dentist always frightens me to death.","She scared me to death when she screamed."],"media":[]}]

name: scared/frightened to death
meanings: [{"name":"very afraid; frightened or anxious","examples":["I don't want to go to the dentist today. I'm frightened to death. ","I'm frightened to death of spiders.","She was scared to death of flying."],"media":[]}]

name: screw loose / loose screw
meanings:
[{"name":"to be silly or eccentric; to seem crazy","examples":["Her brother definitely has a screw loose – I don't really trust him.","He's sort of strange. I think he's got a loose screw. Yes, he has a screw loose somewhere. He wears a heavy jacket in the middle of summer.","Sometimes Mr. Simpson talks to himself, and
sometimes he imagines that he sees creatures from
outer space. I think he has a screw loose."," The old lady on the bench will tell you the story of
her life if you give her a chance. I imagine she's just
lonely or she has a loose screw somewhere."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: bats in (one's) belfry; out to lunch; off (one's)
rocker

name: second-guess
meanings:
[{"name":"to criticize someone's decision after it has been made, and say what you think is wrong with it; to guess what someone will do or what will happen; try to understand someone's reason for doing something","examples":["No one knows for sure why the boss quit so abruptly,

was leaving her husband. She offered no explanation
and told everyone who asked that it was none of

name: second-rate
meanings:
[{"name":"of second or inferior quality or value; mediocre","examples":["This hotel isn't the best. It's really a second-rate
place.","When they remodeled their kitchen, they bought
all new appliances of the best quality. They wanted
nothing that was second-rate."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: third-rate; fourth-rate
Antonym: first-rate
Expressions using rate generally go only as far as fourth-rate.
Second-, third-, and fourth-rate are synonymous. There are
no degrees of inferiority. They are all opposites of first-rate.

name: second thoughts (about someone or something)
meanings: [{"name":"to change your opinion about something or start to doubt it; reconsideration or a revised opinion of a previous often hurried decision","examples":[" I know we've already made the commitment to buy\nthat house, but now I'm having second thoughts\nabout it. Are you sure it was a wise decision?","I'm beginning to get second thoughts about Tom.","You're giving me second thoughts about going there. I'm having second thoughts too.","The audience gave him the raspberry, which gave him some second thoughts about his choice of career."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: cold feet.
Whereas get cold feet means to change one's mind because
of doubts, have second thoughts means only to begin to have
doubts. One may or may not change one's mind based on
second thoughts.
(*Typically: get ~ ; have ~ ; give someone ~ .)

name: Think nothing of it / Don't think anything of it / Don't give it another thought / Don't give it a (second) thought
meanings: [{"name":"You're welcome.; It was nothing.; I was glad to do it","examples":["Mary: Thank you so much for driving me home. John: Think nothing of it.","Sue: It was very kind of you to bring the kids back all the way out here.  Alice: Think nothing of it. I was delighted to do it.","Bob: I really can't begin to thank you.\nTom: Don't think anything of it. It's my pleasure."],"media":[]},{"name":"You did no harm at all. (A very polite way of reassuring someone that an action has not harmed or hurt the speaker.)","examples":["Sue: Oh, sorry. I didn't mean to bump you! Bob: Think nothing of it.","Jane: I hope I didn't hurt your feelings when I said you were too loud. Bill: Don't give it a second thought. I was too loud."],"media":[]}]

name: on second thought
meanings: [{"name":"Fig. after thinking about something again; having given something more thought; having reconsidered something","examples":["Can I have a cup of coffee, please? - actually, on second thought (= after thinking about it further), I will have a glass of water.","On second thought, let's not go to a movie.","On second thought, maybe you should sell your house and move into an apartment. ","You know, on second thought, I won't be driving you to school. The walk will do you good."],"media":[]}]

name: see red
meanings: [{"name":"to get angry","examples":["Whenever I think of the needless destruction of trees, I see red.","Bill really saw red when the tax bill arrived.","John saw red when his boss tried to make everyone\nin the office believe that John had made the mistake.","My father sees red when I come home late."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: fly off the handle; blow (one's) stack; lose (one's)
temper
The expression probably originates from the idea that a bull
is supposed to become enraged when it sees the bullfighter's
red cape.

name: see something through
meanings:
[{"name":"to finish something one has started; to continue doing a job or activity until it is finished, especially when it is difficult","examples":["The boy had said he would do the job, but it was more
work than he had expected. However, he decided to
see the job through because it was the right thing to
do.","It wasn't a pleasant task, but Jane knew she had to

origin: Compare to: see through (something/someone)

name: see through someone or something / see right through someone or something
meanings:
[{"name":"Lit. [for one's vision] to penetrate something clear or opaque or a person.","examples":["Of course, I can see through the window! ","With x-rays, they can see through your body! ","Bob: Can you see through the wall?
Jane: Yeah, I can see right through.","He's looking at me like he can see right through my soul."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. understand or detect the true nature of someone or something; not be fooled by a false front or disguise that someone presents in order to mislead","examples":["The little boy told his mother that he was not the
one who had taken the candy, but his mother saw
through his story because she could see chocolate on
his face."," The pair had everyone convinced they were a
luckless but well-intentioned couple. Very few people
could see through them, and many gave them money,
food, and clothing.","They were very friendly, but it didn't take long to see through them.","She saw through his excuse at once.","Who is she kidding? Like he can't see right through the multiple-book-buying ploy?"],"media":[]}]
origin: Compare to: see (something) through

name: see the light
meanings: [{"name":"to understand something clearly at last; to understand something you did not understand before","examples":[" Wendy was completely fooled by the young man. We\nall wondered when she would see the light.","They finally saw the light when we explained the\nsituation to them.","It wasn't until I was in my thirties that I saw the light and started to work hard.","After a lot of studying and asking many questions, I finally saw the light.","I know that geometry is difficult. Keep working at it. You'll see the light pretty soon."],"media":[]}]

name: see which way the wind is blowing
meanings:
[{"name":"to determine what is the most expedient thing to do under the conditions at hand","examples":["We studied the whole situation to see which way the wind was blowing and decided to avoid any con- flict at that time. ","Sam failed to see which way the wind was blowing and got himself caught up in an argument.","Fred has learned to survive in his job by bending to
the will and desires of each boss he has had. He sees
which way the wind blows and changes his behavior
accordingly.","Her political opinions depend on which way the wind is blowing."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression is often used in reference to a political or
diplomatic situation. It has the negative connotation of being
opportunistic.

name: sell someone a bill of goods
meanings:
[{"name":"Fig. to get someone to believe something that isn't true; to deceive someone. ","examples":["Don't pay any attention to what John says. He's just trying to sell you a bill of goods.","I'm not selling you a bill of goods. What I say is true."," The ring looked real on television, but when it
arrived in the mail, Paula knew she had been sold a
bill of goods.","The project manager told us that construction would
be finished by August; it wasn't until later that we
discovered he had sold us a bill of goods."],"media":[]}]

name: set someone's teeth on edge
meanings:
[{"name":"to irritate; to upset very much","examples":["I wish you wouldn't talk during the movie. The noise
really sets my teeth on edge."," That woman always pretends like she's giving me a
compliment, but I think she's insulting me. It sets my
teeth on edge.","Her overbearing manner usually sets my teeth on edge.","Tom's teeth were set on edge by the incessant screaming of the children.","The very thought of doing that set her teeth on edge."],"media":[]}]

name: in seventh heaven
meanings: [{"name":"blissfully happy","examples":["Ann was really in seventh heaven when she got a car of her own.","I'd be in seventh heaven if I had a million dollars.","When I told her she was going to be a grandmother, she was in seventh heaven."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonyms: on cloud nine; walking on air

name: shoot the breeze
meanings:
[{"name":" to chat casually and without purpose; to talk idly","examples":["During our lunch hour, we like to sit around and
shoot the breeze. We talk about all kinds of things
and nothing in particular.","I sometimes wonder if government employees ever
work. They seem to sit around all day talking to
each other. They always seem to be just shooting the
breeze.","We sat on the porch until late at night, just shooting the breeze.","We spent the entire afternoon just shooting the breeze.","It was good to shoot the breeze with you, Mary."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Shoot the breeze often includes the idea of chatting because
one has some time to “kill” or is waiting for some amount of
time to pass.

name: shot in the dark
meanings:
[{"name":"a wild guess; a very general attempt","examples":["It was just a shot in the dark. I had no idea I was exactly correct. ","Come on, try it. Even a shot in the dark may win.","I don't know what they would like for a wedding gift,
but we could take a shot in the dark and get them
something for the kitchen.","Charles didn't really know the reason why his son was
in a bad mood, but he guessed that perhaps he had
gotten some bad grades. Charles' s guess was a shot
in the dark."],"media":[]}]

name: sit tight
meanings:
[{"name":"to wait; to wait patiently, often in an anxious situation","examples":["The stock market was falling sharply, but Lucy didn't
panic and sell her stocks. Instead she sat tight and
waited for the market to rise again.","Margie called late at night to tell us that her car had
broken down and to ask us to come and pick her up.
We told her to sit tight and we would be there as soon
as possible."," Just relax and sit tight. I'll be right with you.","We were waiting in line for the gates to open when someone came out and told us to sit tight because it wouldn't be much longer before we could go in."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: keep (one's) cool.
The expression sit tight is often used in situations of danger
or panic or in situations where a calm, cool head is needed. It
always uses the adjective “tight” rather than the grammatically
correct “tightly”.

name: sixth sense
meanings:
[{"name":"a supposed power to know or feel things that are not perceptible by the five senses of sight, hear- ing, smell, taste, and touch","examples":["My sixth sense told me to avoid going home by my usual route. Later I discovered there had been a fatal accident on it.","Jane's sixth sense demanded that she not trust Tom, even though he seemed honest enough.","Carrie has an uncanny sense of what's going to
happen in the future. It's almost as though she has a
sixth sense.","They had a terrible feeling that something bad had
happened to their son. They had no rational reason
for thinking it; it was just a sixth sense."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the idea that, whereas
everyone is born with the five senses of sight, hearing, taste,
touch, and smell, some people seem to have an additional
sense that enables them to perceive events or things that
others cannot.

name: sleep like a baby/log/rock
meanings:
[{"name":"to sleep very well; to sleep so soundly that noise doesn't wake the person","examples":["Steve had to have two alarm clocks set to wake him
up because one was never loud enough. He slept like
a log.","As a rule, the baby never wakes up during the night.
She sleeps like a rock, and even the noise of the TV
doesn't wake her.",""How did you sleep?" "So well - I slept like a log, the bed was so comfortable."","Everyone in our family sleeps like a log, so no one heard the thunderstorm in the middle of the night.","Nothing can wake me up. I usually sleep like a baby."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that it is as difficult to wake such a
person as it would be to wake a log or a rock.

name: slip through someone's fingers
meanings:
[{"name":"Lit. to slide through and out of one's grasp","examples":["The glass slipped through his fingers and crashed to the ground.","The rope slipped through
his fingers and followed the anchor to the bottom of the lake."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to escape from someone; to elude someone's capture or control","examples":["The prisoner slipped through the sheriff's fingers.","You shouldn't let a job/man like that slip through your fingers!","We didn't want to let the opportunity slip through our fingers.","They had the opportunity to make a lot of money,
but they didn't act quickly enough and the chance
slipped through their fingers."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: miss the boat.
The expression suggests that the thing or person one wants
to keep is slippery or hard to hold on to, like water or sand.
Despite the fact that one tries to grasp it, it disappears
between one's fingers.

name: slow burn
meanings:
[{"name":"to be quietly angry; a slow, controlled show of anger","examples":["Jack didn't get promoted to a new job and, although
he hasn't said anything about it, I know he's doing a
slow burn.","I do a slow burn every time my husband expects me
to look after the children while he plays golf with his
friends.","When angered, Ellen was given to spontaneous outbursts, while her partner Terry would do a slow burn.","I did a slow burn while I was waiting in line for a refund."],"media":[]}]

name: slow/quick off the mark
meanings: [{"name":"slow/quick to act or understand to an event or a situation","examples":["Katherine succeeds at whatever she attempts\nbecause she‘s very much aware of what's going on\naround her. She's quick off the mark.","As soon as the opportunity arose, he was quick off the mark in exploiting it.","The police were certainly quick off the mark in reaching the scene of the accident.","Yes, I'm afraid Tony is a bit slow off the mark when it comes to trigonometry.","If you are always that slow off the mark you will never win the race."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests a race in which the participants are
slow [or quick] to leave the point of departure (the mark).

name: snowball's chance in hell
meanings:
[{"name":"no chance at all —used in negative statements to say that something is extremely unlikely or impossible","examples":["Let's be honest—there isn't a snowball's chance in hell that we'll win this game.","He doesn't have a snowball's chance in hell of getting the job.","Kay has a snowball's chance in hell of getting into
