scores.","They don't have a snowball's chance in hell of raising
enough money to send him on that trip, because
they don't have anything worth selling.","She doesn't have a snowball's chance in hell of getting it done on time. I know I don't have a hope in hell, but I'll try anyway."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that the likelihood of something
happening is as small as the probability that a snowball will
not melt in the fires of hell.

name: crow about something
meanings:
[{"name":"Lit. [for a rooster] to cry out or squawk about something. ","examples":["The rooster was crowing about something—you never know what. "],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. [for someone] to brag about something (an exceptional accomplishment, achievement, etc)","examples":[" We're really proud of Janie. She got an outstanding
score on her entrance exams. It really is something to
crow about.","If you let Bill win, he'll never let us hear the end of
it. You'll just be giving him something to crow about.","She is crowing over her new car.","It is not the first time he has crowed about his achievements."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: feather in (one's) cap
Antonym: nothing to write home about
The expression suggests the sound a rooster makes to draw
attention to itself.

name: sour grapes
meanings:
[{"name":"something that one cannot have and so disparages as if it were never desirable; a situation where a person criticizes something or someone out of jealousy","examples":["When Nicolas found out that he wasn't going to
be promoted, he told people that he hadn't really
wanted to stay with the company anyway. It was a
case of sour grapes.","I don't think it's such a great job - and that's not just sour grapes because I didn't get it.","I know this sounds like sour grapes, but I'm just as
glad that I didn't get into college. I think I'd rather
get a job.","Of course you want to buy this expensive jacket. Criticizing it is just sour grapes, but you still really want it.","His criticisms are just sour grapes."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from Aesop's fable about a fox that
wanted some grapes from a vine but was unable to jump high
enough to get them. In disgust, he claimed that they weren't
worth having anyway because they were probably sour.

name: speak of the devil / talk of the devil
meanings:
[{"name":"an expression used when someone who is being talked about has just appeared","examples":[""Well, speak of the devil! We were just talking about you!"","Jan brought up the subject of Tom at the meeting
when, all of a sudden, he walked in. “Speak of the
devil!” said Jan. “We were just talking about you.”","“Where's Ernie?” I asked, just as Ernie came through
the door. “Here I am,” said Ernie. “Speak of the
devil,” I said."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression has a slightly negative connotation, because of
the reference to the devil, but it is usually meant humorously.

name: speak one's mind
meanings:
[{"name":"to tell someone how one feels or what one thinks; to say frankly what one thinks","examples":["If you don't agree with him, don't be afraid to speak your mind.","I've always been honest and open with you about
how I feel and what I think. I've never been shy
about speaking my mind.","Donald wondered if he could speak his mind freely,
but decided it would be best if he kept his opinions
to himself. So he didn't tell her what he really
thought about her.","Please let me speak my mind, and then you can do whatever you wish.","You can always depend on John to speak his mind. He'll let you know what
he really thinks. "],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: speak (one's) piece

name: say one's piece / speak one's piece
meanings:
[{"name":"to say what one must say; to express one's opinions or ideas; to say openly what you think; say, especially in public, what you usually say or are expected to say","examples":["Look, just say your piece and get out of here. ","I said my piece and left.","You will all be given a chance to say your piece at the meeting tonight."," I've always been honest with you about how I feel
and what I think. I've never been shy about speaking
my piece.","Bob: Speak your piece.
Kate: Sir, I just cannot accept people talking about Jane that way."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: speak (one's) mind
The expression speak one's piece is usually used to describe
what someone does when he disagrees strongly with someone
else but has little control over the situation. The speaker wants
the person to know his feelings and may present them in an
uninterrupted monologue (piece).

name: spring on
meanings:
[{"name":"to surprise (someone) with (something, such as a request or announcement)","examples":["You have to prepare Mark for surprises or bad news
that he's not expecting. Don't spring anything on
him.","Grace thought she had done well on the test, so it
came as a shock when she discovered that she'd
failed. The teacher sprang it on her very suddenly.","I hate to spring this on you at the last moment, but I will need some money to travel on.","Please don't spring any other demands on me. ","I know I sprung this on you at the last minute.","I didn't want to spring on you like this."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: knock/throw (someone) for a loop
The expression is usually used to describe surprising someone
with some unexpected news.

name: square deal
meanings:
[{"name":"an honest and fair transaction or trade; a fair agreement, fair treatment, or a fair price","examples":[" We bought our car from the dealership in town, and
they gave us a good car at a fair price. It was a square
deal.","The management of this company are always out
to get what they can from the workers without fair
treatment or compensation. They have never given
anyone a square deal.","All the workers want is a square deal, but their boss underpays them.","You always get a square deal with that travel company."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: fair and square
In this expression, square means right.

name: square meal
meanings:
[{"name":"a full or complete meal; a good and nutritious meal","examples":["That man is so thin and gaunt. He looks like he
hasn't had a square meal in weeks.","The children's doctor recommends that they eat
three square meals a day. Each meal should include a
vegetable or fruit, milk or cheese, meat or some form
of protein, and rice or bread.","I need three squares a day—at least."],"media":[]}]
origin: (Always with quantifier when square is used without meal.)

name: stand/hold one's ground
meanings: [{"name":"to stand up for one's rights; to resist an attack; to refuse to change your opinion or give in to an argument","examples":["The lawyer tried to confuse me when I was giving testimony, but I managed to stand my ground.","Some people were trying to crowd us out of the line for tickets, but we held our ground.","I kept trying to get my grandmother to find a smaller house, but she stood her ground.","Clare stood her ground in the meeting and refused to be intimidated even when Michael got angry.","When the goose was threatened by the approaching\nfox, she stood her ground and hissed and pecked at\nhim. She would protect her baby goslings at all costs."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonyms: give in; knuckle under
Compare to: stick to (one's) guns
Stick to one's guns more narrowly means to be firm in one's
resolve, and could be used in sentence 1 but not in sentence 2.
The expression stand one's ground suggests having one's feet
firmly planted on the ground and not giving up any ground to
one's adversary. It is often used to describe the behavior of a
wild animal that is being threatened by its enemy.

name: stand on one's own two feet
meanings: [{"name":"to be independent and self-supporting; to support oneself without help from other people","examples":["Ever since college, Jim has stood on his own two feet.","They told their twenty-year-old son that it was time\nhe found a job and began to support himself. It was\ntime for him to stand on his own two feet.","You can't live with your parents forever. It's time to get a place of your own and learn to stand on your own two feet.","She'll have to get a job and learn to stand on her own two feet sooner or later."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that when a person uses his own two
feet, he is not relying on others for support. The expression
always calls for two feet even when the subject is plural
(sentence 2) and four feet would be more logical.

name: stand out from something
meanings:
[{"name":"to be much better than other similar things or people; to be prominent when compared to someone or something","examples":["Dianne has her own style and rarely follows current
fashion. If you saw her on the street, she would stand
out from the crowd.","Paul does what everyone else does and goes along
with what other people think and say. He doesn't like
to stand out from the crowd.","We had lots of good applicants for the job, but one stood out from the rest.","
As a programmer, she stands out from all the others.","The high quality of these tools makes them stand out from the crowd."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: stick out like a sore thumb
Whereas stand out from the crowd is usually a positive attribute,
stick out like a sore thumb is a negative one. The expression
stand out from the crowd suggests a degree of distinctiveness and
independence.

name: step on it
meanings:
[{"name":"to hurry up; to make a vehicle go faster","examples":["Mother was late for a doctor's appointment and the
children were slow getting into the car. “Step on it!”
she snapped. “We're late.”","As the ambulance left for the hospital with my sick
father in the back, I asked the ambulance driver to
step on it. I wanted him to waste no time getting to
the hospital.","You'd better step on it or we'll be late.","Step on the gas. We are going to be late! ","Step on it! Let's go!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: shake a leg; get a move on
Antonyms: hold (one's) horses; keep (one's) shirt on
The expression is often used when the speaker is annoyed or
short-tempered, and probably stems from
the idea of pressing down hard on the gas pedal to make a
car go faster.

name: stew in one's own juice/juices
meanings:
[{"name":"to suffer the consequences of one's own actions; to be left alone to suffer one's anger or disappointment","examples":["The boss is annoyed that we haven't finished this
report yet, but he really didn't give us enough time
to do it. He's in the office pacing the floor, but I'm
not going to work any faster. Let him stew in his own
juices for a while.","John has such a terrible temper. When he got mad at us, we just let him go away and stew in his own juice.","After John stewed in his own juice for a while, he decided to come back and apologize to us."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression suggests that one is “cooked” (stewed) in one's
own unpleasant but self-made situation.

name: stick/poke/put one's nose in(to something)
meanings:
[{"name":"to try to find out about someone else's private business; to interfere with something; to be nosy about something","examples":["I wish he'd stop sticking his nose into my personal life!","She was too upset for me to stick my nose in and ask what was wrong.","You're always sticking your nose into my business."," Don't stick your nose in where it's not wanted. This
matter is between Pat and me, and it has nothing to
do with you.","I mind my own business, and don't get involved in
other people's personal affairs. I don't stick my nose
in where it doesn't belong."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Antonym: mind (one's) own business
The expression stick one's nose in has a negative connotation.

name: stick out like a sore thumb / stand out like a sore thumb
meanings:
[{"name":"not to blend in; to be very noticeable in usually a bad way; to be obvious and prominent or easily seen","examples":["Everyone else was in jeans and T-shirts and I had my office clothes on - I stuck out like a sore thumb.","John said he planned to wear shorts and a sweatshirt
to the wedding, but I told him it would be completely
inappropriate. I told him he would stick out like a
sore thumb and everyone would notice him.","The paintings of the modern artists stuck out like a
sore thumb in the classical art museum. They just
didn't belong there, grouped together with the old
masters.","That pimple really sticks out like a sore thumb.","Do you think I would stick out like a sore thumb at the party if I wear this coat?"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: stand out from the crowd
Whereas stand out in a crowd is usually a positive attribute,
stick out like a sore thumb is a negative one. It is used to
describe someone (or, less frequently, something) in a
situation where one ought to blend in but doesn't.

name: stonewall
meanings:
[{"name":"to prevent someone from discovering information by not being helpful or by refusing to answer questions","examples":["The newspaper reporter asked the president whether
he intended to seek reelection. The president did
not want to reveal his decision, so he stonewalled by
talking around it.","The interviewer accused the minister of stonewalling on the issue of tax increases.","They're trying to stonewall the media.","We're trying to get the information, but we're being stonewalled."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: beat around the bush; hem and haw
Hem and haw describes being at a loss for words, making only
meaningless sounds, whereas stonewall means talking but
saying little of substance. The expression is usually used to
describe people that want to avoid taking responsibility or
answering a direct question.

name: strange bedfellows
meanings:
[{"name":"an unlikely alliance of people or things; people or things that one does not normally expect to find together","examples":["I never thought I'd see two politicians from opposite
ends of the political spectrum working together
to pass the same law. They certainly are strange
bedfellows.","John and Charlie rarely have the same opinion about
anything, so it was surprising to find them agreeing
on such a controversial issue. Aren't they strange
bedfellows?","The priest and the politician made strange/odd/unlikely bedfellows in their campaign for peace.","Politics indeed makes strange bedfellows."],"media":[]}]

name: strapped for cash/money
meanings:
[{"name":"not having quite enough money","examples":["I am really strapped for cash. Can you lend me some? ","Ted is strapped G for money and cannot pay his bills.","I'd love to have dinner with you, but I'm strapped for
cash and can't afford a restaurant. Maybe we can eat
at home.","Martha got tired of being strapped for cash, so she
made a budget and didn't use more money than she
could afford."],"media":[]}]

name: street smarts
meanings:
[{"name":"the ability to manage or succeed in difficult or dangerous situations, especially in big towns or cities","examples":["You don't have the street smarts to last ten minutes in New York without getting ripped off.","Jim and George drifted from city to city, living off the
streets and stealing. They managed to avoid getting
caught by the police because of their street smarts.","Ms. Howard is a good businesswoman. Although
she studied at Harvard Business School, she's also
picked up some street smarts and can play hardball
when she has to."],"media":[]}]

name: stretch the truth/point
meanings:
[{"name":"to exaggerate; to say something that is not completely honest in order to make someone or something seem better than it really is","examples":["Sally tends to stretch the point when telling tales about her wild teenage years.","Sometimes when people apply for a job, they stretch
the truth about what they did in their previous jobs
in order to make themselves seem more important or
more desirable.","When people asked Peter if he was a manager, he
stretched the truth by telling them that he managed
the office where he worked. What he didn't tell them
was that he was the only person in his office and he
only managed himself."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Compare to: white lie
The expression suggests that one can distort or bend the truth,
so that others are misled, without actually telling a lie.

name: strike it rich
meanings:
[{"name":"to become rich or successful suddenly or unexpectedly; ","examples":["Calvin was very talented when it came to business
and finance, and it was only natural that he would
strike it rich when he invested in the stock market on
Wall Street.","Carol was just trying to get a photograph of the actor,
but she struck it rich when he asked her if she wanted
an exclusive interview, too.","If I could strike it rich, I wouldn't have to work anymore.","Sally ordered a dozen oysters and found a huge pearl in one of them. She struck it rich!"],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: hit pay dirt, hit the jackpot
The expression originated with the idea of miners discovering
precious minerals, but it is also used as a metaphor to describe
finding anything of value.

name: string along someone
meanings: [{"name":"deceive someone for a long time; maintain someone's attention or interest, probably insincerely","examples":["The crook strung the old lady along with the story\nthat he was investing her money in something safe,\nwhen in fact he was stealing from her.","You are just stringing me along because you like to borrow my car. You are not a real friend.","She's been promising to pay back the money for six months, but I think she's just stringing me along.","Were you just stringing me along earlier?"],"media":[]},{"name":"keep waiting","examples":["I strung him along until the boss was back from lunch."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Origin",["This phrase is thought to evoke the image of a puppeteer controlling a marionette by manipulating its strings, symbolizing the manipulation and deception involved in the phrase."]]]

name: swallow one's pride
meanings:
[{"name":"to forget one's pride and accept something humiliating","examples":["I had to swallow my pride and admit that I was wrong. ","When you're trying to master a new skill, you find yourself swallowing your pride quite often.","My aunt is a stubborn woman. She would rather lose
everything than swallow her pride and take money or
help from us.","There's nothing to be ashamed of in being able to
swallow your pride and admit when you are wrong. In
fact, it's a sign of maturity."],"media":[]}]
origin: Compare to: eat crow; eat humble pie

name: sweat blood/bullets
meanings:
[{"name":"to make a great effort; to work intensely","examples":["We sweated blood to get the work finished on time.","I've been sweating blood over this report.","Gary had to work day and night to keep his large
family in food and clothing. He sweat blood for them.","There's no point in sweating blood for some people.
They'll never be happy no matter how hard you try.","In preparing speeches each sweats blood in his own way."],"media":[]},{"name":"be nervous; to worry intensely; to be very anxious and tense","examples":["I didn't know how the
interview would go and was very nervous. I was sweating bullets.","Bob is such a bad driver. I sweat bullets every time I ride with him.","What a terrible test! I was really sweating blood at the last."],"media":[]}]

name: take potluck
meanings: [{"name":"to accept whatever is available","examples":["I know it's short notice but you're welcome to join us\nfor dinner if you don't mind taking potluck.","There isn't much choice left, but I'm not picky. I'm\nhappy to take potluck.","We had no idea which hotel would be best, so we just took pot luck with the first one on the list.","Mary's welcome to stay for dinner if she doesn't mind taking pot luck (= having whatever is available)."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from the idea of a potluck
dinner, where each guest brings one different food or dish
to contribute to everyone's meal. Nobody knows in advance
exactly what foods will be brought. Potluck dinners and
potluck picnics are popular in the U.S. They are informal
gatherings and easy to organize because no one person has
to provide more than one dish.

name: take someone to the cleaners
meanings:
[{"name":"to take a lot of someone's money; to swindle someone; to steal or cheat someone out of all of his or her money","examples":["The unsuspecting woman agreed to invest all her
money with an unethical investment banker. He took
her to the cleaners, and she was left without a penny
to her name.","I made the mistake of giving my dishonest nephew
a blank check from my bank account. Instead of
writing it for the amount we had agreed on, he wrote
it for every cent I had. He took me to the cleaners.","Paul was really taken to the cleaner's on that deal.","Many of us have heard the expression, "She took me to the cleaners." This is certainly a popular belief among [divorced] males."],"media":[]},{"name":"to defeat or best someone; to defeat someone by a very large amount","examples":["In the second half, United were really taken to the cleaner's, and they finally lost the match 6–1.","We took the other team to the cleaners."],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: clean (someone) out

name: take something in stride
meanings:
[{"name":"to accept and adjust to bad fortune or trouble; to deal with (something difficult or upsetting) in a calm way; to accept advances or setbacks as the normal course of events","examples":["When I told them the bad news, I expected them to
be upset, but they took it in stride. It didn't seem to
bother them at all.","Rebecca isn't bothered by unexpected surprises. She
always takes things in stride.","She faced a serious problem, but she was able to take it in her stride.","We were afraid that success would spoil her, but she just took it in stride."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: roll with the punches
Similar to: like water off a duck's back
The expression take something in stride suggests that when one
is confronted by something unexpected, it does not interrupt
one's stride (i.e., the way one walks).

name: take someone or something by storm
meanings: [{"name":"to overwhelm someone or something, often by becoming famous quickly or by spreading very rapidly","examples":["The new fashion has taken London by storm.","The Beatles were rock musicians who took the world\nby storm in the 1960s.","Fear of the disease spread across the country very\nquickly. Panic took the nation by storm."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to conquer someone or something in a fury; to attack and capture (a place) suddenly by using a lot of force or a large number of people","examples":["The soldiers took the castle by storm.","The army took city after city by storm. ","They crashed in and took the general by storm."],"media":[]}]

name: take the wind out of someone's sails
meanings:
[{"name":"to cause someone to lose confidence or energy; to deflate someone's ego; to ruin or destroy someone's high expectations","examples":["The team's star player was injured and it really took the wind out of their sails.","Mary was so sure that she was going to be offered
that job. Wait until I tell her that the position has
been given to Roger instead. That'll take the wind out
of her sails","I was hoping to be accepted by that university. When
the rejection letter arrived, it really took the wind out
of my sails.","John was bragging about how much money he earned until he learned that most of us make more. That took the wind out of his sails."],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression probably originates from the sport of racing
sailboats. When one sailboat cuts in front of another, it literally
takes the wind out of the rear boat's sails, causing it to lose
its speed. The expression can be used to describe one's own
disappointment  or it can be used to express a
somewhat wicked delight that someone else has met with
disappointment.

name: talk a blue streak
meanings:
[{"name":"to talk rapidly and without stopping; to talk fast and at length","examples":["Billy didn't talk until he was two, and then he started talking a blue streak.","No one liked sitting at the lunch table with Phil
because he had only one topic of conversation: his
sports car. When it came to his car, Phil could talk a
blue streak.","You can hardly get a word into a conversation with
Wendy, the way she talks a blue streak.","Sheesh! Your friend really talks a blue streak!"],"media":[]}]
origin: Synonym: talk (someone's) ear off; gift of gab

name: talk someone's ear off
meanings:
[{"name":"to bore someone with one's unending talk; to talk to someone for a long time, usually loudly","examples":["He talks my ear off every time I call him.","I try to keep my office door closed so that Jim won't
come in. When he does, he talks my ear off and I can't
get any work done.","Doug tried to signal me to interrupt his one-way
conversation with Rita. It was obvious that she was
talking his ear off and he was too polite to end the
conversation.","My aunt always talks my ear off when she comes to visit.","Stay away from Mr. Jones. He will talk your ear off if he gets a chance."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonym: bend (someone's) ear
Compare to: talk a blue streak
Talk someone's ear off conveys a sense of boredom that may
or may not be present in talk a blue streak.

name: Dutch uncle
meanings: [{"name":"a man who gives frank and direct advice to someone; person who talks to one like a close relative, giving advice that is sound, well-meant, and sometimes stern","examples":["I would not have to lecture you like a Dutch uncle if you were not so extravagant.","He acts more like a Dutch uncle than a husband. He's forever telling her what to do in public.","The boy's father and mother could talk no sense into\nhim, so they asked a teacher at the boy's school to\ntalk to him like a Dutch uncle."],"media":[]}]

name: talk turkey
meanings:
[{"name":"to talk seriously, usually about a business deal; to talk frankly","examples":["I was ready to get serious about making an offer for
the car. I was ready to talk turkey.","They were in agreement on their business deal; now
all they had to do was work out the details. They sat
down to talk turkey."," Okay, Bob, we have business to discuss. Let's talk turkey.","John wanted to talk turkey, but Jane just wanted to joke around."],"media":[]}]
origin: Compare to: get down to business

name: until one is blue in the face / talk until one is blue in the face
meanings: [{"name":"do something for a very long time, with no results; to talk until one is exhausted","examples":["I talked until I was blue in the face, but I couldn't change her mind.","She had to talk until she was blue in the face in order to convince him.","You can tell her to clean her room until you are blue in the face, but she won't do it.","You can argue with the customer service people until you're blue in the face, but they won't give you your money back.","Well, I've apologized till I'm blue in the face, but they're still leaving in the morning.","Of course. I will talk to him. I'll talk to him till I'm blue in the face."],"media":[]}]
origin: If you say or shout something until you are blue in the face, you are wasting your efforts because you will get no result.

name: tall order
meanings:
[{"name":"something that is very difficult to do; something difficult to accomplish","examples":["My boss wants me to finish all of this work by next
Tuesday. It's a tall order—I'm going to have to work
through the weekend.","My aunt is trying to cook dinner for our entire family
without spending too much money. It's a tall order,
but I think she can do it.","That's a tall order. Do you think anyone can do it? Well, it's a tall order, but I'll do it.","That's a tall order to fill."],"media":[]}]

name: tan someone's hide/britches
meanings:
[{"name":"to beat or whip (someone) very badly; to spank a child's bottom as punishment","examples":["Ricky didn't come home on time from his friend's
house. When he got home, his mother tanned his
hide.","That child is disrespectful and uncontrollable. What
he really needs is for one of his parents to tan his
britches.","He threatened to tan my hide if I didn't do what he told me to do.","I'll tan his hide if I catch him.","Billy's mother said she'd tan Billy's hide if he ever did that again. "],"media":[]}]
origin:
The expression originates from the practice of tanning
(preparing) animal hides (skins) for use as clothing or shoes
by hitting them with a tanning instrument. Hide is also a slang
word used to refer to a person's skin. The alternative britches
(pants) refers to the fact that a person gets spanked on his
bottom. The expression is usually used to describe how parents
might punish their children.

name: third-rate
meanings: [{"name":"of poor quality; extremely low in quality or value; worse than second-rate","examples":["I don't want to work for some third-rate company.","Let's get out of this third-rate hotel now. I know we\ncan find a better one if we try.","The company fired Greg when the management\ndecided that his work was third-rate."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Synonyms: second-rate; fourth-rate

origin: The literal meaning of Italian banca was “bench,” but the word was also used for the benchlike counter at which an early money changer transacted business, and later to describe the money changer's shop itself—the bank. When the banking trade spread from Italy to France, and then to England, the Italian word went with it and became our English bank.

origin:
titivate, spruce up, smarten up, or spiff up?

Titivate, spruce, smarten, and spiff all mean "to make a person or thing neater or more attractive." Titivate often refers to making small additions or alterations in attire ("titivate the costume with sequins and other accessories"), but it can also be used figuratively (as in "titivating the script for Broadway"). Spruce up is sometimes used for cosmetic changes or renovations that give the appearance of newness ("spruce up the house with new shutters and fresh paint before trying to sell it"). Smarten up and spiff up both mean to improve in appearance often by making more neat or stylish ("the tailor smartened up the suit with minor alterations"; "he needed some time to spiff himself up for the party"). The origins of titivate are uncertain, but it may have been formed from the English words tidy and renovate.

Follow the path, or you might get lost.","I got lost in the New York subway system."],"media":[]},{"name":"confused, or not able to understand","examples":["His explanation was so complicated, I got lost after the first example."],"media":[]},{"name":"Go away!","examples":["Stop bothering me. Get lost! ","Get lost! I don't need your help."],"media":[]}]

name: get moving
meanings: [{"name":"to hurry; to start moving or going quickly","examples":["Come on, everybody. Get moving! ","The director is coming. You had better get moving.","We need to get moving or we'll miss the show.","You'll need to get moving if you want to reach the station by three."],"media":[]}]

name: getting/going nowhere fast
meanings: [{"name":"not to make progress; to get nowhere; failing to make progress or to produce a desired result","examples":["I can't seem to make any progress. No matter what I do, I'm just getting nowhere fast. ","Come on. Speed up this car. We're getting nowhere fast.","The plan for a new stadium is going nowhere fast.","I kept asking her the same question, but I was getting nowhere fast."],"media":[]}]

name: get someone down
meanings: [{"name":"to depress a person; to make a person very sad","examples":["My dog ran away, and it really got me down.","Oh, that's too bad. Don't let it get you down.","The weather was getting her down.","Mostly what gets him down is the incredibly long hours he works."],"media":[]}]

name: get with the program
meanings: [{"name":"follow the rules; do what you are supposed to do; to become involved and active in a useful and effective way","examples":["Come on, Mark. Get with the program. Do what you are told.","His boss told him that he'd better get with the program if he wants to keep his job.","Now you get with the program, and fast."],"media":[]},{"name":"to accept new ideas and give more attention to what is happening now; to pay attention to what's going on right now; to be alert to what's happening now","examples":["They've been playing the same old music for ten years now - it's time to get with the program.","Get with the program. Our competitors have all started to outsource their call centers to India to save money, while we're still paying a fortune here."],"media":[]}]
origin:
Implies that there is a clearly known method or “program” that is usually followed.
Usually in orders - used to tell someone that they should change their attitude and do what they are supposed to be doing.

name: get up
meanings: [{"name":"to wake up and get out of bed or to tell or help someone to do this","examples":["What time do you usually get up? I get up when I have to.","He always gets up early.","Could you get me up at 6:30 tomorrow?","I get the boys up at 7 a.m.","It's so hard getting the kids up on school days."],"media":[]},{"name":"to stand up after sitting, lying, etc.","examples":["The class got up when the teacher came in.","He got up and walked over to the window.","She got up and turned off the TV.","I can't get up. Give me a hand, will you?"],"media":[]}]

name: get up something / get something up
meanings: [{"name":"organize, plan, and assemble something","examples":["Let's get a team up and enter the tournament.","I think we can get up a team quite easily.","We got up a party for the newcomers.","You're a little early for the party. We're still getting the decorations up."],"media":[]},{"name":"to make your feelings or your determination stronger in order to do something","examples":["He finally got up his courage to climb the rock wall."],"media":[]},{"name":"to manage to climb something","examples":["I was so tired I couldn't get up the stairs.","The entire group was able to get up the side of the mountain."],"media":[]}]

name: get up to something
meanings:
[{"name":"Lit. climb up to something, at a certain height or level","examples":["We finally got up to the top.","How long will it take to get up to the tenth floor? ","Jane: Kate and I should get going. I was hoping to get up to the top of the hill to get a view of the whole city."],"media":[]},{"name":"reach a particular point","examples":["We got up to page 72 last time.","We got up to the halfway point and stopped.","Will I ever get up to the finish line? I'm so tired of running!","Bob: I've got to get up to that camp.
Tom: I can drive you."],"media":[]},{"name":"do something, often something that is secretive, mischievous, or playful","examples":["Jane: What'd you get up to at school today, Kate?
Kate: Um...not much. Betty and I played princesses.","Bob stays with us for the weekend, and we take photos of all the fun stuff we get up to, and then we stick them in the Bob's book.","Bob: You can trust me.
Jane: Well, gonna have to trust you because we have no way of knowing what you're gonna get up to.","The children are always getting up to some trouble or other when left alone.","What have the kids been getting up to all afternoon?","I wonder what he's getting up to these days."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782264849/phrases/ildvosap6up0rdgjtpg9.mp4","publicId":"phrases/ildvosap6up0rdgjtpg9","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782264869/phrases/jpvidnjknrjbcvdtb9cr.mp4","publicId":"phrases/jpvidnjknrjbcvdtb9cr","type":"video"}]}]

name: get well
meanings: [{"name":"to become healthy again","examples":["Ann had a cold for a week, and then she got well.","Hurry up and get well!"],"media":[]}]

name: get wet
meanings: [{"name":"to become moist or soaked with water","examples":["Get out of the rain or you'll get wet.","Don't get wet, or you'll catch a cold."],"media":[]}]

name: get up (from something)
meanings: [{"name":"to go to a standing position from a lower position.","examples":["She got up from the chair and walked to the door.","I don't want to get up from this hammock unless I just have to."],"media":[]}]

name: get up (off (of) something)
meanings: [{"name":"to rise up and get off something. (Of is usually retained before pronouns.) ","examples":["Please get up off the sofa. I have to turn the cushions over.","Get up off of it!","One of her friends helped her to get up off the floor."],"media":[]}]

name: turn someone or something in (to someone or something)
meanings: [{"name":"to submit or refer someone or something to someone or a group, especially in some official capacity","examples":["The good citizen turned his neighbor in for watering his lawn during the wrong hours.","I turned in the report to the treasurer.","The hit-and-run driver turned himself in to the police the day after the accident.","Don't forget to turn in your papers after class.","He learned that the police were looking for him and turned himself in (= made himself available to them)."],"media":[]}]

name: all things considered
meanings: [{"name":"when all the good and bad parts of something are thought of","examples":["It was a pretty good vacation, all things considered.","All things considered, we're pleased with how the project turned out.","Bob: Did the play turn a profit? \nFred: I suppose that we made a nice profit, all things considered.","I think the party was great, all things considered - I mean we didn't have much time to get ready, but it still went well."],"media":[]}]

name: move over
meanings: [{"name":"to move a bit [away from the speaker]; to cause someone or something to move a little way away","examples":["Would you mind moving over one,\nso my friend and I can sit together?","Move over. I need some space.","Please move over. Part of this space is mine."," Move Tom over a little bit. He is taking too much space. ","Would you move your foot over a little?"],"media":[]}]

name: humanly possible
meanings: [{"name":"within the ability of human beings; able to be done by people; capable of being done","examples":["The doctors tried everything humanly possible to save the patient. (= They did everything they could).","Rescuers are doing everything that is humanly possible to find the lost campers.","My father is gonna do everything humanly possible to acquire Bass Industries.","We'll do everything humanly possible to help."],"media":[]}]

name: have it your (own) way
meanings: [{"name":"to do what one wants to do despite the desires, plans, etc., of other people (often disapproving)","examples":["All right. Have it your way. I'm done arguing with you.","Well, have it your own way.","Tom: I would like to do this room in blue. Sue: I prefer yellow. I really do. Tom: Okay, fine. Have it your way.","Jane: Let's get a pie. Apple would be good. Bob: No, if we are going to buy a whole pie, I want a cherry pie, not apple. Jane: Oh, have it your way!"],"media":[]}]
origin: Usually shows irritation on the part of the speaker

name: face time
meanings: [{"name":"time spent in a face-to-face meeting with someone; time you spend at work talking to people directly, not by email, phone, or online","examples":["He hoped to get more face time with the president.","The CEO likes to get as much face time as possible with junior employees.","A new worker needs face time with coworkers and needs to get to know the company network.","If you put in a little more face-to-face time with your clients, you could improve your sales.","Don't you think we owe the big guy a little face time? Fine, fine. we'll go to temple."],"media":[]},{"name":"time spent at one's place of employment especially beyond normal work hours; the extra time someone spends at work, especially so that their managers will notice them and think they work hard","examples":["Some bosses think lots of face time is a sign of loyalty to the company.","My contract is about going to work, doing my work and then going home - there's nothing about staying overtime or having face time.","Here we reward performance, not face time.","That suggests that young workers are embracing the benefits of in-person work: socialization, mentorship and face time with the boss."],"media":[]}]

name: don't make me laugh
meanings: [{"name":"used as a response to a statement that one thinks is very wrong or foolish; used to show that you think what someone has just said is impossible or stupid; That is a stupid suggestion!","examples":["Bill: I could beat you at chess easily. Mary: Don't make me laugh.","You'll pay? Don't make me laugh!","You a judge? Don't make me laugh! ","Bill: I have this plan to make electricity from garbage. Sally: What a dumb idea! You make me laugh! ","Bill: Can you finish this by tomorrow? Jane: Don't make me laugh!"],"media":[]}]

name: You just don't get it!
meanings: [{"name":"You really don't see what people are trying to tell you!; You really don't understand what people are trying to tell you! ","examples":["You just don't get it! People avoid you because you offend them.","Everyone tells you that you are a bore, but you just don't get it!"],"media":[]}]
origin: Also with subjects other than second person.

name: You heard someone
meanings: [{"name":"Don't argue. You heard your instructions from someone","examples":["Andrew: You heard the man. Get moving. Henry: Don't rush me! ","Bill: What makes her think she can tell me what to do? Bob: She's the boss. Do it! You heard her!","Please leave my house. Tina! You heard me. Get out!","Tom: I sold it.  Mary: What? \nTom: You heard me.\nMary: What about my things?  Tom: All gone. I also sold the car."],"media":[]}]
origin: The someone can be a person's name, a title, or a pronoun.

name: you got it
meanings: [{"name":"Here is what you asked for!; You will get what you want!; I agree to what you asked!","examples":["Bill: Would you get me a coffee? Jane: Sure, you got it!","Don: Can I have a cheeseburger and fries? Andrew: You got it!","Hanna: I'd like weekends off and a higher salary. Isabel: You got it!","You want a green one? You got it! ","This one? You got it! "],"media":[]},{"name":"Good, you understand it!; Finally, you understand it!","examples":["Bill: Does that mean I can't have the car tonight? \nFather: You got it!","Bob: The ax has fallen. You're fired! You don't work here any longer! There are no more paychecks coming to you! \nBill: In other words, I'm out of a job. Bob: You got it! "],"media":[]}]

name: the half of it
meanings: [{"name":"used in negative sentences to say that a situation is worse or more complicated than someone thinks","examples":["Mary: It sounds like you've been having some problems. Sally: You don't know the half of it!","Sales are down but that's only the half of it—the company is closing several stores.","Bob: Poor Ian. You don't know the half of it. I mean, to be betrayed by somebody you love that much."],"media":[]}]

name: you could have fooled me
meanings: [{"name":"I would have thought otherwise.; I would have thought the opposite.; used to tell someone that you do not believe what they have just said; used to say that something seems very surprising or doubtful based on one's own observations","examples":["Henry: Did you know that this land is among the most productive in the entire state? Jane: You could have fooled me. It looks quite barren.","John: I really do like Mary. Andrew: Could have fooled me. You treat her rather badly sometimes.","Bill: He's an expert in his field. Mary: Well, you sure could have fooled me!"],"media":[]}]

name: watch your mouth/language/tongue
meanings: [{"name":"to not say rude or inappropriate things; to be careful what you say in order not to offend someone or make them angry","examples":["Watch your language, young lady!","“Watch your mouth!” warned Sue. “I will not listen to any more of this slime!”","Andrew: Don't talk to me like that! Watch your tongue! Bill: I'll talk to you any way I want.","Hey, don't talk that way! A Watch your mouth!","Watch your tongue, garbage mouth!"],"media":[]}]
origin: Do not talk like that!; Do not say those things!; Do not say those bad words!

name: what's keeping someone
meanings: [{"name":"used to ask why someone is late","examples":["What's keeping them? They should have been here 30 minutes ago.","Bob: Wasn't Mary supposed to be here? Bill: I thought so. Bob: Well, what's keeping her? Bill: How should I know?","Bill: I've been waiting here for an hour for Sally. Sue: What's keeping her?"],"media":[]}]

name: keep someone posted
meanings: [{"name":"to regularly give (someone) the most recent news about something; to make sure someone knows what is happening, esp. in a situation that is quickly changing","examples":["Keep me posted on how the project is coming along.","The doctors kept me posted about her condition.","I'll keep you posted on his progress."],"media":[]}]

name: what's on tap for today?
meanings: [{"name":"What is on the schedule for today?; What is going to happen today?","examples":["Tom: Good morning, Fred. Fred: Morning. What's on tap for today? Tom: Trouble in the morning and difficulty in the afternoon. Fred: So nothing's new.","Sally: Can we have lunch today? Sue: I'll have to look at my schedule and see what's on tap for today."],"media":[]}]

name: What's the damage?
meanings: [{"name":"What are the charges?; How much is the bill?; the amount of money that something costs","examples":["\"What's the damage?\" he asked, pulling out his wallet.","Bill: That was delicious. Waiter, what's the damage? Waiter: I'll get your check, sir. ","Waiter: Your check, sir. Tom: Thanks. Bill: What's the damage, Tom? Let me pay my share. Tom: Nonsense, I'll get it. Bill: Okay this time, but I owe you one."],"media":[]}]

name: the scoop
meanings: [{"name":"the latest information about something; the most recent information or details; information about something that is currently important or happening or that is interesting to many people","examples":["Did you talk to him? What's the scoop?","She always knows the scoop on fashions.","Here's the scoop on how to clean leather.","I was with them when it happened, so I've got the inside scoop.","What's the scoop on the new boss?","Bob: Did you hear about Tom? Mary: No, what's the scoop? "],"media":[]}]

name: good and ...
meanings: [{"name":"very; completely","examples":["She was good and mad.","She doesn't need to come back to work till she's good and ready.","Drink your coffee while it's good and hot.","She won't drink coffee if it's not good and hot.","I'll be there when I'm good and ready.","Ann will finish the job when she's good and ready and not a minute sooner."],"media":[]}]

name: Who do you think you're talking to?
meanings: [{"name":"You can't talk to me that way! ; Do you know the importance of the person who you are talking to? ","examples":["Tom: Get out of the way! Sue: Who do you think you're talking to? Tom: Then move please","Clerk: Look, take it or leave it. Isn't it good enough for you? Sue: Who do you think you're talking to? I want to see the manager!","Who do you think you're talking to? I'm the boss here, you know?","Don't talk to me that way! Who do you think you are talking to?","Who do you think you're talking to? You wicked, ungrateful girl!"],"media":[]}]

name: who would have thought?
meanings: [{"name":"used to say that something is very surprising; a question phrase indicating surprise or amazement; I would never have guessed that something so surprising could happen. (No answer is expected.)","examples":["She's written two novels since graduating? Who'd have thought?","A: The boss's secretary turns out to be an escaped convict who is wanted in three states. B: Wow! Who would have thought?","Tom: Fred just quit his job and went to Africa. Bill: Who would have thought he could do such a thing? ","Andy: They say Bill is training for the Olympics in his spare time. Rachel: Who would have thought?","Who would have thought she'd end up dancing for a living?"],"media":[]}]

name: without further ado
meanings: [{"name":"with no more delay; right away; without waiting any longer","examples":["And now, without further ado, here is our special guest speaker.","Without further ado, I'd like to introduce our speaker.","And without further ado, I would like to introduce Mr. Bill Franklin!","The time has come to leave, so without further ado, good evening and good-bye."],"media":[]}]

name: (Would you) care to join us?
meanings: [{"name":"Do you want to join us?","examples":["Tom and Mary saw Fred and Sally sitting at another table in the restaurant. Tom went over to them and said, “Would you care to join us?”","Mary: Isn't that Bill and Sue over there? John: Yes, it is. Shall I ask them to join us? Mary: Why not? John (after reaching the other table): Hi, you guys! Care to join us? Bill: Love to, but Sue's mom is going to be along any minute. Thanks anyway."],"media":[]}]

name: take a potshot at someone or something
meanings: [{"name":"to criticize someone or something without careful thought; to criticize or censure someone or something, often just to be mean","examples":["Why are you taking potshots at me? What did I do to you?","Everyone in the audience was taking potshots at the comedian's toupee.","Her opponent has taken potshots at her for not being tough enough.","Daily, the media took potshots at the foolish politician.","John is taking potshots at me in his condemnation of office workers."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to shoot at someone or something, as with a shotgun.","examples":["The hunters were taking potshots at each other in the woods.","Someone has been taking potshots at my mailbox!"],"media":[]}]
origin: A potshot refers to the type of shooting done to provide meat for the cooking pot.

name: take a toll / take its toll
meanings: [{"name":"to cause harm or suffering or damage; to have a serious, bad effect on someone or something","examples":["Too much sunlight can take a (heavy) toll on your skin.","Her illness has taken a toll on her marriage.","If you keep working so hard, the stress will eventually take its toll.","Years of sunbathing took a toll on Mary's skin."],"media":[]}]

name: take someone's word for it
meanings: [{"name":"to believe that what someone says is true; to believe what someone says about something without seeking further information or proof","examples":["He said he'd give me a job and I just took him at his word.","If he says there's $500 in the envelope, then I'll take his word for it.","Rachel: No one can cook better than Fred. Take my word for it. Bill: Really? Fred: Oh, yes. It's true.","It's true! Take my word for it.","I can't prove it. You will have to take my word on it."],"media":[]}]
origin: Also: take someone at their word; take someone's word on something

name: take (someone or something) by surprise
meanings: [{"name":"to happen to (someone or something) unexpectedly; to surprise (someone or something)","examples":["Her reaction took me by surprise.","The organization was taken completely by surprise by the announcement.","Filmgoers were taken by surprise when the screening was interrupted by the police."],"media":[]},{"name":"to attack, capture, or approach (someone or something) without warning","examples":["The troops gained an upper hand in the battle by taking their foes by surprise.","Oh! You took me by surprise. I didn't hear you come in. ","Bill took his mother by surprise by coming to the door and pretending to be a solicitor."],"media":[]}]

name: take someone's side
meanings: [{"name":"to support someone in an argument; to agree with or support one person or group and not another","examples":["When my sister and I fight, our dad always takes her side.","You never take my side.","They always took the side of the underdog.","Why do you always take Tom's side?"],"media":[]}]

name: take sides
meanings: [{"name":"to choose one side of an argument; to support one person or group rather than another, in an argument or war","examples":["They were arguing, but I didn't want to take sides, so I left.","Whoa! You can't take sides. Police officers aren't allowed to take sides.","She refuses to take sides on the issue.","All of her friends had taken sides against Dylan.","Listen, I'm not going to take sides. You both have made good points.","Don't force me to take sides between my two children."],"media":[]}]

name: that makes two of us
meanings: [{"name":"The same is true for me; used to say that one has the same thoughts or feelings as someone else","examples":["Bob: I'm hungry.  Mary: That makes two of us.\n","So you're going to the football game? That makes two of us.","Bill: I just passed my biology test. Bob: That makes two of us!","Bill: I have no idea what's going on. Bob: That makes two of us!","A: I think she is being overly harsh with us. B: That makes two of us."],"media":[]}]

name: (that's) easy for you to say
meanings: [{"name":"You can say that easily because it really does not affect you the way it affects others","examples":["Waiter: Here's your check. Mary: Thanks. (turning to others) I'm willing to just split the check evenly. Bob: That's easy for you to say. You had lobster!","Sally: Let's each chip in ten bucks and buy him a sweater. Sue: That's easy for you to say. You make twice what I do.","Mary: Forget about the money. Jane: That's easy for you to say, you still have your trusts. Mine was liquidated years ago."],"media":[]}]

name: news to me
meanings: [{"name":"something one is hearing for the first time; to be very surprising to someone; I did not know that.; I had not been informed of that","examples":["Mary: The concert has been canceled. Jane: Well, that's news to me.","She's expecting a baby? That's news to me.","Bill: They've blocked off Maple Street for some repairs. Tom: That's news to me."],"media":[]}]

name: That's what I say
meanings: [{"name":"I agree with what was just said","examples":["Tom: We've got to get in there and stand up for our rights! Mary: That's what I say.","Bob: They shouldn't do that! They should be put in jail! Mary: That's what I say!"],"media":[]}]

name: that is / that is to say
meanings: [{"name":"in other words; or more exactly; said when you want to give further details or be more exact about something","examples":["Our friends, that is to say our son's friends, will meet us at the airport.","I'll meet you in the city, that is, I will if the trains are running."],"media":[]}]

name: no rest for the wicked
meanings: [{"name":"said when you must continue with your work or other activity although you are very tired; It's because you are wicked that you have to work hard. (Usually jocular)","examples":["Come on. Get up and go back to work. There's no rest for the wicked.","No rest for the wicked. I'm gonna have to leave these here for the day."],"media":[]}]

name: say hello to someone (for me)
meanings: [{"name":"please convey my good wishes to someone","examples":["Andy: Good-bye, Tom. Say hello to your brother for me. Tom: Sure. Bye, Andy.","Sally: Well, good-bye. Mary: Bye. Sally: And say hello to Jane. Mary: Sure. Bye-bye."],"media":[]}]
origin: Also: Give my best to someone, All the best to someone

name: in the neighborhood
meanings: [{"name":"in the area that is close to something","examples":["Is there a grocery store in the neighborhood?","We might as well pay them a visit while we're in the neighborhood."],"media":[]}]

name: in the neighborhood of
meanings: [{"name":"close to (a place)","examples":["An earthquake was reported somewhere in the neighborhood of Los Angeles.","She traveled to a place somewhere in the neighborhood of Helsinki."],"media":[]},{"name":"approximately; about; close to or around (an amount); approximately a particular amount or measurement","examples":["We're hoping to get somewhere in the neighborhood of $150,000 for our house.","The album sold in the neighborhood of 1,000 copies.","A house like this costs somewhere in the neighborhood of $200,000.","My rent is in the neighborhood of $700 per month."],"media":[]}]

name: be/sound like a broken record
meanings: [{"name":"to say the same thing many times; to say the same thing over and over again","examples":["You're such a broken record. We're tired of hearing it!","He'd walk around the house repeating his favourite sayings like a broken record.","He's always complaining about the way she treats him. He sounds like a broken record!","I hate to sound like a broken record, but we just don't have enough people on the payroll to work efficiently."],"media":[]}]
origin: From an earlier age when a crack in a 78 rpm record would cause the needle, or stylus, to stay in the same groove and play it over and over.

name: speak ill of someone
meanings: [{"name":"to say unkind things about someone; to say something bad about someone","examples":["I refuse to speak ill of any of my friends.","I don't like speaking ill of my colleagues, but there are a lot of incompetent people working here.","I realize one shouldn't speak ill of the dead.","I never heard her speak ill of anyone.","He was the only person Alice ever spoke ill of, insisting he was a liar and a thief."],"media":[]}]

name: step aside (for someone)
meanings: [{"name":"Lit. to move out of someone's way; move out of the way so there is a pathway.","examples":["“Step aside. Let the mayor through, please,” called out the mayor's bodyguard. ","Step aside, please - this lady needs a doctor.","Would you step aside for my uncle and his walker?","We had to step aside for the people in wheelchairs to get by."],"media":[]},{"name":"Fig. to retire from an office so someone else can take over; step down; ","examples":["The president retired and stepped aside for someone else. ","Walter stepped aside for a younger person to take over."],"media":[]}]

name: suit oneself
meanings: [{"name":"to do something one's own way; to do something to please oneself; an expression used either humorously or angrily to mean \"do what you want to do\"","examples":["Mary: I don't think I'll come to the party tonight. Jane: All right, suit yourself!","If he doesn't want to do it my way, he can suit himself.","Bob: I don't want to go. Bill: Suit yourself. We'll go without you.","Mary: I think I want the red one. Tom: Suit yourself. ","John (reading the menu): The steak sounds good, but I'm helpless in the face of fried chicken. \nSally: Suit yourself. I'll have the steak."],"media":[]}]

name: in the face of something
meanings: [{"name":"face-to-face with; despite; being threatened with something","examples":["In the face of several lawsuits, the company took the product off the market.","She left home in the face of strong opposition from her parents.","She was fearless in the face of danger.","She found herself helpless in the face of a powerful man.","In the face of such evidence, police have no choice, but to drop the charges against Mike.","No need to apologize. You have behaved with the utmost dignity in the face of unthinkable rudeness. Thank you."],"media":[]}]

name: rise and shine
meanings: [{"name":"used to tell someone to wake up and get out of bed; Get out of bed and be lively and energetic! (Often a command.) ","examples":["Come on, kids! Rise and shine! We're going to the beach.","Father: Come on and get up, Andy. Rise and Shine! You've got to be at school by 7:30! Andy: Dad, today is Saturday! ","Hey, Blanche. The alarm just went off. Rise and shine! Go make some coffee and call me when it's ready.","Father always calls “Rise and shine!” in the morning when we want to go on sleeping."],"media":[]}]

name: put (someone or something) to the test
meanings: [{"name":"to test how good someone or something is, esp. in difficult conditions; to cause (someone or something) to be in a situation that shows how strong, good, etc., that person or thing really is","examples":["Her constant questions put the teacher's patience to the test.","Tomorrow's game will really put the team to the test.","I think I can jump that far, but no one has ever put me to the test.","Those icy roads certainly put my driving to the test.","I'm going to put my car to the test right now, and see how fast it will go."],"media":[]}]

name: on the contrary
meanings: [{"name":"just the opposite; actually the opposite is true;","examples":["Experts predicted the economy would collapse, but, to the contrary, it continues to do extremely well.","Tom: It's rather warm today. Bob: On the contrary, I find it too cool.","Mary: I hear that you aren't too happy about my decision. Sue: On the contrary, I find it fair and reasonable.","\"I thought you said the film was exciting?\" \"On the contrary, I nearly fell asleep half way through it!\"","I'm not angry with you. On the contrary!"],"media":[]}]
origin: Also: to the contrary

name: on the other hand

name: punch up
meanings: [{"name":" to register a figure on a cash register or calculator","examples":[" Jake punched the total up, and the register drawer opened.","He punched up the total too carelessly."],"media":[]},{"name":"to give energy or forcefulness to; to make something more interesting by adding something","examples":["Jokes added to punch up a speech.","He needs some writers to punch up his speeches.","I like to punch my fruit salad up a little, adding pomegranate seeds and lemon juice."],"media":[]}]

name: push away
meanings: [{"name":"to move or force someone or something away from someone or something","examples":["The police pushed the P crowd away from the movie star.","They pushed away the hecklers from the stage.","You pushed me away. name: push against
meanings: [{"name":"to press something against someone or something","examples":["I pushed the chair up against the door to prevent the robber from getting in","Accidentally, I pushed the door against Donna and hurt her sore elbow."],"media":[]},{"name":"to put pressure on someone or something","examples":["The small dog pushed up against me, wagging its tail. ","Push up against the ceiling tile while I try to tack it back in place."],"media":[]}]

name: push down
meanings: [{"name":"to press down on something, such as a button, stamp, lever, etc; to force someone or something downward.","examples":["Push down on this button if you want room service."," Don't push down on the door handle too hard. meanings: [{"name":"to request or demand something; to demand something repeatedly, or to take strong action to try to make it happen","examples":["Business leaders are pushing for a change in tax laws.","Local residents are pushing for the road to be made safer.","My secretary is pushing for a raise.","The citizens are pushing for an investigation of the police department."],"media":[]}]

name: push forward
meanings: [{"name":"to move forward; to move onward toward a goal","examples":["We have lots to do. We must push forward!","They are pushing forward, hoping to complete the project on time."],"media":[]},{"name":"to shove or move someone or something to the front","examples":["Mary's mother pushed her forward where she would be seen","Let me push the piano bench forward for you."],"media":[]}]

name: push into
meanings: [{"name":"to force someone into a situation; to force someone to do something","examples":["They are trying to push me into signing the contract.","Please don't push me into it! name: push off
meanings: [{"name":"to leave; set out","examples":["We pushed off for home.","I'd better be pushing off now – I've got work to do.","Let's push off while it's still early enough to beat the evening rush."],"media":[]},{"name":"to apply pressure to and force someone or something off someone or something","examples":["He continued to come at me, but I managed to push him off me and escape.","I pushed off the attacker.","Bob pushed me off the swing."],"media":[]},{"name":"to place one's task onto another person; to make someone else do an unwanted job","examples":["Don't push the dirty work off onto me.","Kelly pushed some of her workload off on me."],"media":[]}]

name: push on
meanings: [{"name":"to put pressure on someone or something","examples":["Don't push on me! I can't move any faster than the person in front of me!","Push on this button if you want the steward to come.","Push on the door a little. name: push out
meanings: [{"name":"to spread out; to expand outward","examples":["The sides of the box pushed out, and I was afraid it would break.","His little tummy pushed out when he was full."],"media":[]},{"name":"to force someone or something out of something","examples":["Nick pushed the intruder out of the house.","Tony pushed out the intruder."],"media":[]}]

name: push over
meanings: [{"name":"to cause someone or something to move over something","examples":["The convict pushed his buddy over the wall and followed after him.","He climbed up to the top of the fence and I pushed him over."],"media":[]},{"name":"to make someone or something fall over or fall down","examples":["When you ran into me, you nearly pushed me over.","You nearly pushed over your friend."],"media":[]}]

name: pushover
meanings: [{"name":"something easy to do or win, or someone who is easily persuaded, influenced, or defeated; someone unable to resist an attraction or appeal","examples":["The exam was a pushover.","Dad's a pushover. name: push through
meanings: [{"name":"to force something to penetrate something","examples":["Tony pushed the needle through the cloth, and drew the thread tight.","He pushed the needle through just like a tailor."],"media":[]},{"name":"to work through or force one's way through something","examples":["I pushed through the snow, trying to get to the post office on time.","The snow was very deep, but I pushed through."],"media":[]},{"name":"to make a plan or suggestion be officially accepted or put into use; to force passage of a motion or law","examples":["The committee chairman managed to push the bill through the committee.","With a little lobbying, they pushed it through.","We are trying to push this deal through as quickly as possible.","The president is trying to push through various tax reforms."],"media":[]}]

name: put a cap on
meanings: [{"name":"to put a limit on something","examples":["We need to put a cap on spending in every department.","The city put a cap on the amount each landlord could charge."],"media":[]}]

name: put a hold on
meanings: [{"name":"to place restriction on something so that it is reserved, delayed, or inactivated; to order that something is to be kept for a particular person or time","examples":["The bank put a hold on my credit card until I paid my bill.","The committee agreed to put a hold on the troublesome piece of business.","I asked the library to put a hold on the book for me."],"media":[]}]

name: put a lid on
meanings: [{"name":"to stop (something) from growing or becoming worse","examples":["These changes are intended to put a lid on rising medical costs.","We've got to keep a lid on our credit-card purchases"],"media":[]},{"name":"to stop doing or saying (something)","examples":["He angrily told them to put a lid on their complaints.","I'm tired of listening to your complaints, so just put a lid on it!"],"media":[]}]

name: put a price on
meanings: [{"name":"to ask for a particular amount of money for (something one is selling); to say how much something costs, or is worth","examples":["The owners have not yet put a price on the house.","The latest development makes it difficult to put a price on other bonds and loans."],"media":[]},{"name":"to say how important or valuable something is — usually used in negative statements to say that something is extremely important and valuable","examples":["Staff loyalty is something that you can't really put a price on.","When she smiles at me, you can't put a price on it.","You can't put a price tag on beauty.","Could you really put a price on your kids' safety?"],"media":[]}]

name: put a smile on someone's face
meanings: [{"name":"to please someone; to make someone happy","examples":["We are going to give Andy a pretty good raise, and I know that'll put a smile on his face.","The surprise birthday party really put a smile on my dad's face."],"media":[]}]

name: put a stop to / put an end to
meanings: [{"name":"to end (something) ; to bring something to an end; to bring (something) to a state in which no further activity happens","examples":["I want you to put a stop to all this bad behavior.","Please put an end to this conversation.","Negotiations brought a stop to the conflict.","She wanted to put a stop to the rumors.","We need to put a stop to these practices.","They promise to put an end to unfair policies.","The new mayor vowed to put an end to the violence."],"media":[]}]

name: put a strain on
meanings: [{"name":"to burden or overload someone or something","examples":["All this bad economic news puts a strain on everyone's nerves.","The epidemic put a strain on the resources of the hospital.","Look, I know this new job's put a bit of a strain on us."],"media":[]}]

name: put away
meanings: [{"name":"Lit. to return something to its proper storage place; to store things where they are usually stored","examples":["When you are finished with the hammer, please put it away. Don't leave it out.","Put away this mess!","You never put away your toys. Put your toys away now."],"media":[]},{"name":"to eat or drink up; to eat a lot of food","examples":["He put away a whole box of chocolates in one evening.","He put away a whole pie in one sitting.","Are you going to put this last piece of cake away?","Did you put away that whole pizza?"],"media":[]},{"name":"to bury someone","examples":["My uncle died last week. ","The judge put away the whole gang.","After what he did, he deserves to be put away for life."],"media":[]},{"name":"to save money to spend later or for a special purpose","examples":["Parents should start early to put something away for their children - for college, etc."],"media":[]}]

name: put across
meanings: [{"name":"to make something clear to someone; to convince someone of something; to get a plan accepted; to express an idea, opinion, etc. clearly so that people can easily understand it","examples":["Jane put her viewpoint across subtly.","I do expect standards to be met and, if I have to, I can put the point across strongly.","What's the most important thing you try to put across in your book?","I don't know how to put this point across to my class. Can you help?","Can you help me get this across?","I don't think I managed to put myself across very well in my interview."],"media":[]}]
origin: Same as: get something across (to someone)

name: put aside
meanings: [{"name":"to set or place something to the side","examples":["I put the magazine aside and began reading a book.","Put aside your work for a minute and listen to what I have to tell you."],"media":[]},{"name":"to save or keep (something, such as money) to be used at a later time; to hold something in reserve for some purpose","examples":["She's been putting aside some money for a vacation.","Can you put a few minutes aside for a short meeting?","I put aside a little every month for a deposit on a house.","He tries to put some time aside every evening to read to the kids.","You should put a little of the sugar aside for your coffee in the morning.","Please put aside some money for me.  I can put a little aside."],"media":[]},{"name":"to stop worrying or thinking about (something)","examples":["We need to put these problems aside for now and get the work done.","It's time to put aside our differences and start working together. Let's put aside our differences.","Can we put that question aside for now?"],"media":[]}]

name: put among
meanings: [{"name":"to place someone or something in the midst of people or things","examples":["The martial arts instructor put Fred among the strongest students to see what he would do.","The shopkeeper put the green pears among the ripe ones and tried to sell them."],"media":[]}]

name: put before
meanings: [{"name":"to ask (a person or group) to make a decision about (something)","examples":["The problem of downtown parking was put before the mayor/council.","We should put this question before the voters.","We have to put our proposal before the committee."],"media":[]},{"name":"Lit. to put someone or something in front of someone or something, especially in a line","examples":["The teacher put/placed George before Bob, because Bob was a little taller.
