name: sit up and take notice
meanings: [{"name":"suddenly pay attention to something because it is surprising, impressive, important, or unexpected; suddenly give attention to something when you had not done so before","examples":["The losses in the election have made party leaders finally sit up and take notice.","The startup was ignored for years, but their latest innovation made the entire industry sit up and take notice.","She had been a quiet employee until her presentation on cost-saving made the CEO sit up and take notice.","When the small team defeated the champions, everyone sat up and took notice.","The company's profits caused competitors to sit up and take notice."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Origin",["The phrase likely evokes the image of a person (or a dog) physically straightening their posture from a relaxed or lying position to a vertical, alert stance to better see or hear something.","This physical act of \"sitting up\" is universally associated with becoming attentive. ","Over time, it became a fixed idiom meaning to take serious notice of something noteworthy."]]]

name: write up something
meanings: [{"name":"prepare a bill, order, or statement; record something completely on paper or on a computer, often using notes that you have made; prepare a full report, document, etc. to record ideas, discussions, or meetings you had earlier","examples":["We have to write up the lab report for chemistry.","Please write the order up and send me a copy.","As soon as I finish writing up your check, I'll bring you some more coffee.","I need to write up the minutes of the meeting."],"media":[]},{"name":"write an article about something","examples":["The product didn't get a very good write-up in which magazine?","The paper didn't give the show a very good write-up.","I wrote up a local business and sent the story to a magazine, but they didn't buy the story."],"media":[]}]

name: add on something / add (something) on(to) something
meanings: [{"name":"add to an existing thing, often to increase the size; include or build something extra; extend something by providing more (of something). (This use of on with add is colloquial.)","examples":["You added nearly one thousand dollars onto the total.","You added on a thousand dollars to the total!","We had to add on an extra room.","They added on an extra room to their house","The company added on several new employees."],"media":[]}]

name: give off
meanings: [{"name":"release, send out  or produce something, such as a smell, heat, light, sound, or a particular impression/vibe.","examples":["Jasmines give off a wonderful scent.","Halogen lamps give off a lot of bright light.","The fire gives off a lot of heat."],"media":[]},{"name":"convey or create a particular impression/vibe, feeling, or atmosphere","examples":["He gives off an air of confidence.","The room gives off a creepy vibe.","The empty house gave off such a spooky feeling that we decided not to go inside","Despite the chaos, the team leader gave off a sense of calm that reassured everyone."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Origin",["The phrase is built from: give (= produce or provide) and off (= outward, away from the source)","So give off literally means send something outward from oneself or from a source, which naturally led to its modern meanings of emit and project."]]]

name: there's nothing like it
meanings: [{"name":"unusual; extraordinary; the best. If you say there is nothing like it (something), you think it is better than anything else.","examples":["There's nothing like a good cup of coffee.","If you've never tried river rafting, you should. There's nothing like it!"],"media":[]}]

name: go under the knife
meanings: [{"name":"have surgery; undergo surgery; have a medical operation","examples":["She's going under the knife tomorrow.","Bob: You can donate part of your liver for our dad.\nJane: There's no way I'm going under the knife for him."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782386347/phrases/ft9hm6sfwxh4dpxlvizh.mp4","publicId":"phrases/ft9hm6sfwxh4dpxlvizh","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782386357/phrases/wfzsazvnzb3fdtbrhc6m.mp4","publicId":"phrases/wfzsazvnzb3fdtbrhc6m","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",[" It is commonly used in casual conversation and media to describe everything from minor outpatient procedures to major operations (e.g., \"He's going under the knife tomorrow to fix his knee\").","The phrase can be used for both necessary medical surgeries and elective cosmetic surgeries."]],["Origin",["The expression comes from the fact that surgeons traditionally used a surgical knife (scalpel) to perform operations.","Knife refers to the surgeon's cutting instrument.","Under refers to being subjected to or placed beneath the action of the surgeon's knife."]]]

name: get ahead of it

extraDetails: [["Literal idea - Breaking it down",["get ahead = move in front of something","it = the problem, event, trend, or situation"]],["Usage",["The phrase is common in business, workplace, news, and everyday conversations"]],["\"get ahead of oneself\" vs \"get ahead of  it\"",["get ahead of oneself -  act prematurely or overconfidently","get ahead of  it -  is generally positive, suggesting competence and preparedness"]]]

name: be a long way from
meanings: [{"name":"Literally, to be physically far away from a place","examples":["The village is a long way from the nearest hospital.","My school is a long way from my house."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782435654/phrases/sji1wobq4w0hpueggdij.mp4","publicId":"phrases/sji1wobq4w0hpueggdij","type":"video"}]},{"name":"used to indicate that someone or something is very far from achieving a specific state, condition, or goal","examples":["We're still a long way from finishing the project. name: apply yourself / apply oneself to something
meanings: [{"name":"make a serious effort, work diligently, or use your abilities fully, especially when you are capable of doing better but haven't been trying hard enough;  work hard, focus diligently, and put serious effort into a task or study","examples":["You can solve any problem if you apply yourself.","If I had applied myself, I think I could have passed those exams.","People assumed he was simply not applying himself to his studies.","I'm sure the business will thrive if we apply ourselves and work together.","She applied herself to learning Spanish and became fluent within two years.","You have a lot of potential—you just need to apply yourself.","He finally applied himself to the project and completed it ahead of schedule."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782611235/phrases/gbxoqbhhgtsfctawvpbv.mp4","publicId":"phrases/gbxoqbhhgtsfctawvpbv","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782611243/phrases/cmama1bgn4f806kaffl4.mp4","publicId":"phrases/cmama1bgn4f806kaffl4","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["To apply yourself is to dedicate your mental or physical energy to a specific activity with the intention of succeeding or improving."," It implies a shift from casual effort to concentrated work."]],["\"buckle down\" vs \"apply yourself\"",["Buckle down = Start working seriously, often after procrastinating.","Apply yourself = Make a sustained, genuine effort and use your abilities well."]]]

(if it's early morning)"]]]

name: head in / head into
meanings: [{"name":"go toward or enter a place; move or travel towards a specific place with the intention of entering it.","examples":["Let's head into the city before traffic gets worse.","She headed into the office at 9 a.m.","We headed into the restaurant for lunch.","It's getting cold; let's head in. extraDetails: [["Common patterns",["Head into + place: \"head into the office,\" \"head into town\"","Head into + time period: \"head into winter,\" \"head into the weekend\"","Head into + situation/event: \"head into an exam,\" \"head into a meeting\""]],["\"head in\" vs \"go in\"",["\"Go in\" = Neutral and literal. Let's head in.\"","\"I'm going to head in and make dinner.\"","  ","But in directions or commands, go in is usually more natural:","\"The doctor will see you now. Go in.\"","\"Go in through the front door.\""]]]

name: I'm through
meanings: [{"name":"I am done; I'm finished; I'm fed up; I've had enough.","examples":["\"I'm through with my homework.\" → I have finished my homework.","\"I'm through with you.\" → I don't want to continue this relationship or deal with you anymore.","\"I'm through listening to excuses.\" → I've had enough of listening to excuses.","\"Are you through eating?\" → Have you finished eating?","\"I'm through trying to convince him.\" → I've given up trying to convince him."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1782897946/phrases/egkg4vmf3qps2wwoswbg.mp4","publicId":"phrases/egkg4vmf3qps2wwoswbg","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["\"I'm through\" vs \"I'm done\"",["\"I'm done\" is often more neutral and casual.","\"I'm through\" can sound more final, formal, or emotionally charged, especially when expressing frustration."]]]

name: Do you see (someone or something)?
meanings: [{"name":"Can you see someone or something right now?","examples":["Do you see that man over there?","Jane: Do you see him?\nKate: There he is.","Look around. Do you see a sign?","I hear a train. Do you see any train tracks?"],"media":[]},{"name":"Do you understand?; Do you get what I mean?","examples":["Do you see what I'm dealing with?","Do you see what I have to put up with?","If we cut the budget here, we lose quality there. Do you see the problem?"],"media":[]},{"name":"Do you notice or recognize something?","examples":["Do you see the difference between these two pictures?","Do you see what's wrong with this sentence?","Do you see a problem with this plan?","Do you see any errors in the report?"],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["\"Do you see\"  vs \"Have you seen\" ",["\"Do you see\" → is used when asking about immediate visual contact. The speaker expects the listener to look around right now to verify if someone or something is in sight. ","\"Have you seen\" → Did you see someone or something at any time before now (usually recently)?","In everyday conversation, if you're trying to locate someone, \"Have you seen him?\" is much more common.","If you're asking whether the person is currently visible, use \"Do you see him?\""]],["Common expressions",["Do you see him? → Can you see him right now?","Do you see it? → Can you see it? / Do you understand it? (depending on context)","Do you see what I mean? → Do you understand what I'm saying?","Do you see the point? → Do you understand the reason or importance?","Do you see the difference? → Can you recognize how they differ?"]]]

name: in more ways than one
meanings: [{"name":"for multiple reasons; for more than one reason. It's commonly used to suggest there's an additional meaning beyond what was just said.","examples":["The new park was a gift in more ways than one; it provided a place for children to play and increased local property values.","Jane: How was your first day at work?\nKate: It was exhausting in more ways than one. (= Physically tiring and mentally or emotionally draining.)","Winter hit us hard in more ways than one. (Cold weather was difficult. It also caused financial problems, power outages, or emotional stress.)","His visit was timely in more ways than one, offering both financial advice and emotional support."],"media":[]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["The phrase is especially effective when the speaker wants to hint at an additional meaning without explaining it immediately, creating a bit of curiosity."]]]

name: real good
meanings: [{"name":"really good; very good; excellent","examples":["The pizza was real good.","She did a real good job on the presentation.","That movie is real good—you should watch it.","I'm feeling real good today.","That was a real good movie."],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783941429/phrases/rvrfgbswgllp1gm4yaju.mp4","publicId":"phrases/rvrfgbswgllp1gm4yaju","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783941447/phrases/t7argsrpz1kvxgoiwzgz.mp4","publicId":"phrases/t7argsrpz1kvxgoiwzgz","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783941464/phrases/jcthoqklsmv7pkazxo1b.mp4","publicId":"phrases/jcthoqklsmv7pkazxo1b","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["It's common in everyday spoken English, especially in American English","Technically incorrect in formal English because real is an adjective and should not modify another adjective. The standard form is really good (adverb + adjective). "]]]

name: try and
meanings: [{"name":"try to","examples":["I'll try and call you tomorrow. (= I'll try to call you tomorrow.)","Please try and be on time. (= Please try to be on time.)","Let's try and solve this problem together. (= Let's try to solve this problem together.)","I'll try and finish the report today. (= I'll try to finish the report today.)"],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783942201/phrases/oztvr6th9f4gzw9j2tst.mp4","publicId":"phrases/oztvr6th9f4gzw9j2tst","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783942214/phrases/fpcecy1pxwqj77xucn9w.mp4","publicId":"phrases/fpcecy1pxwqj77xucn9w","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1783942229/phrases/gayqx4cvledyuvo0ga3m.mp4","publicId":"phrases/gayqx4cvledyuvo0ga3m","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["It's widely used in casual speech.","It only works when \"try\" is in its base form (present tense or imperative).","If you need to use the past tense, continuous form, or third-person singular, you must switch to \"try to.\""]],["Rule of Thumb",["If you are writing an email, essay, or report, always use \"try to.\"","If you are chatting with friends, \"try and\" is natural and acceptable. "]]]

name: almost never
meanings: [{"name":"hardly ever","examples":["She almost never misses a game.","I know. It almost never works.","You know what? She's almost never right.","Jane: How often does that happen?\nKate: Almost never."],"media":[]}]

name: which is what?
meanings:
[{"name":"What does that mean? or What exactly is that?","examples":["Jane: I want you to do the right thing. Kate: Which is what?
Jane: Give us our chocolate back.","Bob: The issue is with the middleware. Tom: Which is what?
Bob: It's software that connects different applications.","Jane: Pride is what made us and strong, and that all starts with one thing. Kate: Which is what?
Jane: A job.
"],"media":[{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1784099318/phrases/combvrrpzpopzmcjmdvl.mp4","publicId":"phrases/combvrrpzpopzmcjmdvl","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1784099333/phrases/h8b7ev5r7kp6lzeo2hhb.mp4","publicId":"phrases/h8b7ev5r7kp6lzeo2hhb","type":"video"},{"url":"https://res.cloudinary.com/sriniavoz/video/upload/v1784112235/phrases/dgvftyqj8t2ss0jnat1l.mp4","publicId":"phrases/dgvftyqj8t2ss0jnat1l","type":"video"}]}]
extraDetails: [["Usage",["Use \"Which is what?\" when someone has just mentioned a term or concept and you want them to say or explain it."]],["Note - For asking someone to explain an unfamiliar term, native speakers also commonly say:",["\"What's that?\"","\"What do you mean by that?\"","\"What is X?\" (e.g., \"What is middleware?\")","\"Can you explain what that is?\""]]]
